papers_seen.author: Morales
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central Tool for Compression and Adaptation in Deep Learning and NLP: Strengths, Limits, and Practical Extensions
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a core technique for producing compact, efficient models and for enabling cross-model, cross-modal, and privacy-sensitive transfer in deep learning and NLP. KD can be implemented at the logit, feature, and layer levels, and extended to ensemble teachers, data-free scenarios, federated settings, and task-adaptive architecture search. While KD often yields large efficiency gains with small accuracy loss, its effectiveness depends on data properties, teacher–student alignment, and training choices; addressing limitations such as data heterogeneity, low-frequency token degradation, and mismatched inputs requires tailored methods (e.g., feature mimicking, teacher adaptation, multi-teacher weighting, and specialized divergences). Building on empirical and methodological work across modalities, I argue that KD should be treated as a versatile, application-driven toolkit rather than a single recipe, and that future progress will come from combining representational-level distillation, teacher-aware training, and methods that reduce reliance on original training data.

papers_seen.author: Ellis
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Theory, and Applications
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and model compression comprise a diverse set of techniques to produce smaller, faster, or more private models by transferring information from larger or auxiliary models. Research spans supervised teacher-student frameworks, self-distillation, multi-teacher and task-adaptive compression, and distillation combined with pruning, architecture search, adversarial training, and data augmentation. Practical work demonstrates benefits across vision, multimodal, graph, and NLP tasks, while theoretical analyses connect distillation to label smoothing, ensemble behavior, and bias–variance tradeoffs. Open challenges include aligning heterogeneous inputs and modalities, preserving robustness and privacy, and handling low-resource or low-frequency phenomena.

papers_seen.author: Lynch
papers_seen.title: Revisiting Knowledge Distillation via Label Smoothing Regularization
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge Distillation (KD) aims to distill the knowledge of a cumbersome teacher model into a lightweight student model. Its success is generally attributed to the privileged information on similarities among categories provided by the teacher model, and in this sense, only strong teacher models are deployed to teach weaker students in practice. In this work, we challenge this common belief by following experimental observations: 1) beyond the acknowledgment that the teacher can improve the student, the student can also enhance the teacher significantly by reversing the KD procedure; 2) a poorly-trained teacher with much lower accuracy than the student can still improve the latter significantly. To explain these observations, we provide a theoretical analysis of the relationships between KD and label smoothing regularization. We prove that 1) KD is a type of learned label smoothing regularization and 2) label smoothing regularization provides a virtual teacher model for KD. From these results, we argue that the success of KD is not fully due to the similarity information between categories from teachers, but also to the regularization of soft targets, which is equally or even more important.   Based on these analyses, we further propose a novel Teacher-free Knowledge Distillation (Tf-KD) framework, where a student model learns from itself or manuallydesigned regularization distribution. The Tf-KD achieves comparable performance with normal KD from a superior teacher, which is well applied when a stronger teacher model is unavailable. Meanwhile, Tf-KD is generic and can be directly deployed for training deep neural networks. Without any extra computation cost, Tf-KD achieves up to 0.65\% improvement on ImageNet over well-established baseline models, which is superior to label smoothing regularization.

papers_seen.author: Pierce
papers_seen.title: Survey of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP (Selected 2017–2022 Literature)
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model-compression techniques have become central tools for producing compact, efficient models from larger teachers across vision, language, and multimodal tasks. Methods include soft-label distillation, feature- and representation-level matching, adversarial and ensemble-based transfer, data-free or privacy-aware distillation, curriculum and selective-sample strategies, and task-adaptive architecture search. These approaches target deployment constraints (latency, memory, on-device compute), data-availability and privacy limitations, robustness, and domain-continuity, and have been adapted to detectors, generative models, retrieval systems, federated settings, and pre-trained language models. Empirical work demonstrates that careful choice of what to transfer (logits, internal features, relational/contrastive signals) and when/how to train (online, teacher-free, curriculum, few-shot) materially affects student performance and robustness. Open challenges include heterogeneity of data and architectures in distributed settings, theoretical understanding of what aspects of teacher knowledge are most valuable across tasks, and extending distillation to privacy- and domain-constrained deployments.

papers_seen.author: Jones
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and model compression have become central strategies for deploying large deep models under resource, latency, and privacy constraints. A diverse set of methods—ranging from soft-label distillation, intermediate feature and attention matching, layer mapping, adversarial and data-free techniques, to task-adaptive architecture search and meta-learning of teachers—have been proposed to transfer performance from bulky teachers to compact students. These approaches are applied across domains including vision, language, multi-modal systems, recommender systems, and domain-specific NLP, and they trade off fidelity to the teacher, generalization, and computational efficiency. Empirical results show that properly designed distillation pipelines can recover a large fraction of teacher performance while yielding substantial speedups and memory reductions, and in some settings can even improve fairness, robustness, or downstream generalization. Remaining challenges include aligning heterogeneous inputs and representations across teacher and student, coping with absent or private training data, and automatically selecting what and how to transfer for specific tasks and deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Adams
papers_seen.title: Is Label Smoothing Truly Incompatible with Knowledge Distillation: An Empirical Study
papers_seen.abstract: This work aims to empirically clarify a recently discovered perspective that label smoothing is incompatible with knowledge distillation. We begin by introducing the motivation behind on how this incompatibility is raised, i.e., label smoothing erases relative information between teacher logits. We provide a novel connection on how label smoothing affects distributions of semantically similar and dissimilar classes. Then we propose a metric to quantitatively measure the degree of erased information in sample's representation. After that, we study its one-sidedness and imperfection of the incompatibility view through massive analyses, visualizations and comprehensive experiments on Image Classification, Binary Networks, and Neural Machine Translation. Finally, we broadly discuss several circumstances wherein label smoothing will indeed lose its effectiveness. Project page: http://zhiqiangshen.com/projects/LS_and_KD/index.html.

papers_seen.author: Wright
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques have matured into a diverse set of methods for transferring information from larger or more expensive models to smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained models. Methods span from classic logit-based distillation to feature- and representation-level matching, adversarial and projector-based strategies, module-replacement and pruning approaches, and specialized protocols for cross-modal, federated, data-free, and generative settings. Applications range across NLP (BERT compression, machine translation, non-autoregressive models), speech and paralinguistic embeddings, vision (image translation, novel-view synthesis), 3D detection, recommender systems, and graph neural networks. Research highlights include analyses that explain why distillation works, techniques that mitigate transfer of teacher errors, curricula and selection mechanisms for better sample usage, and approaches that adapt distillation to privacy- or resource-constrained environments. Together, these works map an ecosystem of practical techniques and open challenges for deploying compact, high-performing models in real-world systems.

papers_seen.author: Ramirez
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a central technique for compressing large neural models and transferring knowledge across architectures, tasks, and deployment constraints. Work across vision, language, graphs, and generative representations shows diverse KD objectives (soft-target, feature, relational, contrastive, and layer-matching), a range of data regimes (full-data, limited-data, data-free/zero-shot), and many complementary compression mechanisms (pruning, architecture search, block-structured sparsity, and cheap operators). Empirical and theoretical studies clarify when KD helps, how it interacts with data-augmentation and teacher imperfection, and how KD can be adapted for privacy-preserving or federated scenarios. This review summarizes these practical methods, observed trade-offs, and open challenges for robust, efficient, and private model compression.

papers_seen.author: Henderson
papers_seen.title: Graph-less Neural Networks: Teaching Old MLPs New Tricks via Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are popular for graph machine learning and have shown great results on wide node classification tasks. Yet, they are less popular for practical deployments in the industry owing to their scalability challenges incurred by data dependency. Namely, GNN inference depends on neighbor nodes multiple hops away from the target, and fetching them burdens latency-constrained applications. Existing inference acceleration methods like pruning and quantization can speed up GNNs by reducing Multiplication-and-ACcumulation (MAC) operations, but the improvements are limited given the data dependency is not resolved. Conversely, multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) have no graph dependency and infer much faster than GNNs, even though they are less accurate than GNNs for node classification in general. Motivated by these complementary strengths and weaknesses, we bring GNNs and MLPs together via knowledge distillation (KD). Our work shows that the performance of MLPs can be improved by large margins with GNN KD. We call the distilled MLPs Graph-less Neural Networks (GLNNs) as they have no inference graph dependency. We show that GLNNs with competitive accuracy infer faster than GNNs by 146X-273X and faster than other acceleration methods by 14X-27X. Under a production setting involving both transductive and inductive predictions across 7 datasets, GLNN accuracies improve over stand-alone MLPs by 12.36% on average and match GNNs on 6/7 datasets. Comprehensive analysis shows when and why GLNNs can achieve competitive accuracies to GNNs and suggests GLNN as a handy choice for latency-constrained applications.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: The Case for Pragmatic, Task-Aware Knowledge Distillation in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically validated set of techniques for producing smaller, faster models from larger teachers. Across vision, language, multimodal, and distributed settings, distillation can preserve or even improve accuracy while enabling deployments with constrained compute, memory, latency, and privacy requirements. However, its success depends on matching distillation objectives and procedures to task constraints (e.g., robustness, heterogeneity, data availability). When applied thoughtfully—using feature-based objectives, ensemble or adversarial strategies, data augmentation or data-free approaches, and task-adaptive compression—KD reliably delivers practical trade-offs between efficiency and effectiveness.

papers_seen.author: Caldwell
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Effectiveness, Limitations, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a practical and flexible method for compressing large models into smaller, faster, and often more interpretable models across vision, language, speech, and recommendation systems. KD works both as a stand-alone compression technique and as a complementary tool that combines well with pruning, quantization, multi-teacher strategies, and privacy-aware or federated settings. While highly effective in practice, KD has limits—especially around data availability, heterogeneity, and theoretical understanding—that recent work addresses with data-free methods, meta-learning teachers, and principled analyses.

papers_seen.author: Walton
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central Tool for Efficient and Robust Deep Models: Evidence, Techniques, and Recommendations
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has evolved from a simple teacher→student transfer recipe into a broad set of methods that enable model compression, robustness, domain adaptation, privacy-preserving training, and architectural search. Across modalities and tasks—NLP, speech, vision, graphs, ranking and recommender systems—KD-based approaches consistently trade minimal performance loss for large gains in speed, memory, interpretability or deployability. The diversity of KD formulations (feature-based, layer-mapping, data-free, online/mutual, multi-teacher, meta-learned teachers, and task-adaptive compression) provides practitioners with targeted tools to address constraints such as limited data, non-iid federated shards, low-frequency tokens in translation, and privacy requirements. Based on empirical results across the literature, KD should be considered a first-order technique in any pipeline that must deliver high-quality models under resource, privacy, or latency constraints.

papers_seen.author: James
papers_seen.title: Robust Cross-Modal Representation Learning with Progressive Self-Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: The learning objective of vision-language approach of CLIP does not effectively account for the noisy many-to-many correspondences found in web-harvested image captioning datasets, which contributes to its compute and data inefficiency. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel training framework based on cross-modal contrastive learning that uses progressive self-distillation and soft image-text alignments to more efficiently learn robust representations from noisy data. Our model distills its own knowledge to dynamically generate soft-alignment targets for a subset of images and captions in every minibatch, which are then used to update its parameters. Extensive evaluation across 14 benchmark datasets shows that our method consistently outperforms its CLIP counterpart in multiple settings, including: (a) zero-shot classification, (b) linear probe transfer, and (c) image-text retrieval, without incurring added computational cost. Analysis using an ImageNet-based robustness test-bed reveals that our method offers better effective robustness to natural distribution shifts compared to both ImageNet-trained models and CLIP itself. Lastly, pretraining with datasets spanning two orders of magnitude in size shows that our improvements over CLIP tend to scale with number of training examples.

papers_seen.author: Ramirez
papers_seen.title: Self-Knowledge Distillation with Progressive Refinement of Targets
papers_seen.abstract: The generalization capability of deep neural networks has been substantially improved by applying a wide spectrum of regularization methods, e.g., restricting function space, injecting randomness during training, augmenting data, etc. In this work, we propose a simple yet effective regularization method named progressive self-knowledge distillation (PS-KD), which progressively distills a model's own knowledge to soften hard targets (i.e., one-hot vectors) during training. Hence, it can be interpreted within a framework of knowledge distillation as a student becomes a teacher itself. Specifically, targets are adjusted adaptively by combining the ground-truth and past predictions from the model itself. We show that PS-KD provides an effect of hard example mining by rescaling gradients according to difficulty in classifying examples. The proposed method is applicable to any supervised learning tasks with hard targets and can be easily combined with existing regularization methods to further enhance the generalization performance. Furthermore, it is confirmed that PS-KD achieves not only better accuracy, but also provides high quality of confidence estimates in terms of calibration as well as ordinal ranking. Extensive experimental results on three different tasks, image classification, object detection, and machine translation, demonstrate that our method consistently improves the performance of the state-of-the-art baselines. The code is available at https://github.com/lgcnsai/PS-KD-Pytorch.

papers_seen.author: Cannon
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression strategies have become central to deploying large neural networks in resource-constrained settings. Across vision, multimodal, and language domains, researchers have developed approaches that transfer information from larger teacher models to smaller students via logits, intermediate representations, attention maps, or adversarial objectives. Work spans supervised and unsupervised settings, data-free or black-box scenarios, continual and federated use-cases, and concerns such as privacy and adversarial robustness. Practical recipes combine distillation with pruning, structured sparsity, progressive module replacement, and many-to-many layer mapping to balance accuracy, latency, and memory. Open challenges remain in data- and domain-limited regimes, robust and private compression, and principled selection of which teacher knowledge to transfer for a given downstream task.

papers_seen.author: Le
papers_seen.title: VPN++: Rethinking Video-Pose embeddings for understanding Activities of Daily Living
papers_seen.abstract: Many attempts have been made towards combining RGB and 3D poses for the recognition of Activities of Daily Living (ADL). ADL may look very similar and often necessitate to model fine-grained details to distinguish them. Because the recent 3D ConvNets are too rigid to capture the subtle visual patterns across an action, this research direction is dominated by methods combining RGB and 3D Poses. But the cost of computing 3D poses from RGB stream is high in the absence of appropriate sensors. This limits the usage of aforementioned approaches in real-world applications requiring low latency. Then, how to best take advantage of 3D Poses for recognizing ADL? To this end, we propose an extension of a pose driven attention mechanism: Video-Pose Network (VPN), exploring two distinct directions. One is to transfer the Pose knowledge into RGB through a feature-level distillation and the other towards mimicking pose driven attention through an attention-level distillation. Finally, these two approaches are integrated into a single model, we call VPN++. We show that VPN++ is not only effective but also provides a high speed up and high resilience to noisy Poses. VPN++, with or without 3D Poses, outperforms the representative baselines on 4 public datasets. Code is available at https://github.com/srijandas07/vpnplusplus.

papers_seen.author: Blair
papers_seen.title: Distilling Policy Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: The transfer of knowledge from one policy to another is an important tool in Deep Reinforcement Learning. This process, referred to as distillation, has been used to great success, for example, by enhancing the optimisation of agents, leading to stronger performance faster, on harder domains [26, 32, 5, 8]. Despite the widespread use and conceptual simplicity of distillation, many different formulations are used in practice, and the subtle variations between them can often drastically change the performance and the resulting objective that is being optimised. In this work, we rigorously explore the entire landscape of policy distillation, comparing the motivations and strengths of each variant through theoretical and empirical analysis. Our results point to three distillation techniques, that are preferred depending on specifics of the task. Specifically a newly proposed expected entropy regularised distillation allows for quicker learning in a wide range of situations, while still guaranteeing convergence.

papers_seen.author: Evans
papers_seen.title: Learning Compact Metrics for MT
papers_seen.abstract: Recent developments in machine translation and multilingual text generation have led researchers to adopt trained metrics such as COMET or BLEURT, which treat evaluation as a regression problem and use representations from multilingual pre-trained models such as XLM-RoBERTa or mBERT. Yet studies on related tasks suggest that these models are most efficient when they are large, which is costly and impractical for evaluation. We investigate the trade-off between multilinguality and model capacity with RemBERT, a state-of-the-art multilingual language model, using data from the WMT Metrics Shared Task. We present a series of experiments which show that model size is indeed a bottleneck for cross-lingual transfer, then demonstrate how distillation can help addressing this bottleneck, by leveraging synthetic data generation and transferring knowledge from one teacher to multiple students trained on related languages. Our method yields up to 10.5% improvement over vanilla fine-tuning and reaches 92.6% of RemBERT's performance using only a third of its parameters.

papers_seen.author: Higgins
papers_seen.title: The Case for Knowledge Distillation as a Core Tool for Model Compression and Transfer in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile technique that compresses large models into smaller, faster models while preserving or even improving task performance. Beyond simple size reduction, KD enables domain adaptation, multimodal capability lifting, robustness transfer, privacy-aware compression, and practical deployment on constrained hardware. The technique is complementary to pruning and quantization and can be adapted to settings with limited or no original training data, few-shot samples, and heterogeneous teacher ensembles. However, realizing KD's benefits reliably requires attention to teacher quality, sample selection, layer-mapping strategies, and interactions with regularization techniques such as label smoothing.

papers_seen.author: Bright
papers_seen.title: Towards Practical Lipreading with Distilled and Efficient Models
papers_seen.abstract: Lipreading has witnessed a lot of progress due to the resurgence of neural networks. Recent works have placed emphasis on aspects such as improving performance by finding the optimal architecture or improving generalization. However, there is still a significant gap between the current methodologies and the requirements for an effective deployment of lipreading in practical scenarios. In this work, we propose a series of innovations that significantly bridge that gap: first, we raise the state-of-the-art performance by a wide margin on LRW and LRW-1000 to 88.5% and 46.6%, respectively using self-distillation. Secondly, we propose a series of architectural changes, including a novel Depthwise Separable Temporal Convolutional Network (DS-TCN) head, that slashes the computational cost to a fraction of the (already quite efficient) original model. Thirdly, we show that knowledge distillation is a very effective tool for recovering performance of the lightweight models. This results in a range of models with different accuracy-efficiency trade-offs. However, our most promising lightweight models are on par with the current state-of-the-art while showing a reduction of 8.2x and 3.9x in terms of computational cost and number of parameters, respectively, which we hope will enable the deployment of lipreading models in practical applications.

papers_seen.author: Roberts
papers_seen.title: Improving the Interpretability of Deep Neural Networks with Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Deep Neural Networks have achieved huge success at a wide spectrum of applications from language modeling, computer vision to speech recognition. However, nowadays, good performance alone is not sufficient to satisfy the needs of practical deployment where interpretability is demanded for cases involving ethics and mission critical applications. The complex models of Deep Neural Networks make it hard to understand and reason the predictions, which hinders its further progress. To tackle this problem, we apply the Knowledge Distillation technique to distill Deep Neural Networks into decision trees in order to attain good performance and interpretability simultaneously. We formulate the problem at hand as a multi-output regression problem and the experiments demonstrate that the student model achieves significantly better accuracy performance (about 1\% to 5\%) than vanilla decision trees at the same level of tree depth. The experiments are implemented on the TensorFlow platform to make it scalable to big datasets. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to distill Deep Neural Networks into vanilla decision trees on multi-class datasets.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: Explaining Knowledge Distillation by Quantifying the Knowledge
papers_seen.abstract: This paper presents a method to interpret the success of knowledge distillation by quantifying and analyzing task-relevant and task-irrelevant visual concepts that are encoded in intermediate layers of a deep neural network (DNN). More specifically, three hypotheses are proposed as follows. 1. Knowledge distillation makes the DNN learn more visual concepts than learning from raw data. 2. Knowledge distillation ensures that the DNN is prone to learning various visual concepts simultaneously. Whereas, in the scenario of learning from raw data, the DNN learns visual concepts sequentially. 3. Knowledge distillation yields more stable optimization directions than learning from raw data. Accordingly, we design three types of mathematical metrics to evaluate feature representations of the DNN. In experiments, we diagnosed various DNNs, and above hypotheses were verified.

papers_seen.author: Brown
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Practices in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model-compression techniques have become central tools for deploying large deep models in resource-constrained settings. Across modalities and tasks, distillation is used to transfer predictive behavior or internal representations from larger, more accurate teachers to smaller, faster students; it also appears within automated model search, pruning and distributed training workflows. Work in this area spans logit matching, representation-level objectives, data-free and few-shot regimes, multi-/online-teacher schemes, and task- or architecture-aware compression. Empirical results demonstrate that carefully designed distillation strategies can yield compact models that approach teacher accuracy while enabling large reductions in memory and compute, but limitations remain around optimization, data availability, and the preservation or mitigation of undesirable biases.

papers_seen.author: Walker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Versatile Tool for Compression, Adaptation, Privacy, and Robustness in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is more than a single compression recipe: it is a flexible family of techniques that transfers predictive behavior and internal representations from one set of models to another. KD enables production of compact, fast models that retain much of a larger model's performance, and it can be adapted to address domain shift, limited or private data, modality-specific constraints, and even fairness or robustness objectives. This paper argues that KD should be treated as a core component of model deployment pipelines across modalities (vision, language, graphs, generative models, and sequential tasks) and that careful selection among KD variants (logit, feature, ensemble, online, adversarial, data-free, teacher-free, and task-aware distillation) lets practitioners balance accuracy, latency, privacy, and fairness requirements.

papers_seen.author: Harrell
papers_seen.title: No One Left Behind: Inclusive Federated Learning over Heterogeneous Devices
papers_seen.abstract: Federated learning (FL) is an important paradigm for training global models from decentralized data in a privacy-preserving way. Existing FL methods usually assume the global model can be trained on any participating client. However, in real applications, the devices of clients are usually heterogeneous, and have different computing power. Although big models like BERT have achieved huge success in AI, it is difficult to apply them to heterogeneous FL with weak clients. The straightforward solutions like removing the weak clients or using a small model to fit all clients will lead to some problems, such as under-representation of dropped clients and inferior accuracy due to data loss or limited model representation ability. In this work, we propose InclusiveFL, a client-inclusive federated learning method to handle this problem. The core idea of InclusiveFL is to assign models of different sizes to clients with different computing capabilities, bigger models for powerful clients and smaller ones for weak clients. We also propose an effective method to share the knowledge among multiple local models with different sizes. In this way, all the clients can participate in the model learning in FL, and the final model can be big and powerful enough. Besides, we propose a momentum knowledge distillation method to better transfer knowledge in big models on powerful clients to the small models on weak clients. Extensive experiments on many real-world benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in learning accurate models from clients with heterogeneous devices under the FL framework.

papers_seen.author: Herrera
papers_seen.title: Distilling Object Detectors with Fine-grained Feature Imitation
papers_seen.abstract: State-of-the-art CNN based recognition models are often computationally prohibitive to deploy on low-end devices. A promising high level approach tackling this limitation is knowledge distillation, which let small student model mimic cumbersome teacher model's output to get improved generalization. However, related methods mainly focus on simple task of classification while do not consider complex tasks like object detection. We show applying the vanilla knowledge distillation to detection model gets minor gain. To address the challenge of distilling knowledge in detection model, we propose a fine-grained feature imitation method exploiting the cross-location discrepancy of feature response. Our intuition is that detectors care more about local near object regions. Thus the discrepancy of feature response on the near object anchor locations reveals important information of how teacher model tends to generalize. We design a novel mechanism to estimate those locations and let student model imitate the teacher on them to get enhanced performance. We first validate the idea on a developed lightweight toy detector which carries simplest notion of current state-of-the-art anchor based detection models on challenging KITTI dataset, our method generates up to 15% boost of mAP for the student model compared to the non-imitated counterpart. We then extensively evaluate the method with Faster R-CNN model under various scenarios with common object detection benchmark of Pascal VOC and COCO, imitation alleviates up to 74% performance drop of student model compared to teacher. Codes released at https://github.com/twangnh/Distilling-Object-Detectors

papers_seen.author: Gray
papers_seen.title: Improved Feature Distillation via Projector Ensemble
papers_seen.abstract: In knowledge distillation, previous feature distillation methods mainly focus on the design of loss functions and the selection of the distilled layers, while the effect of the feature projector between the student and the teacher remains under-explored. In this paper, we first discuss a plausible mechanism of the projector with empirical evidence and then propose a new feature distillation method based on a projector ensemble for further performance improvement. We observe that the student network benefits from a projector even if the feature dimensions of the student and the teacher are the same. Training a student backbone without a projector can be considered as a multi-task learning process, namely achieving discriminative feature extraction for classification and feature matching between the student and the teacher for distillation at the same time. We hypothesize and empirically verify that without a projector, the student network tends to overfit the teacher's feature distributions despite having different architecture and weights initialization. This leads to degradation on the quality of the student's deep features that are eventually used in classification. Adding a projector, on the other hand, disentangles the two learning tasks and helps the student network to focus better on the main feature extraction task while still being able to utilize teacher features as a guidance through the projector. Motivated by the positive effect of the projector in feature distillation, we propose an ensemble of projectors to further improve the quality of student features. Experimental results on different datasets with a series of teacher-student pairs illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

papers_seen.author: Chapman
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Approaches and Findings
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a practical and versatile family of techniques for producing smaller, faster, or otherwise specialized models by transferring information from larger or alternative teacher models. KD variants include offline teacher-student distillation, online mutual distillation, ensemble-to-student distillation, cross-task distillation, and teacher-aware or student-aware training. Beyond the canonical logit-matching objective, modern work distills intermediate representations, relational and contrastive structures, and task-specific signals to improve accuracy, robustness, fairness, privacy, generation, and inference latency. Empirical results across computer vision, speech, machine translation, retrieval, graph learning, and routing problems show KD can both compress models without large accuracy loss and improve distilled students in multiple dimensions (robustness, fairness, generalization, and deployment cost). However, distillation is not a panacea: its effectiveness depends on teacher quality and compatibility, the choice of distilled knowledge (logits vs features vs relations), data complexity, and careful training strategies (sample selection, curriculum, annealing, or joint teacher-student learning). This synthesis summarizes methods, motivations, practical techniques, and empirical patterns observed across recent studies.

papers_seen.author: Hicks
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Adaptation: Teaching to Adapt
papers_seen.abstract: Domain adaptation is crucial in many real-world applications where the distribution of the training data differs from the distribution of the test data. Previous Deep Learning-based approaches to domain adaptation need to be trained jointly on source and target domain data and are therefore unappealing in scenarios where models need to be adapted to a large number of domains or where a domain is evolving, e.g. spam detection where attackers continuously change their tactics.   To fill this gap, we propose Knowledge Adaptation, an extension of Knowledge Distillation (Bucilua et al., 2006; Hinton et al., 2015) to the domain adaptation scenario. We show how a student model achieves state-of-the-art results on unsupervised domain adaptation from multiple sources on a standard sentiment analysis benchmark by taking into account the domain-specific expertise of multiple teachers and the similarities between their domains.   When learning from a single teacher, using domain similarity to gauge trustworthiness is inadequate. To this end, we propose a simple metric that correlates well with the teacher's accuracy in the target domain. We demonstrate that incorporating high-confidence examples selected by this metric enables the student model to achieve state-of-the-art performance in the single-source scenario.

papers_seen.author: Ryan
papers_seen.title: The Central Role of Knowledge Distillation for Practical Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Modalities, and Recommendations
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model compression techniques are now essential for deploying high-performing deep learning models under resource, privacy, and latency constraints. A broad set of distillation strategies—ranging from soft-label supervision and feature mimicking to data-free (zero-shot) distillation, adversarially guided feature transfer, self-distillation, and automated architecture search guided by teacher models—enable substantial reductions in model size and computational cost while preserving or even improving performance across vision, language, multimodal, and sequence tasks. Best practice combines input-side methods (data augmentation and mixup), representation-level transfer, and careful teacher-student design choices to match the deployment objectives (efficiency, fairness, interpretability, or privacy).

This review summarizes these practical methods, observed trade-offs, and open challenges for robust, efficient, and private model compression.'}, {'author': 'Henderson', 'year': 2021, 'title': 'Graph-less Neural Networks: Teaching Old MLPs New Tricks via Distillation', 'abstract': 'Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are popular for graph machine learning and have shown great results on wide node classification tasks. This paper argues that KD should be treated as a core component of model deployment pipelines across modalities (vision, language, graphs, generative models, and sequential tasks) and that careful selection among KD variants (logit, feature, ensemble, online, adversarial, data-free, teacher-free, and task-aware distillation) lets practitioners balance accuracy, latency, privacy, and fairness requirements."}, {'author': 'Harrell', 'year': 2022, 'title': 'No One Left Behind: Inclusive Federated Learning over Heterogeneous Devices', 'abstract': 'Federated learning (FL) is an important paradigm for training global models from decentralized data in a privacy-preserving way. Existing FL methods usually assume the global model can be trained on any participating client. However, in real applications, the devices of clients are usually heterogeneous, and have different computing power. In this way, all the clients can participate in the model learning in FL, and the final model can be big and powerful enough. papers_seen.author: Pacheco
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation with Adversarial Samples Supporting Decision Boundary
papers_seen.abstract: Many recent works on knowledge distillation have provided ways to transfer the knowledge of a trained network for improving the learning process of a new one, but finding a good technique for knowledge distillation is still an open problem. In this paper, we provide a new perspective based on a decision boundary, which is one of the most important component of a classifier. The generalization performance of a classifier is closely related to the adequacy of its decision boundary, so a good classifier bears a good decision boundary. Therefore, transferring information closely related to the decision boundary can be a good attempt for knowledge distillation. To realize this goal, we utilize an adversarial attack to discover samples supporting a decision boundary. Based on this idea, to transfer more accurate information about the decision boundary, the proposed algorithm trains a student classifier based on the adversarial samples supporting the decision boundary. Experiments show that the proposed method indeed improves knowledge distillation and achieves the state-of-the-arts performance.

papers_seen.author: Pierce
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression methods provide practical routes to deploy high-performing deep models under resource, privacy, and latency constraints. The literature has developed diverse approaches that transfer information via soft logits, intermediate features, attentional maps, channel-wise statistics, and online mutual learning; adaptations address task-specific compression, data-free or few-shot regimes, large-scale distributed training, and teacher-student co-optimization. Empirical and theoretical analyses highlight that distillation combines information transfer with regularization effects, and that selecting what, when, and how to transfer knowledge (e.g., logits vs. features, offline vs. online, task-aware filtering) is crucial to achieve favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-offs across vision and language tasks.

papers_seen.author: Chavez
papers_seen.title: Data-Free Knowledge Distillation for Deep Neural Networks
papers_seen.abstract: Recent advances in model compression have provided procedures for compressing large neural networks to a fraction of their original size while retaining most if not all of their accuracy. However, all of these approaches rely on access to the original training set, which might not always be possible if the network to be compressed was trained on a very large dataset, or on a dataset whose release poses privacy or safety concerns as may be the case for biometrics tasks. We present a method for data-free knowledge distillation, which is able to compress deep neural networks trained on large-scale datasets to a fraction of their size leveraging only some extra metadata to be provided with a pretrained model release. We also explore different kinds of metadata that can be used with our method, and discuss tradeoffs involved in using each of them.

papers_seen.author: Bernard
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Approaches and Findings
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and model compression have matured into a versatile set of techniques for transferring predictive capacity from large, expensive models into smaller, faster, or more private models. Across computer vision, NLP, multimodal systems, federated settings, and generative models, researchers have combined soft-label (logit) distillation, intermediate feature/hint transfer, architecture transformation, quantization, pruning, and automated search to achieve significant reductions in memory, computation, or communication while largely preserving accuracy. Empirical work demonstrates that distillation can enable high-quality low-precision models, speed up inference and training, unify heterogeneous models without shared data, and make distributed learning more communication- and privacy-efficient. The field continues to refine when and what knowledge to transfer (e.g., logits vs. features vs. attention), how to handle multiple or unreliable teachers, how to design student-friendly teachers, and how to integrate distillation with other compression methods such as pruning and search.

papers_seen.author: Maldonado
papers_seen.title: Distilling Knowledge by Mimicking Features
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a popular method to train efficient networks ("student") with the help of high-capacity networks ("teacher"). Traditional methods use the teacher's soft logits as extra supervision to train the student network. In this paper, we argue that it is more advantageous to make the student mimic the teacher's features in the penultimate layer. Not only the student can directly learn more effective information from the teacher feature, feature mimicking can also be applied for teachers trained without a softmax layer. Experiments show that it can achieve higher accuracy than traditional KD. To further facilitate feature mimicking, we decompose a feature vector into the magnitude and the direction. We argue that the teacher should give more freedom to the student feature's magnitude, and let the student pay more attention on mimicking the feature direction. To meet this requirement, we propose a loss term based on locality-sensitive hashing (LSH). With the help of this new loss, our method indeed mimics feature directions more accurately, relaxes constraints on feature magnitudes, and achieves state-of-the-art distillation accuracy. We provide theoretical analyses of how LSH facilitates feature direction mimicking, and further extend feature mimicking to multi-label recognition and object detection.

papers_seen.author: Miller
papers_seen.title: Understanding BERT Rankers Under Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Deep language models such as BERT pre-trained on large corpus have given a huge performance boost to the state-of-the-art information retrieval ranking systems. Knowledge embedded in such models allows them to pick up complex matching signals between passages and queries. However, the high computation cost during inference limits their deployment in real-world search scenarios. In this paper, we study if and how the knowledge for search within BERT can be transferred to a smaller ranker through distillation. Our experiments demonstrate that it is crucial to use a proper distillation procedure, which produces up to nine times speedup while preserving the state-of-the-art performance.

papers_seen.author: Adams
papers_seen.title: Is Label Smoothing Truly Incompatible with Knowledge Distillation: An Empirical Study
papers_seen.abstract: This work aims to empirically clarify a recently discovered perspective that label smoothing is incompatible with knowledge distillation. We begin by introducing the motivation behind on how this incompatibility is raised, i.e., label smoothing erases relative information between teacher logits. We provide a novel connection on how label smoothing affects distributions of semantically similar and dissimilar classes. Then we propose a metric to quantitatively measure the degree of erased information in sample's representation. After that, we study its one-sidedness and imperfection of the incompatibility view through massive analyses, visualizations and comprehensive experiments on Image Classification, Binary Networks, and Neural Machine Translation. Finally, we broadly discuss several circumstances wherein label smoothing will indeed lose its effectiveness. Project page: http://zhiqiangshen.com/projects/LS_and_KD/index.html.

papers_seen.author: Mueller
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Work
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a central technique for compressing and accelerating deep models by transferring knowledge from larger (teacher) models to smaller (student) models. Beyond straightforward parameter reduction, KD is used to improve student generalization, robustness, interpretability, domain adaptation, continual learning, and to enable deployment in latency- or resource-constrained settings. The literature shows a wide variety of KD objectives (logit/soft-label matching, feature imitation, relational losses), training protocols (multi-teacher, curriculum, adversarial or zero-shot data generation, teacher-free/self-distillation), and application-specific adaptations (detection, retrieval, GANs, speech, lipreading, 3D vision, recommender systems, and NLP). Empirical results demonstrate that carefully designed distillation pipelines can recover much of teacher performance and in some cases surpass teachers on efficiency-accuracy trade-offs, but raise challenges including heterogeneous teacher-student alignment, data availability, preserving low-frequency or fine-grained behaviors, and transferring robustness and domain-general knowledge.

papers_seen.author: Parsons
papers_seen.title: Curriculum Learning for Dense Retrieval Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Recent work has shown that more effective dense retrieval models can be obtained by distilling ranking knowledge from an existing base re-ranking model. In this paper, we propose a generic curriculum learning based optimization framework called CL-DRD that controls the difficulty level of training data produced by the re-ranking (teacher) model. CL-DRD iteratively optimizes the dense retrieval (student) model by increasing the difficulty of the knowledge distillation data made available to it. In more detail, we initially provide the student model coarse-grained preference pairs between documents in the teacher's ranking and progressively move towards finer-grained pairwise document ordering requirements. In our experiments, we apply a simple implementation of the CL-DRD framework to enhance two state-of-the-art dense retrieval models. Experiments on three public passage retrieval datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed framework.

papers_seen.author: Cowan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Approaches
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques aim to transfer knowledge from large, expensive models to smaller, efficient models while preserving performance. Across vision, language, multimodal, and federated settings, researchers have applied KD for inference speedup, deployment on resource-constrained devices, privacy-preserving model release, and enhanced robustness or interpretability. Methods vary from standard teacher–student soft-label supervision to data-free distillation, adversarially chosen boundary samples, many-to-many layer mappings, generative replay, and architecture-aware compression. Empirical results show KD can yield large efficiency gains with modest accuracy loss when combined with task-aware design, careful sample selection, and appropriate optimization; challenges remain around distributional mismatch, low-frequency token handling, heterogeneous architectures, and privacy/validation in data-free scenarios. Emerging directions include task-adaptive compressed models, joint optimization of pruning and KD, federated/distilled learning across heterogeneous devices, and cross-modal distillation for generative capabilities.

papers_seen.author: Jones
papers_seen.title: The Case for Task- and Data-Aware Knowledge Distillation: Principles, Pitfalls, and Practical Extensions for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a central tool for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. Its practical success across vision, language, graph, and generative models depends not only on the generic teacher→student paradigm but on task-aware selection of transferred information, choices about data access (including data-free and privacy-preserving variants), and the use of auxiliary techniques (adversarial training, ensembling, pruning, and architecture search). When these dimensions are addressed explicitly, distillation can produce compact models that approach teacher performance while offering improved robustness, interpretability, or resource-efficiency. However, naive distillation can fail due to optimization difficulties, domain shift, and heterogeneous teacher-student mismatches, so practitioners must adopt targeted strategies that consider the learning objective, available data, and student capacity.

papers_seen.author: Henderson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning: Methods, Domains, and Practical Considerations
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques transfer information from larger or multi-source models to smaller, faster, or modality-restricted models to reduce memory, compute, and latency while retaining performance. Approaches vary from matching teacher logits to mimicking internal features, and extend to self-distillation, many-to-many layer mapping, adversarial and contrastive objectives, and adaptations for few-shot, federated, and multimodal settings. Empirical work across vision, language, graphs, speech, and generative models shows KD can enable compact models that approach teacher accuracy, improve calibration and fairness, and make deployment on resource-constrained and heterogeneous devices practical. Ongoing challenges include selecting what to transfer (logits, features, relations), aligning heterogeneous architectures, and designing KD protocols robust to limited data, domain shifts, and privacy constraints.

papers_seen.author: Richards
papers_seen.title: TextKD-GAN: Text Generation using KnowledgeDistillation and Generative Adversarial Networks
papers_seen.abstract: Text generation is of particular interest in many NLP applications such as machine translation, language modeling, and text summarization. Generative adversarial networks (GANs) achieved a remarkable success in high quality image generation in computer vision,and recently, GANs have gained lots of interest from the NLP community as well. However, achieving similar success in NLP would be more challenging due to the discrete nature of text. In this work, we introduce a method using knowledge distillation to effectively exploit GAN setup for text generation. We demonstrate how autoencoders (AEs) can be used for providing a continuous representation of sentences, which is a smooth representation that assign non-zero probabilities to more than one word. We distill this representation to train the generator to synthesize similar smooth representations. We perform a number of experiments to validate our idea using different datasets and show that our proposed approach yields better performance in terms of the BLEU score and Jensen-Shannon distance (JSD) measure compared to traditional GAN-based text generation approaches without pre-training.

papers_seen.author: Duncan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Analyses, and Applications
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a central technique for compressing and adapting large neural models into smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained models while retaining much of their performance. A diverse set of KD approaches operate at the level of final outputs (logits), intermediate features, layer relations, or via adversarial and data-generation mechanisms. KD has been adapted across modalities and tasks — from NLP transformer compression to GAN and speech-model compression, cross-modal transfer, federated settings, and domain-specific applications — and interacts strongly with concerns about robustness, fairness, and transfer of inductive biases. Empirical and theoretical work has clarified when and why various KD variants help, and highlights open challenges in data heterogeneity, teacher-student mismatch, and automatic discovery of compact architectures.

papers_seen.author: Novak
papers_seen.title: The Central Role of Knowledge Distillation for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, practical strategy for compressing large models into smaller, faster, and often more deployable students across modalities and tasks. KD techniques extend beyond matching logits: they include internal-representation distillation, adversarial and relational approaches, multi-teacher and online schemes, data-free and privacy-aware methods, and architecture-aware replacements. Empirical and theoretical work shows KD can preserve or even improve generalization, enable domain adaptation, and permit deployment under resource, privacy, or latency constraints—provided practitioners attend to known failure modes such as teacher bias, low-frequency lexical errors, and domain shift.

papers_seen.author: Rocha
papers_seen.title: Few Shot Network Compression via Cross Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Model compression has been widely adopted to obtain light-weighted deep neural networks. Most prevalent methods, however, require fine-tuning with sufficient training data to ensure accuracy, which could be challenged by privacy and security issues. As a compromise between privacy and performance, in this paper we investigate few shot network compression: given few samples per class, how can we effectively compress the network with negligible performance drop? The core challenge of few shot network compression lies in high estimation errors from the original network during inference, since the compressed network can easily over-fits on the few training instances. The estimation errors could propagate and accumulate layer-wisely and finally deteriorate the network output. To address the problem, we propose cross distillation, a novel layer-wise knowledge distillation approach. By interweaving hidden layers of teacher and student network, layer-wisely accumulated estimation errors can be effectively reduced.The proposed method offers a general framework compatible with prevalent network compression techniques such as pruning. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that cross distillation can significantly improve the student network's accuracy when only a few training instances are available.

papers_seen.author: Clark
papers_seen.title: Towards Model Agnostic Federated Learning Using Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Is it possible to design an universal API for federated learning using which an ad-hoc group of data-holders (agents) collaborate with each other and perform federated learning? Such an API would necessarily need to be model-agnostic i.e. make no assumption about the model architecture being used by the agents, and also cannot rely on having representative public data at hand. Knowledge distillation (KD) is the obvious tool of choice to design such protocols. However, surprisingly, we show that most natural KD-based federated learning protocols have poor performance.   To investigate this, we propose a new theoretical framework, Federated Kernel ridge regression, which can capture both model heterogeneity as well as data heterogeneity. Our analysis shows that the degradation is largely due to a fundamental limitation of knowledge distillation under data heterogeneity. We further validate our framework by analyzing and designing new protocols based on KD. Their performance on real world experiments using neural networks, though still unsatisfactory, closely matches our theoretical predictions.

papers_seen.author: Humphrey
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Multi-Modal Tool for Compression and Adaptation in Deep Learning: Strengths, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a broadly applicable approach for compressing and adapting deep models across modalities (text, vision, graphs, speech) and deployment scenarios (edge devices, federated clients, domain shifts). Empirical evidence shows KD can improve student generalization, enable small-footprint models, and facilitate domain- or modality-transfer when combined with representation-level objectives or adversarial/contrastive methods. However, its success depends on optimization, teacher-student design, data availability, and fairness considerations. I argue that KD should be treated as a flexible framework—one that combines logit-level supervision with representation-aware objectives, domain-aware selection of teacher signals, and explicit measures to mitigate undesirable side effects (e.g., lexical errors or bias)—to reliably produce compact, high-quality models for NLP and beyond.

papers_seen.author: Munoz
papers_seen.title: Zero-Shot Knowledge Distillation in Deep Networks
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation deals with the problem of training a smaller model (Student) from a high capacity source model (Teacher) so as to retain most of its performance. Existing approaches use either the training data or meta-data extracted from it in order to train the Student. However, accessing the dataset on which the Teacher has been trained may not always be feasible if the dataset is very large or it poses privacy or safety concerns (e.g., bio-metric or medical data). Hence, in this paper, we propose a novel data-free method to train the Student from the Teacher. Without even using any meta-data, we synthesize the Data Impressions from the complex Teacher model and utilize these as surrogates for the original training data samples to transfer its learning to Student via knowledge distillation. We, therefore, dub our method "Zero-Shot Knowledge Distillation" and demonstrate that our framework results in competitive generalization performance as achieved by distillation using the actual training data samples on multiple benchmark datasets.

papers_seen.author: Powell
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central Tool for Model Compression and Transfer: Strengths, Limits, and Practical Directions
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a versatile set of techniques that enable model compression, domain- and task-level transfer, privacy-preserving distillation, and improvements in interpretability and fairness. Empirical and methodological work shows KD can compress large models into efficient students, transfer inductive biases, support multi-task and lifelong learning, and enable data-free or zero-shot distillation when training data are unavailable. At the same time, KD faces concrete limitations due to data heterogeneity, teacher-student capacity mismatch, and the need to select or synthesize appropriate supervision; hybrid solutions that combine feature-level matching, adversarial sample synthesis, curriculum strategies, and architectural compression achieve the best practical results. Based on evidence across domains (vision, language, graphs, retrieval, reinforcement learning), we argue that KD should be used as part of an integrated compression pipeline that is task-aware, data-aware, and often combined with pruning, layer skipping, or module replacement to meet deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Jones
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and model compression have become central strategies for deploying large deep models under resource, latency, and privacy constraints. A diverse set of methods—ranging from soft-label distillation, intermediate feature and attention matching, layer mapping, adversarial and data-free techniques, to task-adaptive architecture search and meta-learning of teachers—have been proposed to transfer performance from bulky teachers to compact students. These approaches are applied across domains including vision, language, multi-modal systems, recommender systems, and domain-specific NLP, and they trade off fidelity to the teacher, generalization, and computational efficiency. Empirical results show that properly designed distillation pipelines can recover a large fraction of teacher performance while yielding substantial speedups and memory reductions, and in some settings can even improve fairness, robustness, or downstream generalization. Remaining challenges include aligning heterogeneous inputs and representations across teacher and student, coping with absent or private training data, and automatically selecting what and how to transfer for specific tasks and deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Edwards
papers_seen.title: Preserving Privacy in Federated Learning with Ensemble Cross-Domain Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Federated Learning (FL) is a machine learning paradigm where local nodes collaboratively train a central model while the training data remains decentralized. Existing FL methods typically share model parameters or employ co-distillation to address the issue of unbalanced data distribution. However, they suffer from communication bottlenecks. More importantly, they risk privacy leakage. In this work, we develop a privacy preserving and communication efficient method in a FL framework with one-shot offline knowledge distillation using unlabeled, cross-domain public data. We propose a quantized and noisy ensemble of local predictions from completely trained local models for stronger privacy guarantees without sacrificing accuracy. Based on extensive experiments on image classification and text classification tasks, we show that our privacy-preserving method outperforms baseline FL algorithms with superior performance in both accuracy and communication efficiency.

papers_seen.author: Bright
papers_seen.title: Towards Practical Lipreading with Distilled and Efficient Models
papers_seen.abstract: Lipreading has witnessed a lot of progress due to the resurgence of neural networks. Recent works have placed emphasis on aspects such as improving performance by finding the optimal architecture or improving generalization. However, there is still a significant gap between the current methodologies and the requirements for an effective deployment of lipreading in practical scenarios. In this work, we propose a series of innovations that significantly bridge that gap: first, we raise the state-of-the-art performance by a wide margin on LRW and LRW-1000 to 88.5% and 46.6%, respectively using self-distillation. Secondly, we propose a series of architectural changes, including a novel Depthwise Separable Temporal Convolutional Network (DS-TCN) head, that slashes the computational cost to a fraction of the (already quite efficient) original model. Thirdly, we show that knowledge distillation is a very effective tool for recovering performance of the lightweight models. This results in a range of models with different accuracy-efficiency trade-offs. However, our most promising lightweight models are on par with the current state-of-the-art while showing a reduction of 8.2x and 3.9x in terms of computational cost and number of parameters, respectively, which we hope will enable the deployment of lipreading models in practical applications.

papers_seen.author: Brown
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Approaches
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques have become central tools for deploying high-performing deep models in resource-constrained or privacy-sensitive settings. Work in this area has progressed beyond the original formulation of training a small student to match a teacher's output probabilities: modern approaches distill internal representations, perform many-to-many layer alignment, operate without access to original training data, combine multiple teachers or ensembles, and adapt to particular architectures and tasks (including graph networks, detectors, generative models, and language models). Practical concerns such as data heterogeneity, privacy guarantees, and robustness to distribution shift have motivated methods that use synthetic data, private perturbations, generative replay, and federated or online distillation protocols. The field continues to trade off fidelity to teacher behavior, compactness, task specificity, and deployability, with task-adaptive compression and representation-alignment methods emerging as especially effective for NLP and other structured prediction tasks.

papers_seen.author: Chapman
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Approaches and Findings
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a practical and versatile family of techniques for producing smaller, faster, or otherwise specialized models by transferring information from larger or alternative teacher models. KD variants include offline teacher-student distillation, online mutual distillation, ensemble-to-student distillation, cross-task distillation, and teacher-aware or student-aware training. Beyond the canonical logit-matching objective, modern work distills intermediate representations, relational and contrastive structures, and task-specific signals to improve accuracy, robustness, fairness, privacy, generation, and inference latency. Empirical results across computer vision, speech, machine translation, retrieval, graph learning, and routing problems show KD can both compress models without large accuracy loss and improve distilled students in multiple dimensions (robustness, fairness, generalization, and deployment cost). However, distillation is not a panacea: its effectiveness depends on teacher quality and compatibility, the choice of distilled knowledge (logits vs features vs relations), data complexity, and careful training strategies (sample selection, curriculum, annealing, or joint teacher-student learning). This synthesis summarizes methods, motivations, practical techniques, and empirical patterns observed across recent studies.

papers_seen.author: Rodriguez
papers_seen.title: Extract the Knowledge of Graph Neural Networks and Go Beyond it: An Effective Knowledge Distillation Framework
papers_seen.abstract: Semi-supervised learning on graphs is an important problem in the machine learning area. In recent years, state-of-the-art classification methods based on graph neural networks (GNNs) have shown their superiority over traditional ones such as label propagation. However, the sophisticated architectures of these neural models will lead to a complex prediction mechanism, which could not make full use of valuable prior knowledge lying in the data, e.g., structurally correlated nodes tend to have the same class. In this paper, we propose a framework based on knowledge distillation to address the above issues. Our framework extracts the knowledge of an arbitrary learned GNN model (teacher model), and injects it into a well-designed student model. The student model is built with two simple prediction mechanisms, i.e., label propagation and feature transformation, which naturally preserves structure-based and feature-based prior knowledge, respectively. In specific, we design the student model as a trainable combination of parameterized label propagation and feature transformation modules. As a result, the learned student can benefit from both prior knowledge and the knowledge in GNN teachers for more effective predictions. Moreover, the learned student model has a more interpretable prediction process than GNNs. We conduct experiments on five public benchmark datasets and employ seven GNN models including GCN, GAT, APPNP, SAGE, SGC, GCNII and GLP as the teacher models. Experimental results show that the learned student model can consistently outperform its corresponding teacher model by 1.4% - 4.7% on average. Code and data are available at https://github.com/BUPT-GAMMA/CPF

papers_seen.author: Callahan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical and Versatile Path for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a practical toolkit for compressing large models into smaller, faster models while preserving much of their performance. Across modalities and tasks—classification, detection, generation, retrieval, recommendation, graph learning, and language modeling—KD enables deployment on resource-constrained devices and latency-sensitive pipelines. However, maximizing benefits requires addressing teacher-student capacity gaps, computational cost of teacher supervision, and task-specific information selection; a variety of methodological extensions (multi-teacher schedules, feature/projector design, adversarial or decision-boundary driven samples, layer- and task-aware filtering, self-distillation, and meta-learned teachers) have been developed to meet these needs. When combined appropriately with other compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search), distillation yields state-of-the-art trade-offs for real applications.

papers_seen.author: Moore
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central Tool for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a practical and versatile approach to compressing large models for deployment and domain-specific use. Across modalities and tasks, KD can preserve much of the teacher's performance in compact students, but it must be combined with task-aware engineering—such as teacher adaptation, layer-wise selection, data augmentation, and hardware-aware pruning—to address heterogeneity, domain shift, and efficiency constraints. This article argues that KD is necessary but not sufficient: best results come from integrating KD with complementary techniques chosen for the target modality, deployment constraints, and learning scenario.

papers_seen.author: Rios
papers_seen.title: Improving Neural Topic Models using Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Topic models are often used to identify human-interpretable topics to help make sense of large document collections. We use knowledge distillation to combine the best attributes of probabilistic topic models and pretrained transformers. Our modular method can be straightforwardly applied with any neural topic model to improve topic quality, which we demonstrate using two models having disparate architectures, obtaining state-of-the-art topic coherence. We show that our adaptable framework not only improves performance in the aggregate over all estimated topics, as is commonly reported, but also in head-to-head comparisons of aligned topics.

papers_seen.author: Higgins
papers_seen.title: The Case for Knowledge Distillation as a Core Tool for Model Compression and Transfer in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile technique that compresses large models into smaller, faster models while preserving or even improving task performance. Beyond simple size reduction, KD enables domain adaptation, multimodal capability lifting, robustness transfer, privacy-aware compression, and practical deployment on constrained hardware. The technique is complementary to pruning and quantization and can be adapted to settings with limited or no original training data, few-shot samples, and heterogeneous teacher ensembles. However, realizing KD's benefits reliably requires attention to teacher quality, sample selection, layer-mapping strategies, and interactions with regularization techniques such as label smoothing.

Project page: http://zhiqiangshen.com/projects/LS_and_KD/index.html."}, {'author': 'Mueller', 'year': 2024, 'title': 'Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Work', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a central technique for compressing and accelerating deep models by transferring knowledge from larger (teacher) models to smaller (student) models.
