papers_seen.author: Fowler
papers_seen.title: SEED: Self-supervised Distillation For Visual Representation
papers_seen.abstract: This paper is concerned with self-supervised learning for small models. The problem is motivated by our empirical studies that while the widely used contrastive self-supervised learning method has shown great progress on large model training, it does not work well for small models. To address this problem, we propose a new learning paradigm, named SElf-SupErvised Distillation (SEED), where we leverage a larger network (as Teacher) to transfer its representational knowledge into a smaller architecture (as Student) in a self-supervised fashion. Instead of directly learning from unlabeled data, we train a student encoder to mimic the similarity score distribution inferred by a teacher over a set of instances. We show that SEED dramatically boosts the performance of small networks on downstream tasks. Compared with self-supervised baselines, SEED improves the top-1 accuracy from 42.2% to 67.6% on EfficientNet-B0 and from 36.3% to 68.2% on MobileNet-v3-Large on the ImageNet-1k dataset.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: The Case for Pragmatic, Task-Aware Knowledge Distillation in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically validated set of techniques for producing smaller, faster models from larger teachers. Across vision, language, multimodal, and distributed settings, distillation can preserve or even improve accuracy while enabling deployments with constrained compute, memory, latency, and privacy requirements. However, its success depends on matching distillation objectives and procedures to task constraints (e.g., robustness, heterogeneity, data availability). When applied thoughtfully—using feature-based objectives, ensemble or adversarial strategies, data augmentation or data-free approaches, and task-adaptive compression—KD reliably delivers practical trade-offs between efficiency and effectiveness.

papers_seen.author: Daniel
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques have become primary approaches for deploying high-performing deep models in resource-constrained settings. The literature spans methods that transfer soft-labels, internal feature representations, and ensemble knowledge; extensions address teacher imperfections, data scarcity or privacy, task-specific adaptations for NLP and vision, and hardware-aware compression. Empirical work demonstrates that careful design choices—such as which signals to transfer, how to align teacher and student layers, whether to incorporate self-distillation or multi-teacher training, and how to combine pruning or low-precision numerics—substantially affect final accuracy and efficiency. The field also benefits from theoretical analyses that clarify when and why distillation helps. Remaining challenges include distilling robust semantics for low-frequency phenomena, distillation without access to original data, and co-design for hardware deployment.

papers_seen.author: Alvarez
papers_seen.title: The Central Role of Knowledge Distillation for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a foundational technique for compressing large models into efficient, deployable students while preserving much of teacher performance. KD is effective across modalities (graphs, vision, speech, and NLP), supports privacy- and communication-constrained settings, can work without original training data, and admits algorithmic and theoretical refinements that improve robustness, interpretability, and efficiency. Combining representation-level objectives, adversarial or data-free sample generation, and task-aware layer mapping yields practical recipes for real-world compression and adaptation.

papers_seen.author: House
papers_seen.title: The Centrality of Knowledge Distillation for Practical Deep and NLP Models
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques are indispensable for moving state-of-the-art deep models from research to real-world deployment. By transferring predictive behavior, representations, or relational structure from larger or specialized teachers to smaller students, KD enables faster inference, smaller footprints, better generalization across domains, privacy-preserving sharing, and adaptation to heterogeneous hardware and data constraints. Realizing these benefits in practice requires combining algorithmic advances (multi-teacher regimes, curriculum and projector design, augmentation and adversarial synthesis), systems thinking (federated and client-inclusive protocols), and attention to pitfalls (mismatched objectives, erased class relations). Together, the literature shows KD is not a niche trick but a broad, flexible toolkit for addressing latency, capacity, distribution shift, privacy, and interpretability in deep learning and NLP.

papers_seen.author: Walls
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related compression techniques have been adapted across modalities (vision, language, graphs, and generative models) to produce smaller, faster, or more robust models while attempting to retain performance of larger teachers. Approaches vary in what is transferred (soft logits, intermediate features, relational information, or structural/topological properties), how transfer is scheduled or weighted (confidence-aware, progressive replacement, or multi-teacher aggregation), and how distillation is combined with other compression methods (pruning, architecture search, or compact operator substitution). Empirical work shows strong practical benefits—improved runtime, memory, and sometimes robustness or fairness—while theoretical and analytical work begins to explain when and why distillation helps (e.g., role of soft targets, label smoothing analogies, and behavior with imperfect teachers). Remaining challenges include transferring rare-word or low-frequency information in sequence tasks, preserving relational/global structure in graph and link tasks, adapting to evolving domains, and automating generator compression for GANs. This synthesis summarizes key methods, insights, and open directions from recent literature.

papers_seen.author: Joyce
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Theory, and Applications
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related compression techniques have become central for deploying large deep models in latency- and resource-constrained settings. Across modalities and tasks, a consistent pattern is that distilled students can recover much of teacher performance when distillation addresses mismatches in architecture, data distribution, and input representations. Practical advances include multi-teacher and ensemble distillation, online and distributed distillation, data-free and zero-shot approaches, layer-wise and many-to-many layer mappings, task-aware selection of distilled information, and distillation formulations tailored to domain adaptation and federated settings. Theoretical and empirical analyses point to KD acting both as knowledge transfer and as a form of regularization; performance depends strongly on teacher quality, student capacity, data augmentation, and instance-level selection of teacher signals. Remaining challenges include robust distillation under data heterogeneity, principled teacher selection, and aligning intermediate representations across heterogeneous detectors or modalities.

papers_seen.author: Mckay
papers_seen.title: MixKD: Towards Efficient Distillation of Large-scale Language Models
papers_seen.abstract: Large-scale language models have recently demonstrated impressive empirical performance. Nevertheless, the improved results are attained at the price of bigger models, more power consumption, and slower inference, which hinder their applicability to low-resource (both memory and computation) platforms. Knowledge distillation (KD) has been demonstrated as an effective framework for compressing such big models. However, large-scale neural network systems are prone to memorize training instances, and thus tend to make inconsistent predictions when the data distribution is altered slightly. Moreover, the student model has few opportunities to request useful information from the teacher model when there is limited task-specific data available. To address these issues, we propose MixKD, a data-agnostic distillation framework that leverages mixup, a simple yet efficient data augmentation approach, to endow the resulting model with stronger generalization ability. Concretely, in addition to the original training examples, the student model is encouraged to mimic the teacher's behavior on the linear interpolation of example pairs as well. We prove from a theoretical perspective that under reasonable conditions MixKD gives rise to a smaller gap between the generalization error and the empirical error. To verify its effectiveness, we conduct experiments on the GLUE benchmark, where MixKD consistently leads to significant gains over the standard KD training, and outperforms several competitive baselines. Experiments under a limited-data setting and ablation studies further demonstrate the advantages of the proposed approach.

papers_seen.author: Rocha
papers_seen.title: Few Shot Network Compression via Cross Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Model compression has been widely adopted to obtain light-weighted deep neural networks. Most prevalent methods, however, require fine-tuning with sufficient training data to ensure accuracy, which could be challenged by privacy and security issues. As a compromise between privacy and performance, in this paper we investigate few shot network compression: given few samples per class, how can we effectively compress the network with negligible performance drop? The core challenge of few shot network compression lies in high estimation errors from the original network during inference, since the compressed network can easily over-fits on the few training instances. The estimation errors could propagate and accumulate layer-wisely and finally deteriorate the network output. To address the problem, we propose cross distillation, a novel layer-wise knowledge distillation approach. By interweaving hidden layers of teacher and student network, layer-wisely accumulated estimation errors can be effectively reduced.The proposed method offers a general framework compatible with prevalent network compression techniques such as pruning. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that cross distillation can significantly improve the student network's accuracy when only a few training instances are available.

papers_seen.author: Mayo
papers_seen.title: Rethinking Soft Labels for Knowledge Distillation: A Bias-Variance Tradeoff Perspective
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is an effective approach to leverage a well-trained network or an ensemble of them, named as the teacher, to guide the training of a student network. The outputs from the teacher network are used as soft labels for supervising the training of a new network. Recent studies \citep{muller2019does,yuan2020revisiting} revealed an intriguing property of the soft labels that making labels soft serves as a good regularization to the student network. From the perspective of statistical learning, regularization aims to reduce the variance, however how bias and variance change is not clear for training with soft labels. In this paper, we investigate the bias-variance tradeoff brought by distillation with soft labels. Specifically, we observe that during training the bias-variance tradeoff varies sample-wisely. Further, under the same distillation temperature setting, we observe that the distillation performance is negatively associated with the number of some specific samples, which are named as regularization samples since these samples lead to bias increasing and variance decreasing. Nevertheless, we empirically find that completely filtering out regularization samples also deteriorates distillation performance. Our discoveries inspired us to propose the novel weighted soft labels to help the network adaptively handle the sample-wise bias-variance tradeoff. Experiments on standard evaluation benchmarks validate the effectiveness of our method. Our code is available at \url{https://github.com/bellymonster/Weighted-Soft-Label-Distillation}.

papers_seen.author: Foster
papers_seen.title: Ensemble Knowledge Distillation for CTR Prediction
papers_seen.abstract: Recently, deep learning-based models have been widely studied for click-through rate (CTR) prediction and lead to improved prediction accuracy in many industrial applications. However, current research focuses primarily on building complex network architectures to better capture sophisticated feature interactions and dynamic user behaviors. The increased model complexity may slow down online inference and hinder its adoption in real-time applications. Instead, our work targets at a new model training strategy based on knowledge distillation (KD). KD is a teacher-student learning framework to transfer knowledge learned from a teacher model to a student model. The KD strategy not only allows us to simplify the student model as a vanilla DNN model but also achieves significant accuracy improvements over the state-of-the-art teacher models. The benefits thus motivate us to further explore the use of a powerful ensemble of teachers for more accurate student model training. We also propose some novel techniques to facilitate ensembled CTR prediction, including teacher gating and early stopping by distillation loss. We conduct comprehensive experiments against 12 existing models and across three industrial datasets. Both offline and online A/B testing results show the effectiveness of our KD-based training strategy.

papers_seen.author: Brown
papers_seen.title: The Strengths, Limits, and Best Practices of Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable technique for compressing large models into smaller, faster, or more interpretable students across vision, language, graph, and multimodal domains. KD can be combined with pruning, quantization, architecture search, and progressive replacement to yield compact models that preserve much of teacher performance, but its effectiveness depends on dataset complexity, teacher quality, and the choice of what and how to transfer. Addressing pitfalls such as harmful teacher supervision on particular samples, degraded signals for low-frequency outputs, data unavailability, privacy concerns, and fairness requires targeted strategies (selective distillation, adapted teachers, self-distillation, generative replay, or tailored objectives).

papers_seen.author: Kim
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Multifaceted Strategy for Model Compression, Adaptation and Privacy
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is more than a single recipe for shrinking large models: it is a flexible family of techniques that enables accurate, efficient and deployable models across modalities and tasks. KD can compress huge pretrained language and vision models into lightweight architectures with large speed and memory gains while retaining most of the teacher performance. It also supports variant protocols—online, self-distillation, multi-teacher, representation-level and contrastive forms—that trade off efficiency, robustness, and generalization. Beyond raw compression, KD can enable domain adaptation, privacy-preserving model release, and fairness-aware training when combined with appropriate design choices. However, KD is not a panacea: teacher quality, data heterogeneity, and mismatch between teacher and student inputs/architectures can limit gains and must be addressed by specific strategies such as multi-teacher ensembles, confidence weighting, input alignment, or theoretical safeguards.

papers_seen.author: Brown
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Practices in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model-compression techniques have become central tools for deploying large deep models in resource-constrained settings. Across modalities and tasks, distillation is used to transfer predictive behavior or internal representations from larger, more accurate teachers to smaller, faster students; it also appears within automated model search, pruning and distributed training workflows. Work in this area spans logit matching, representation-level objectives, data-free and few-shot regimes, multi-/online-teacher schemes, and task- or architecture-aware compression. Empirical results demonstrate that carefully designed distillation strategies can yield compact models that approach teacher accuracy while enabling large reductions in memory and compute, but limitations remain around optimization, data availability, and the preservation or mitigation of undesirable biases.

papers_seen.author: Silva
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large models into smaller, faster models by transferring information from a teacher to a student. Approaches vary from matching output soft-labels to imitating internal representations, attention maps, or relational structure. Distillation has been applied across modalities and tasks — NLP, vision, detection, generation, ranking, CTR prediction, graph learning, reinforcement learning and federated settings — and can be combined with architecture search and task- or domain-adaptation to produce compact models that preserve much of the teacher’s performance while reducing latency, memory and compute. Practical constraints such as unavailable training data, mismatched inputs or architectures, privacy requirements, and distribution shift motivate specialized techniques including data-free distillation, student-friendly teacher training, adversarial sample generation, many-to-many layer mapping, and generative replay. Empirical results show substantial size and speed gains with modest degradation in performance in many settings, but trade-offs remain and several directions for more robust, automated and privacy-aware distillation remain active.

papers_seen.author: Shaw
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Insights, and Applications
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model compression techniques reduce the size and computational cost of large deep models while retaining much of their performance. Across classification, sequence modeling, generation, and structured prediction, researchers have developed soft-label distillation, intermediate-feature guidance, adversarial and contrastive objectives, projector and embedding modules, and privacy-aware mechanisms to transfer knowledge from large teacher models to smaller students. Empirical and theoretical work highlights trade-offs among bias, variance, teacher quality, and data complexity, and shows that distillation interacts with pre-training, label smoothing, and modality differences. Applications span speech and machine translation to GANs and graph neural networks; complementary methods such as pruning and block-structured compression can further improve deployment on constrained hardware.

papers_seen.author: Chapman
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Approaches and Findings
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a practical and versatile family of techniques for producing smaller, faster, or otherwise specialized models by transferring information from larger or alternative teacher models. KD variants include offline teacher-student distillation, online mutual distillation, ensemble-to-student distillation, cross-task distillation, and teacher-aware or student-aware training. Beyond the canonical logit-matching objective, modern work distills intermediate representations, relational and contrastive structures, and task-specific signals to improve accuracy, robustness, fairness, privacy, generation, and inference latency. Empirical results across computer vision, speech, machine translation, retrieval, graph learning, and routing problems show KD can both compress models without large accuracy loss and improve distilled students in multiple dimensions (robustness, fairness, generalization, and deployment cost). However, distillation is not a panacea: its effectiveness depends on teacher quality and compatibility, the choice of distilled knowledge (logits vs features vs relations), data complexity, and careful training strategies (sample selection, curriculum, annealing, or joint teacher-student learning). This synthesis summarizes methods, motivations, practical techniques, and empirical patterns observed across recent studies.

papers_seen.author: Callahan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical and Versatile Path for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a practical toolkit for compressing large models into smaller, faster models while preserving much of their performance. Across modalities and tasks—classification, detection, generation, retrieval, recommendation, graph learning, and language modeling—KD enables deployment on resource-constrained devices and latency-sensitive pipelines. However, maximizing benefits requires addressing teacher-student capacity gaps, computational cost of teacher supervision, and task-specific information selection; a variety of methodological extensions (multi-teacher schedules, feature/projector design, adversarial or decision-boundary driven samples, layer- and task-aware filtering, self-distillation, and meta-learned teachers) have been developed to meet these needs. When combined appropriately with other compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search), distillation yields state-of-the-art trade-offs for real applications.

papers_seen.author: Adkins
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Approaches, Applications, and Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: This synthesis summarizes methods, extensions, and applications of knowledge distillation and related model compression techniques in deep learning and NLP. It covers teacher-student paradigms (offline and online), multi-teacher and ensemble strategies, layer- and feature-based distillation, data-free and privacy-aware distillation, task-aware and architecture-aware adaptations, theoretical perspectives, and applications beyond classification (e.g., generation, detection, graph learning, and machine reading). The review highlights recurrent practical challenges—capacity mismatch, optimization difficulty, redundant teacher information, data and privacy constraints—and points to promising directions such as task-aware filtering, many-to-many layer mappings, and adversarial/data-free sample generation to enable distillation under limited resources or access.

papers_seen.author: Barnes
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques have become central to making large deep models practical for deployment. Research has explored diverse teacher-student architectures, alternatives to relying on original training data, adaptations to heterogeneous devices and federated settings, methods that transfer intermediate representations (features, relations, attention), adversarial and ensemble strategies, and task- or domain-specific compression. Empirical work across NLP, vision, reinforcement learning, recommendation, graph and 3D detection demonstrates that careful design of the distillation objective, choice of teacher(s), and selection of data (real, synthetic, or none) strongly affect student performance and efficiency. Remaining challenges include handling data heterogeneity, preserving low-frequency or minority information, and designing teacher models that are optimal for transfer. This review synthesizes findings across these directions and highlights practical approaches and open problems.

papers_seen.author: Tucker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Multi-Modal Strategy for Model Compression: Strengths, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a broadly applicable technique for compressing and adapting large neural models into smaller, faster models while retaining much of their performance. Across computer vision, generative modeling, cross-modal systems, and NLP, distillation can be combined with complementary methods (pre-training, pruning, quantization, adversarial training, and feature alignment) to meet deployment constraints and domain requirements. Success depends on teacher design, the availability and nature of data used for transfer, careful alignment of representations, and training objectives that address optimization challenges.

papers_seen.author: Sanchez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques are widely used to transfer behavior from larger, high-capacity teacher models to smaller, deployable student models. Work across vision, generative modeling, reinforcement learning, recommendation, and language has developed diverse objectives and mechanisms — soft-label matching, internal-representation matching, adversarial synthesis of training data, multi-teacher/ensemble supervision, layer-wise and task-adaptive compression, and data-augmentation-enhanced distillation. These approaches trade off accuracy, inference cost, and robustness and address practical constraints such as lack of access to original training data, domain shift, fairness, and heterogeneous model architectures. Empirical results show distilled students can approach or sometimes match teacher performance while substantially reducing FLOPs, parameters, or latency, but limitations remain in data heterogeneity, low-frequency token transfer, and privacy-constrained settings. This synthesis summarizes methods, empirical findings, applications, and open challenges documented in the provided literature.

papers_seen.author: Ellis
papers_seen.title: On Representation Knowledge Distillation for Graph Neural Networks
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a learning paradigm for boosting resource-efficient graph neural networks (GNNs) using more expressive yet cumbersome teacher models. Past work on distillation for GNNs proposed the Local Structure Preserving loss (LSP), which matches local structural relationships defined over edges across the student and teacher's node embeddings. This paper studies whether preserving the global topology of how the teacher embeds graph data can be a more effective distillation objective for GNNs, as real-world graphs often contain latent interactions and noisy edges. We propose Graph Contrastive Representation Distillation (G-CRD), which uses contrastive learning to implicitly preserve global topology by aligning the student node embeddings to those of the teacher in a shared representation space. Additionally, we introduce an expanded set of benchmarks on large-scale real-world datasets where the performance gap between teacher and student GNNs is non-negligible. Experiments across 4 datasets and 14 heterogeneous GNN architectures show that G-CRD consistently boosts the performance and robustness of lightweight GNNs, outperforming LSP (and a global structure preserving variant of LSP) as well as baselines from 2D computer vision. An analysis of the representational similarity among teacher and student embedding spaces reveals that G-CRD balances preserving local and global relationships, while structure preserving approaches are best at preserving one or the other. Our code is available at https://github.com/chaitjo/efficient-gnns

papers_seen.author: Cannon
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression strategies have become central to deploying large neural networks in resource-constrained settings. Across vision, multimodal, and language domains, researchers have developed approaches that transfer information from larger teacher models to smaller students via logits, intermediate representations, attention maps, or adversarial objectives. Work spans supervised and unsupervised settings, data-free or black-box scenarios, continual and federated use-cases, and concerns such as privacy and adversarial robustness. Practical recipes combine distillation with pruning, structured sparsity, progressive module replacement, and many-to-many layer mapping to balance accuracy, latency, and memory. Open challenges remain in data- and domain-limited regimes, robust and private compression, and principled selection of which teacher knowledge to transfer for a given downstream task.

papers_seen.author: Diaz
papers_seen.title: Model Compression with Two-stage Multi-teacher Knowledge Distillation for Web Question Answering System
papers_seen.abstract: Deep pre-training and fine-tuning models (such as BERT and OpenAI GPT) have demonstrated excellent results in question answering areas. However, due to the sheer amount of model parameters, the inference speed of these models is very slow. How to apply these complex models to real business scenarios becomes a challenging but practical problem. Previous model compression methods usually suffer from information loss during the model compression procedure, leading to inferior models compared with the original one. To tackle this challenge, we propose a Two-stage Multi-teacher Knowledge Distillation (TMKD for short) method for web Question Answering system. We first develop a general Q\&A distillation task for student model pre-training, and further fine-tune this pre-trained student model with multi-teacher knowledge distillation on downstream tasks (like Web Q\&A task, MNLI, SNLI, RTE tasks from GLUE), which effectively reduces the overfitting bias in individual teacher models, and transfers more general knowledge to the student model. The experiment results show that our method can significantly outperform the baseline methods and even achieve comparable results with the original teacher models, along with substantial speedup of model inference.

papers_seen.author: Stewart
papers_seen.title: Private Model Compression via Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: The soaring demand for intelligent mobile applications calls for deploying powerful deep neural networks (DNNs) on mobile devices. However, the outstanding performance of DNNs notoriously relies on increasingly complex models, which in turn is associated with an increase in computational expense far surpassing mobile devices' capacity. What is worse, app service providers need to collect and utilize a large volume of users' data, which contain sensitive information, to build the sophisticated DNN models. Directly deploying these models on public mobile devices presents prohibitive privacy risk. To benefit from the on-device deep learning without the capacity and privacy concerns, we design a private model compression framework RONA. Following the knowledge distillation paradigm, we jointly use hint learning, distillation learning, and self learning to train a compact and fast neural network. The knowledge distilled from the cumbersome model is adaptively bounded and carefully perturbed to enforce differential privacy. We further propose an elegant query sample selection method to reduce the number of queries and control the privacy loss. A series of empirical evaluations as well as the implementation on an Android mobile device show that RONA can not only compress cumbersome models efficiently but also provide a strong privacy guarantee. For example, on SVHN, when a meaningful $(9.83,10^{-6})$-differential privacy is guaranteed, the compact model trained by RONA can obtain 20$\times$ compression ratio and 19$\times$ speed-up with merely 0.97% accuracy loss.

papers_seen.author: Holmes
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques are widely used to produce smaller, faster models while preserving much of the performance of large teachers. Approaches vary from matching final logits to transferring internal representations, attention maps, or layer-wise information, and they are applied across modalities including NLP, vision, speech, and reinforcement learning. Practical extensions address multi-teacher setups, data-free scenarios, domain adaptation, quantization, and architecture-aware compression; remaining challenges include handling heterogeneous architectures, data heterogeneity, fairness, and reliably preserving inductive biases.

papers_seen.author: Herrera
papers_seen.title: Compressing GANs using Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have been used in several machine learning tasks such as domain transfer, super resolution, and synthetic data generation. State-of-the-art GANs often use tens of millions of parameters, making them expensive to deploy for applications in low SWAP (size, weight, and power) hardware, such as mobile devices, and for applications with real time capabilities. There has been no work found to reduce the number of parameters used in GANs. Therefore, we propose a method to compress GANs using knowledge distillation techniques, in which a smaller "student" GAN learns to mimic a larger "teacher" GAN. We show that the distillation methods used on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and Celeb-A datasets can compress teacher GANs at ratios of 1669:1, 58:1, and 87:1, respectively, while retaining the quality of the generated image. From our experiments, we observe a qualitative limit for GAN's compression. Moreover, we observe that, with a fixed parameter budget, compressed GANs outperform GANs trained using standard training methods. We conjecture that this is partially owing to the optimization landscape of over-parameterized GANs which allows efficient training using alternating gradient descent. Thus, training an over-parameterized GAN followed by our proposed compression scheme provides a high quality generative model with a small number of parameters.

papers_seen.author: Powell
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central Tool for Model Compression and Transfer: Strengths, Limits, and Practical Directions
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a versatile set of techniques that enable model compression, domain- and task-level transfer, privacy-preserving distillation, and improvements in interpretability and fairness. Empirical and methodological work shows KD can compress large models into efficient students, transfer inductive biases, support multi-task and lifelong learning, and enable data-free or zero-shot distillation when training data are unavailable. At the same time, KD faces concrete limitations due to data heterogeneity, teacher-student capacity mismatch, and the need to select or synthesize appropriate supervision; hybrid solutions that combine feature-level matching, adversarial sample synthesis, curriculum strategies, and architectural compression achieve the best practical results. Based on evidence across domains (vision, language, graphs, retrieval, reinforcement learning), we argue that KD should be used as part of an integrated compression pipeline that is task-aware, data-aware, and often combined with pruning, layer skipping, or module replacement to meet deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Nunez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Foundational Tool for Model Compression and Beyond
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation has matured from a technique for compressing large models into smaller, faster ones into a broad set of methods that address efficiency, domain adaptation, privacy, robustness, fairness, and cross-modal transfer. By moving beyond simple logits matching to layer- and feature-level alignment, multi-teacher schemes, data-free and few-shot settings, and meta-learned teachers, distillation can both preserve performance and add functional guarantees (e.g., robustness, fairness) that are crucial for real-world deployment. This paper argues that knowledge distillation should be considered a foundational component of model compression pipelines and of strategies for adapting large pre-trained models to constrained, specialized, or sensitive applications.

papers_seen.author: Moore
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression: Powerful, Versatile, but Context-Dependent
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a core technique for compressing large models and transferring their knowledge into smaller, faster models for deployment in resource-constrained settings and domain-specific applications. Advances in layer- and feature-level transfer, many-to-many layer mapping, data- and augmentation-aware practices, and federated or privacy-sensitive adaptations have expanded KD's applicability across vision, NLP, and graph domains. However, KD is not a universal remedy: it can propagate teacher errors, struggle under data heterogeneity, and depend critically on teacher quality, data choices, and optimization design. Best outcomes follow when practitioners combine KD with complementary techniques (careful layer matching, feature mimicking, data selection/augmentation, and pruning or quantization) and explicitly address heterogeneity and teacher reliability.

papers_seen.author: Moore
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central Tool for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a practical and versatile approach to compressing large models for deployment and domain-specific use. Across modalities and tasks, KD can preserve much of the teacher's performance in compact students, but it must be combined with task-aware engineering—such as teacher adaptation, layer-wise selection, data augmentation, and hardware-aware pruning—to address heterogeneity, domain shift, and efficiency constraints. This article argues that KD is necessary but not sufficient: best results come from integrating KD with complementary techniques chosen for the target modality, deployment constraints, and learning scenario.

papers_seen.author: Fowler
papers_seen.title: SEED: Self-supervised Distillation For Visual Representation
papers_seen.abstract: This paper is concerned with self-supervised learning for small models. The problem is motivated by our empirical studies that while the widely used contrastive self-supervised learning method has shown great progress on large model training, it does not work well for small models. To address this problem, we propose a new learning paradigm, named SElf-SupErvised Distillation (SEED), where we leverage a larger network (as Teacher) to transfer its representational knowledge into a smaller architecture (as Student) in a self-supervised fashion. Instead of directly learning from unlabeled data, we train a student encoder to mimic the similarity score distribution inferred by a teacher over a set of instances. We show that SEED dramatically boosts the performance of small networks on downstream tasks. Compared with self-supervised baselines, SEED improves the top-1 accuracy from 42.2% to 67.6% on EfficientNet-B0 and from 36.3% to 68.2% on MobileNet-v3-Large on the ImageNet-1k dataset.

papers_seen.author: Wright
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques have matured into a diverse set of methods for transferring information from larger or more expensive models to smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained models. Methods span from classic logit-based distillation to feature- and representation-level matching, adversarial and projector-based strategies, module-replacement and pruning approaches, and specialized protocols for cross-modal, federated, data-free, and generative settings. Applications range across NLP (BERT compression, machine translation, non-autoregressive models), speech and paralinguistic embeddings, vision (image translation, novel-view synthesis), 3D detection, recommender systems, and graph neural networks. Research highlights include analyses that explain why distillation works, techniques that mitigate transfer of teacher errors, curricula and selection mechanisms for better sample usage, and approaches that adapt distillation to privacy- or resource-constrained environments. Together, these works map an ecosystem of practical techniques and open challenges for deploying compact, high-performing models in real-world systems.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: Adapt-and-Distill: Developing Small, Fast and Effective Pretrained Language Models for Domains
papers_seen.abstract: Large pre-trained models have achieved great success in many natural language processing tasks. However, when they are applied in specific domains, these models suffer from domain shift and bring challenges in fine-tuning and online serving for latency and capacity constraints. In this paper, we present a general approach to developing small, fast and effective pre-trained models for specific domains. This is achieved by adapting the off-the-shelf general pre-trained models and performing task-agnostic knowledge distillation in target domains. Specifically, we propose domain-specific vocabulary expansion in the adaptation stage and employ corpus level occurrence probability to choose the size of incremental vocabulary automatically. Then we systematically explore different strategies to compress the large pre-trained models for specific domains. We conduct our experiments in the biomedical and computer science domain. The experimental results demonstrate that our approach achieves better performance over the BERT BASE model in domain-specific tasks while 3.3x smaller and 5.1x faster than BERT BASE. The code and pre-trained models are available at https://aka.ms/adalm.

papers_seen.author: Bowers
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques are widely used to reduce the resource footprint of large neural networks while preserving performance. The literature surveys a range of approaches — from vanilla teacher-student soft-target transfers to layer-wise, attention- and channel-wise methods, multi-teacher and online schemes, data-free and privacy-preserving variants, and combinations with pruning and adversarial training — and demonstrates successful applications across NLP, speech, vision, graph, and multimodal problems. Empirical results show effective speedups and parameter reductions with modest accuracy loss; theoretical and empirical analyses also connect KD to label-smoothing and regularization effects that can improve generalization.

papers_seen.author: Allen
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Flexible Path to Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, practically effective family of techniques for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster, and often more socially or operationally suitable models. Across vision, speech, and NLP tasks KD has been shown to preserve much of teacher performance while enabling deployment on constrained hardware and in privacy-sensitive or distributed settings. KD is most effective when combined with complementary practices such as pre-training, data augmentation, careful layer-matching, ensemble guidance, and hardware-aware pruning.

papers_seen.author: Bernard
papers_seen.title: Reinforced Multi-Teacher Selection for Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: In natural language processing (NLP) tasks, slow inference speed and huge footprints in GPU usage remain the bottleneck of applying pre-trained deep models in production. As a popular method for model compression, knowledge distillation transfers knowledge from one or multiple large (teacher) models to a small (student) model. When multiple teacher models are available in distillation, the state-of-the-art methods assign a fixed weight to a teacher model in the whole distillation. Furthermore, most of the existing methods allocate an equal weight to every teacher model. In this paper, we observe that, due to the complexity of training examples and the differences in student model capability, learning differentially from teacher models can lead to better performance of student models distilled. We systematically develop a reinforced method to dynamically assign weights to teacher models for different training instances and optimize the performance of student model. Our extensive experimental results on several NLP tasks clearly verify the feasibility and effectiveness of our approach.

papers_seen.author: Diaz
papers_seen.title: Model Compression with Two-stage Multi-teacher Knowledge Distillation for Web Question Answering System
papers_seen.abstract: Deep pre-training and fine-tuning models (such as BERT and OpenAI GPT) have demonstrated excellent results in question answering areas. However, due to the sheer amount of model parameters, the inference speed of these models is very slow. How to apply these complex models to real business scenarios becomes a challenging but practical problem. Previous model compression methods usually suffer from information loss during the model compression procedure, leading to inferior models compared with the original one. To tackle this challenge, we propose a Two-stage Multi-teacher Knowledge Distillation (TMKD for short) method for web Question Answering system. We first develop a general Q\&A distillation task for student model pre-training, and further fine-tune this pre-trained student model with multi-teacher knowledge distillation on downstream tasks (like Web Q\&A task, MNLI, SNLI, RTE tasks from GLUE), which effectively reduces the overfitting bias in individual teacher models, and transfers more general knowledge to the student model. The experiment results show that our method can significantly outperform the baseline methods and even achieve comparable results with the original teacher models, along with substantial speedup of model inference.

papers_seen.author: Parker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Approaches and Findings
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a broad family of techniques for compressing large or expensive models into smaller, faster, or more deployable ones by transferring information from a teacher to a student. Methods differ in the form of transferred knowledge (soft logits, hidden features, contrastive distributions, synthetic data, or cross-modal alignments), in how and when distillation is applied (offline, online, layer-wise, task-adaptive, or data-free), and in the problems they target (classification, detection, generation, language tasks, graph learning, or novel-view synthesis). Empirical work demonstrates that appropriate choices about teacher signals, data manipulation, and architectural search can yield compact models that retain much of teacher performance across modalities; theoretical work begins to clarify when soft labels help and when hard labels or mixed supervision are needed. Remaining challenges include optimization gaps between teacher and student, dataset and fairness concerns, and scaling distillation reliably in large distributed settings.

papers_seen.author: Jones
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and model compression have become central strategies for deploying large deep models under resource, latency, and privacy constraints. A diverse set of methods—ranging from soft-label distillation, intermediate feature and attention matching, layer mapping, adversarial and data-free techniques, to task-adaptive architecture search and meta-learning of teachers—have been proposed to transfer performance from bulky teachers to compact students. These approaches are applied across domains including vision, language, multi-modal systems, recommender systems, and domain-specific NLP, and they trade off fidelity to the teacher, generalization, and computational efficiency. Empirical results show that properly designed distillation pipelines can recover a large fraction of teacher performance while yielding substantial speedups and memory reductions, and in some settings can even improve fairness, robustness, or downstream generalization. Remaining challenges include aligning heterogeneous inputs and representations across teacher and student, coping with absent or private training data, and automatically selecting what and how to transfer for specific tasks and deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: AutoGAN-Distiller: Searching to Compress Generative Adversarial Networks
papers_seen.abstract: The compression of Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) has lately drawn attention, due to the increasing demand for deploying GANs into mobile devices for numerous applications such as image translation, enhancement and editing. However, compared to the substantial efforts to compressing other deep models, the research on compressing GANs (usually the generators) remains at its infancy stage. Existing GAN compression algorithms are limited to handling specific GAN architectures and losses. Inspired by the recent success of AutoML in deep compression, we introduce AutoML to GAN compression and develop an AutoGAN-Distiller (AGD) framework. Starting with a specifically designed efficient search space, AGD performs an end-to-end discovery for new efficient generators, given the target computational resource constraints. The search is guided by the original GAN model via knowledge distillation, therefore fulfilling the compression. AGD is fully automatic, standalone (i.e., needing no trained discriminators), and generically applicable to various GAN models. We evaluate AGD in two representative GAN tasks: image translation and super resolution. Without bells and whistles, AGD yields remarkably lightweight yet more competitive compressed models, that largely outperform existing alternatives. Our codes and pretrained models are available at https://github.com/TAMU-VITA/AGD.

papers_seen.author: Cameron
papers_seen.title: Well-Read Students Learn Better: On the Importance of Pre-training Compact Models
papers_seen.abstract: Recent developments in natural language representations have been accompanied by large and expensive models that leverage vast amounts of general-domain text through self-supervised pre-training. Due to the cost of applying such models to down-stream tasks, several model compression techniques on pre-trained language representations have been proposed (Sun et al., 2019; Sanh, 2019). However, surprisingly, the simple baseline of just pre-training and fine-tuning compact models has been overlooked. In this paper, we first show that pre-training remains important in the context of smaller architectures, and fine-tuning pre-trained compact models can be competitive to more elaborate methods proposed in concurrent work. Starting with pre-trained compact models, we then explore transferring task knowledge from large fine-tuned models through standard knowledge distillation. The resulting simple, yet effective and general algorithm, Pre-trained Distillation, brings further improvements. Through extensive experiments, we more generally explore the interaction between pre-training and distillation under two variables that have been under-studied: model size and properties of unlabeled task data. One surprising observation is that they have a compound effect even when sequentially applied on the same data. To accelerate future research, we will make our 24 pre-trained miniature BERT models publicly available.

papers_seen.author: Brown
papers_seen.title: Unified Visual Transformer Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Vision transformers (ViTs) have gained popularity recently. Even without customized image operators such as convolutions, ViTs can yield competitive performance when properly trained on massive data. However, the computational overhead of ViTs remains prohibitive, due to stacking multi-head self-attention modules and else. Compared to the vast literature and prevailing success in compressing convolutional neural networks, the study of Vision Transformer compression has also just emerged, and existing works focused on one or two aspects of compression. This paper proposes a unified ViT compression framework that seamlessly assembles three effective techniques: pruning, layer skipping, and knowledge distillation. We formulate a budget-constrained, end-to-end optimization framework, targeting jointly learning model weights, layer-wise pruning ratios/masks, and skip configurations, under a distillation loss. The optimization problem is then solved using the primal-dual algorithm. Experiments are conducted with several ViT variants, e.g. DeiT and T2T-ViT backbones on the ImageNet dataset, and our approach consistently outperforms recent competitors. For example, DeiT-Tiny can be trimmed down to 50\% of the original FLOPs almost without losing accuracy. Codes are available online:~\url{https://github.com/VITA-Group/UVC}.

papers_seen.author: Walker
papers_seen.title: BERT Learns to Teach: Knowledge Distillation with Meta Learning
papers_seen.abstract: We present Knowledge Distillation with Meta Learning (MetaDistil), a simple yet effective alternative to traditional knowledge distillation (KD) methods where the teacher model is fixed during training. We show the teacher network can learn to better transfer knowledge to the student network (i.e., learning to teach) with the feedback from the performance of the distilled student network in a meta learning framework. Moreover, we introduce a pilot update mechanism to improve the alignment between the inner-learner and meta-learner in meta learning algorithms that focus on an improved inner-learner. Experiments on various benchmarks show that MetaDistil can yield significant improvements compared with traditional KD algorithms and is less sensitive to the choice of different student capacity and hyperparameters, facilitating the use of KD on different tasks and models.

papers_seen.author: Tucker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Multi-Modal Strategy for Model Compression: Strengths, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a broadly applicable technique for compressing and adapting large neural models into smaller, faster models while retaining much of their performance. Across computer vision, generative modeling, cross-modal systems, and NLP, distillation can be combined with complementary methods (pre-training, pruning, quantization, adversarial training, and feature alignment) to meet deployment constraints and domain requirements. Success depends on teacher design, the availability and nature of data used for transfer, careful alignment of representations, and training objectives that address optimization challenges.

papers_seen.author: Wilson
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad and practical set of techniques for transferring behaviors and representations from larger or otherwise stronger models (teachers) to smaller or more constrained models (students). KD has been adapted across modalities and tasks—classification, generation, retrieval, speech, graph learning, reinforcement and lifelong learning—yielding work on algorithmic variants (self-distillation, multi-teacher, curriculum, adversarial, relational and loss-function innovations), data- and privacy-aware designs, and hardware-aware/low-precision deployments. Empirical work demonstrates KD can substantially reduce model size and latency while preserving much of the teacher performance, but theoretical and optimization limits remain: students often cannot perfectly match teachers and training/data choices matter greatly. Practical advances address these limits through better supervision signals, input-side design (data augmentation), alternate discrepancy measures, and privacy/communication constraints. The field continues to move toward more efficient, fair, private and domain-robust distilled models suitable for real-world deployment.

papers_seen.author: Hawkins
papers_seen.title: A Fast Knowledge Distillation Framework for Visual Recognition
papers_seen.abstract: While Knowledge Distillation (KD) has been recognized as a useful tool in many visual tasks, such as supervised classification and self-supervised representation learning, the main drawback of a vanilla KD framework is its mechanism, which consumes the majority of the computational overhead on forwarding through the giant teacher networks, making the entire learning procedure inefficient and costly. ReLabel, a recently proposed solution, suggests creating a label map for the entire image. During training, it receives the cropped region-level label by RoI aligning on a pre-generated entire label map, allowing for efficient supervision generation without having to pass through the teachers many times. However, as the KD teachers are from conventional multi-crop training, there are various mismatches between the global label-map and region-level label in this technique, resulting in performance deterioration. In this study, we present a Fast Knowledge Distillation (FKD) framework that replicates the distillation training phase and generates soft labels using the multi-crop KD approach, while training faster than ReLabel since no post-processes such as RoI align and softmax operations are used. When conducting multi-crop in the same image for data loading, our FKD is even more efficient than the traditional image classification framework. On ImageNet-1K, we obtain 79.8% with ResNet-50, outperforming ReLabel by ~1.0% while being faster. On the self-supervised learning task, we also show that FKD has an efficiency advantage. Our project page: http://zhiqiangshen.com/projects/FKD/index.html, source code and models are available at: https://github.com/szq0214/FKD.

papers_seen.author: Callahan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical and Versatile Path for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a practical toolkit for compressing large models into smaller, faster models while preserving much of their performance. Across modalities and tasks—classification, detection, generation, retrieval, recommendation, graph learning, and language modeling—KD enables deployment on resource-constrained devices and latency-sensitive pipelines. However, maximizing benefits requires addressing teacher-student capacity gaps, computational cost of teacher supervision, and task-specific information selection; a variety of methodological extensions (multi-teacher schedules, feature/projector design, adversarial or decision-boundary driven samples, layer- and task-aware filtering, self-distillation, and meta-learned teachers) have been developed to meet these needs. When combined appropriately with other compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search), distillation yields state-of-the-art trade-offs for real applications.

papers_seen.author: Arnold
papers_seen.title: Does Knowledge Distillation Really Work?
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a popular technique for training a small student network to emulate a larger teacher model, such as an ensemble of networks. We show that while knowledge distillation can improve student generalization, it does not typically work as it is commonly understood: there often remains a surprisingly large discrepancy between the predictive distributions of the teacher and the student, even in cases when the student has the capacity to perfectly match the teacher. We identify difficulties in optimization as a key reason for why the student is unable to match the teacher. We also show how the details of the dataset used for distillation play a role in how closely the student matches the teacher -- and that more closely matching the teacher paradoxically does not always lead to better student generalization.

papers_seen.author: Kim
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Multifaceted Strategy for Model Compression, Adaptation and Privacy
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is more than a single recipe for shrinking large models: it is a flexible family of techniques that enables accurate, efficient and deployable models across modalities and tasks. KD can compress huge pretrained language and vision models into lightweight architectures with large speed and memory gains while retaining most of the teacher performance. It also supports variant protocols—online, self-distillation, multi-teacher, representation-level and contrastive forms—that trade off efficiency, robustness, and generalization. Beyond raw compression, KD can enable domain adaptation, privacy-preserving model release, and fairness-aware training when combined with appropriate design choices. However, KD is not a panacea: teacher quality, data heterogeneity, and mismatch between teacher and student inputs/architectures can limit gains and must be addressed by specific strategies such as multi-teacher ensembles, confidence weighting, input alignment, or theoretical safeguards.

papers_seen.author: Baker
papers_seen.title: Rejuvenating Low-Frequency Words: Making the Most of Parallel Data in Non-Autoregressive Translation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is commonly used to construct synthetic data for training non-autoregressive translation (NAT) models. However, there exists a discrepancy on low-frequency words between the distilled and the original data, leading to more errors on predicting low-frequency words. To alleviate the problem, we directly expose the raw data into NAT by leveraging pretraining. By analyzing directed alignments, we found that KD makes low-frequency source words aligned with targets more deterministically but fails to align sufficient low-frequency words from target to source. Accordingly, we propose reverse KD to rejuvenate more alignments for low-frequency target words. To make the most of authentic and synthetic data, we combine these complementary approaches as a new training strategy for further boosting NAT performance. We conduct experiments on five translation benchmarks over two advanced architectures. Results demonstrate that the proposed approach can significantly and universally improve translation quality by reducing translation errors on low-frequency words. Encouragingly, our approach achieves 28.2 and 33.9 BLEU points on the WMT14 English-German and WMT16 Romanian-English datasets, respectively. Our code, data, and trained models are available at \url{https://github.com/alphadl/RLFW-NAT}.

papers_seen.author: Daniel
papers_seen.title: Data-Free Adversarial Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge Distillation (KD) has made remarkable progress in the last few years and become a popular paradigm for model compression and knowledge transfer. However, almost all existing KD algorithms are data-driven, i.e., relying on a large amount of original training data or alternative data, which is usually unavailable in real-world scenarios. In this paper, we devote ourselves to this challenging problem and propose a novel adversarial distillation mechanism to craft a compact student model without any real-world data. We introduce a model discrepancy to quantificationally measure the difference between student and teacher models and construct an optimizable upper bound. In our work, the student and the teacher jointly act the role of the discriminator to reduce this discrepancy, when a generator adversarially produces some "hard samples" to enlarge it. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed data-free method yields comparable performance to existing data-driven methods. More strikingly, our approach can be directly extended to semantic segmentation, which is more complicated than classification, and our approach achieves state-of-the-art results. Code and pretrained models are available at https://github.com/VainF/Data-Free-Adversarial-Distillation.

papers_seen.author: Mills
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, and Practical Insights
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques have matured into a diverse set of methods for transferring information from large, expensive models (or ensembles) to smaller, efficient models. Methods include logit-based distillation, feature- or representation-based matching, self-distillation, multi-teacher strategies, data-free and privacy-preserving approaches, and combinations with pruning or architecture search. KD has been applied across modalities and domains—vision, language, graphs, reinforcement learning, generative models, and healthcare—demonstrating gains in inference efficiency, robustness, generalization, and interpretability when appropriately designed. Open challenges remain around data availability, teacher–student mismatch, selection of distilled signals and samples, and principled integration with other compression techniques; recent work proposes meta-learning teachers, adaptive teacher weighting, projector modules, and task-adaptive compression as practical remedies.

papers_seen.author: Johnson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation in Wide Neural Networks: Risk Bound, Data Efficiency and Imperfect Teacher
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a strategy of training a student network with guide of the soft output from a teacher network. It has been a successful method of model compression and knowledge transfer. However, currently knowledge distillation lacks a convincing theoretical understanding. On the other hand, recent finding on neural tangent kernel enables us to approximate a wide neural network with a linear model of the network's random features. In this paper, we theoretically analyze the knowledge distillation of a wide neural network. First we provide a transfer risk bound for the linearized model of the network. Then we propose a metric of the task's training difficulty, called data inefficiency. Based on this metric, we show that for a perfect teacher, a high ratio of teacher's soft labels can be beneficial. Finally, for the case of imperfect teacher, we find that hard labels can correct teacher's wrong prediction, which explains the practice of mixing hard and soft labels.

papers_seen.author: Stewart
papers_seen.title: Private Model Compression via Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: The soaring demand for intelligent mobile applications calls for deploying powerful deep neural networks (DNNs) on mobile devices. However, the outstanding performance of DNNs notoriously relies on increasingly complex models, which in turn is associated with an increase in computational expense far surpassing mobile devices' capacity. What is worse, app service providers need to collect and utilize a large volume of users' data, which contain sensitive information, to build the sophisticated DNN models. Directly deploying these models on public mobile devices presents prohibitive privacy risk. To benefit from the on-device deep learning without the capacity and privacy concerns, we design a private model compression framework RONA. Following the knowledge distillation paradigm, we jointly use hint learning, distillation learning, and self learning to train a compact and fast neural network. The knowledge distilled from the cumbersome model is adaptively bounded and carefully perturbed to enforce differential privacy. We further propose an elegant query sample selection method to reduce the number of queries and control the privacy loss. A series of empirical evaluations as well as the implementation on an Android mobile device show that RONA can not only compress cumbersome models efficiently but also provide a strong privacy guarantee. For example, on SVHN, when a meaningful $(9.83,10^{-6})$-differential privacy is guaranteed, the compact model trained by RONA can obtain 20$\times$ compression ratio and 19$\times$ speed-up with merely 0.97% accuracy loss.

papers_seen.author: Riley
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Methods and Findings
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a central technique for compressing large neural models and transferring knowledge from high-capacity teachers to compact students across vision, language, multimodal, and generative settings. Research has diversified beyond the original logits-based recipes into feature- and layer-level matching, many-to-many layer mappings, self-supervised distillation, data-free and online KD, task- and domain-adaptive compression, and combinations with architecture search and low-precision inference. Empirical and theoretical work highlights trade-offs involving teacher quality, the role of soft targets as regularizers, and practical constraints such as limited data, privacy, and inference latency. This synthesis summarizes key methods, empirical patterns, and open directions drawn from the provided literature.

papers_seen.author: Hoffman
papers_seen.title: Federated Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Distributed learning frameworks often rely on exchanging model parameters across workers, instead of revealing their raw data. A prime example is federated learning that exchanges the gradients or weights of each neural network model. Under limited communication resources, however, such a method becomes extremely costly particularly for modern deep neural networks having a huge number of model parameters. In this regard, federated distillation (FD) is a compelling distributed learning solution that only exchanges the model outputs whose dimensions are commonly much smaller than the model sizes (e.g., 10 labels in the MNIST dataset). The goal of this chapter is to provide a deep understanding of FD while demonstrating its communication efficiency and applicability to a variety of tasks. To this end, towards demystifying the operational principle of FD, the first part of this chapter provides a novel asymptotic analysis for two foundational algorithms of FD, namely knowledge distillation (KD) and co-distillation (CD), by exploiting the theory of neural tangent kernel (NTK). Next, the second part elaborates on a baseline implementation of FD for a classification task, and illustrates its performance in terms of accuracy and communication efficiency compared to FL. Lastly, to demonstrate the applicability of FD to various distributed learning tasks and environments, the third part presents two selected applications, namely FD over asymmetric uplink-and-downlink wireless channels and FD for reinforcement learning.

papers_seen.author: Lewis
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central Paradigm for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, practical, and theoretically grounded approach to compressing and adapting deep models. Across modalities and tasks, KD enables compact students to inherit predictive performance, inductive biases, and application-specific properties (privacy, fairness, task-adaptivity) from larger or specialized teachers. Best practice combines logit-level, feature-level, and architecture-aware strategies, often augmented by multi-teacher, curriculum, or meta-learning schemes; privacy-preserving and data-free variants make KD suitable for sensitive or decentralized settings. We argue that KD should be a first-class tool in compression toolkits and outline concrete practices that are supported by empirical and theoretical work.

papers_seen.author: Alvarez
papers_seen.title: The Central Role of Knowledge Distillation for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a foundational technique for compressing large models into efficient, deployable students while preserving much of teacher performance. KD is effective across modalities (graphs, vision, speech, and NLP), supports privacy- and communication-constrained settings, can work without original training data, and admits algorithmic and theoretical refinements that improve robustness, interpretability, and efficiency. Combining representation-level objectives, adversarial or data-free sample generation, and task-aware layer mapping yields practical recipes for real-world compression and adaptation.
