papers_seen.author: Nguyen
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Small-footprint Highway Networks
papers_seen.abstract: Deep learning has significantly advanced state-of-the-art of speech recognition in the past few years. However, compared to conventional Gaussian mixture acoustic models, neural network models are usually much larger, and are therefore not very deployable in embedded devices. Previously, we investigated a compact highway deep neural network (HDNN) for acoustic modelling, which is a type of depth-gated feedforward neural network. We have shown that HDNN-based acoustic models can achieve comparable recognition accuracy with much smaller number of model parameters compared to plain deep neural network (DNN) acoustic models. In this paper, we push the boundary further by leveraging on the knowledge distillation technique that is also known as {\it teacher-student} training, i.e., we train the compact HDNN model with the supervision of a high accuracy cumbersome model. Furthermore, we also investigate sequence training and adaptation in the context of teacher-student training. Our experiments were performed on the AMI meeting speech recognition corpus. With this technique, we significantly improved the recognition accuracy of the HDNN acoustic model with less than 0.8 million parameters, and narrowed the gap between this model and the plain DNN with 30 million parameters.

papers_seen.author: Morgan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Challenges, and Practical Strategies
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques seek to transfer knowledge from larger or more expensive models (teachers) to smaller, faster, or more interpretable students. Over the past decade these approaches have been adapted across modalities and tasks — from image classification and object detection to sequence models and large pretrained language models — and have been combined with complementary compression methods such as pruning and low-precision quantization. Empirical and theoretical work has highlighted both the practical gains of distillation (improved student generalization, reduced latency and memory, enabling deployment) and key limitations (optimization gaps, distribution mismatch, loss of certain types of information). A range of innovations — feature- and attention-based matching, layer-wise/task-aware distillation, self-distillation, data-free distillation with generative replay, teacher adaptation, and weighted/importance-aware soft labels — have been proposed to close these gaps and extend KD to settings such as domain adaptation, privacy-preserving federated learning, cross-modal transfer, and low-resource devices.

papers_seen.author: Pierce
papers_seen.title: Survey of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP (Selected 2017–2022 Literature)
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model-compression techniques have become central tools for producing compact, efficient models from larger teachers across vision, language, and multimodal tasks. Methods include soft-label distillation, feature- and representation-level matching, adversarial and ensemble-based transfer, data-free or privacy-aware distillation, curriculum and selective-sample strategies, and task-adaptive architecture search. These approaches target deployment constraints (latency, memory, on-device compute), data-availability and privacy limitations, robustness, and domain-continuity, and have been adapted to detectors, generative models, retrieval systems, federated settings, and pre-trained language models. Empirical work demonstrates that careful choice of what to transfer (logits, internal features, relational/contrastive signals) and when/how to train (online, teacher-free, curriculum, few-shot) materially affects student performance and robustness. Open challenges include heterogeneity of data and architectures in distributed settings, theoretical understanding of what aspects of teacher knowledge are most valuable across tasks, and extending distillation to privacy- and domain-constrained deployments.

papers_seen.author: Ramirez
papers_seen.title: Self-Knowledge Distillation with Progressive Refinement of Targets
papers_seen.abstract: The generalization capability of deep neural networks has been substantially improved by applying a wide spectrum of regularization methods, e.g., restricting function space, injecting randomness during training, augmenting data, etc. In this work, we propose a simple yet effective regularization method named progressive self-knowledge distillation (PS-KD), which progressively distills a model's own knowledge to soften hard targets (i.e., one-hot vectors) during training. Hence, it can be interpreted within a framework of knowledge distillation as a student becomes a teacher itself. Specifically, targets are adjusted adaptively by combining the ground-truth and past predictions from the model itself. We show that PS-KD provides an effect of hard example mining by rescaling gradients according to difficulty in classifying examples. The proposed method is applicable to any supervised learning tasks with hard targets and can be easily combined with existing regularization methods to further enhance the generalization performance. Furthermore, it is confirmed that PS-KD achieves not only better accuracy, but also provides high quality of confidence estimates in terms of calibration as well as ordinal ranking. Extensive experimental results on three different tasks, image classification, object detection, and machine translation, demonstrate that our method consistently improves the performance of the state-of-the-art baselines. The code is available at https://github.com/lgcnsai/PS-KD-Pytorch.

papers_seen.author: Holmes
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques are widely used to produce smaller, faster models while preserving much of the performance of large teachers. Approaches vary from matching final logits to transferring internal representations, attention maps, or layer-wise information, and they are applied across modalities including NLP, vision, speech, and reinforcement learning. Practical extensions address multi-teacher setups, data-free scenarios, domain adaptation, quantization, and architecture-aware compression; remaining challenges include handling heterogeneous architectures, data heterogeneity, fairness, and reliably preserving inductive biases.

papers_seen.author: Anderson
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques form a diverse set of methods for producing smaller, faster, or more deployable models by transferring knowledge from larger or specialized models. Approaches span from simple soft-label supervision to richer transfers of internal representations, intermediate-layer mappings, attention-guided projections, adversarial feature alignment, and task- or device-aware compression. KD is used across domains—image classification, detection (2D and 3D), recommendation/CTR, language model compression, federated and heterogeneous-device learning, and reinforcement learning—and is frequently combined with pruning, quantization, architecture search, or curriculum strategies. Recent work examines theoretical aspects (e.g., bias–variance tradeoffs and statistical interactions with data augmentation), practical design choices (teacher-student layer alignment, many-to-many mappings, ensemble teachers), and extensions that address privacy, fairness, and low-data regimes. Despite strong empirical success, open problems remain in understanding when particular KD variants best transfer generalization, how to measure and mitigate transferred biases, and how to optimally combine KD with other compression primitives for different constraints.

papers_seen.author: Hoffman
papers_seen.title: Federated Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Distributed learning frameworks often rely on exchanging model parameters across workers, instead of revealing their raw data. A prime example is federated learning that exchanges the gradients or weights of each neural network model. Under limited communication resources, however, such a method becomes extremely costly particularly for modern deep neural networks having a huge number of model parameters. In this regard, federated distillation (FD) is a compelling distributed learning solution that only exchanges the model outputs whose dimensions are commonly much smaller than the model sizes (e.g., 10 labels in the MNIST dataset). The goal of this chapter is to provide a deep understanding of FD while demonstrating its communication efficiency and applicability to a variety of tasks. To this end, towards demystifying the operational principle of FD, the first part of this chapter provides a novel asymptotic analysis for two foundational algorithms of FD, namely knowledge distillation (KD) and co-distillation (CD), by exploiting the theory of neural tangent kernel (NTK). Next, the second part elaborates on a baseline implementation of FD for a classification task, and illustrates its performance in terms of accuracy and communication efficiency compared to FL. Lastly, to demonstrate the applicability of FD to various distributed learning tasks and environments, the third part presents two selected applications, namely FD over asymmetric uplink-and-downlink wireless channels and FD for reinforcement learning.

papers_seen.author: Williams
papers_seen.title: Zero-shot Knowledge Transfer via Adversarial Belief Matching
papers_seen.abstract: Performing knowledge transfer from a large teacher network to a smaller student is a popular task in modern deep learning applications. However, due to growing dataset sizes and stricter privacy regulations, it is increasingly common not to have access to the data that was used to train the teacher. We propose a novel method which trains a student to match the predictions of its teacher without using any data or metadata. We achieve this by training an adversarial generator to search for images on which the student poorly matches the teacher, and then using them to train the student. Our resulting student closely approximates its teacher for simple datasets like SVHN, and on CIFAR10 we improve on the state-of-the-art for few-shot distillation (with 100 images per class), despite using no data. Finally, we also propose a metric to quantify the degree of belief matching between teacher and student in the vicinity of decision boundaries, and observe a significantly higher match between our zero-shot student and the teacher, than between a student distilled with real data and the teacher. Code available at: https://github.com/polo5/ZeroShotKnowledgeTransfer

papers_seen.author: Whitehead
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Approaches, Theory, and Applications
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression methods transfer knowledge from larger, more expensive models to smaller, efficient ones. The approaches span soft-logit supervision, feature- and layer-level matching, contrastive and relational objectives, and adaptations for special settings such as low-precision inference, multimodal models, graph data, federated learning, and heterogeneous-device training. Empirical work shows KD can improve student accuracy, robustness, and latency while theoretical analyses connect KD to label smoothing and regularization effects. Best practice choices (which teacher signals to match, which samples or augmentations to use, and how to align heterogeneous inputs) materially affect outcomes. This synthesis summarizes known methods, insights about why KD helps, and practical considerations for deploying KD in real-world ML systems.

papers_seen.author: Hawkins
papers_seen.title: A Fast Knowledge Distillation Framework for Visual Recognition
papers_seen.abstract: While Knowledge Distillation (KD) has been recognized as a useful tool in many visual tasks, such as supervised classification and self-supervised representation learning, the main drawback of a vanilla KD framework is its mechanism, which consumes the majority of the computational overhead on forwarding through the giant teacher networks, making the entire learning procedure inefficient and costly. ReLabel, a recently proposed solution, suggests creating a label map for the entire image. During training, it receives the cropped region-level label by RoI aligning on a pre-generated entire label map, allowing for efficient supervision generation without having to pass through the teachers many times. However, as the KD teachers are from conventional multi-crop training, there are various mismatches between the global label-map and region-level label in this technique, resulting in performance deterioration. In this study, we present a Fast Knowledge Distillation (FKD) framework that replicates the distillation training phase and generates soft labels using the multi-crop KD approach, while training faster than ReLabel since no post-processes such as RoI align and softmax operations are used. When conducting multi-crop in the same image for data loading, our FKD is even more efficient than the traditional image classification framework. On ImageNet-1K, we obtain 79.8% with ResNet-50, outperforming ReLabel by ~1.0% while being faster. On the self-supervised learning task, we also show that FKD has an efficiency advantage. Our project page: http://zhiqiangshen.com/projects/FKD/index.html, source code and models are available at: https://github.com/szq0214/FKD.

papers_seen.author: Powers
papers_seen.title: The Central Role of Knowledge Distillation for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a practical, flexible, and widely applicable approach to compressing large neural models into smaller, faster students while retaining much of their performance. Across domains and tasks—language modeling and translation, recommendation, graph learning, vision, continual and domain adaptation, and resource-constrained deployment—KD enables trade-offs between accuracy, latency, memory, privacy, and train-time complexity. Variants such as feature mimicking, self- and teacher-free distillation, ensemble and online distillation, data-free and privacy-aware schemes, and task- or domain-aware adaptations extend KD’s applicability. At the same time, careful choice of training targets, treatment of low-frequency phenomena, and consideration of the teacher-student mismatch are necessary to avoid transferring teacher errors and to realize the full benefits of distillation.

papers_seen.author: Farmer
papers_seen.title: Towards Efficient 3D Object Detection with Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Despite substantial progress in 3D object detection, advanced 3D detectors often suffer from heavy computation overheads. To this end, we explore the potential of knowledge distillation (KD) for developing efficient 3D object detectors, focusing on popular pillar- and voxel-based detectors.In the absence of well-developed teacher-student pairs, we first study how to obtain student models with good trade offs between accuracy and efficiency from the perspectives of model compression and input resolution reduction. Then, we build a benchmark to assess existing KD methods developed in the 2D domain for 3D object detection upon six well-constructed teacher-student pairs. Further, we propose an improved KD pipeline incorporating an enhanced logit KD method that performs KD on only a few pivotal positions determined by teacher classification response, and a teacher-guided student model initialization to facilitate transferring teacher model's feature extraction ability to students through weight inheritance. Finally, we conduct extensive experiments on the Waymo dataset. Our best performing model achieves $65.75\%$ LEVEL 2 mAPH, surpassing its teacher model and requiring only $44\%$ of teacher flops. Our most efficient model runs 51 FPS on an NVIDIA A100, which is $2.2\times$ faster than PointPillar with even higher accuracy. Code is available at \url{https://github.com/CVMI-Lab/SparseKD}.

papers_seen.author: Baker
papers_seen.title: Rejuvenating Low-Frequency Words: Making the Most of Parallel Data in Non-Autoregressive Translation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is commonly used to construct synthetic data for training non-autoregressive translation (NAT) models. However, there exists a discrepancy on low-frequency words between the distilled and the original data, leading to more errors on predicting low-frequency words. To alleviate the problem, we directly expose the raw data into NAT by leveraging pretraining. By analyzing directed alignments, we found that KD makes low-frequency source words aligned with targets more deterministically but fails to align sufficient low-frequency words from target to source. Accordingly, we propose reverse KD to rejuvenate more alignments for low-frequency target words. To make the most of authentic and synthetic data, we combine these complementary approaches as a new training strategy for further boosting NAT performance. We conduct experiments on five translation benchmarks over two advanced architectures. Results demonstrate that the proposed approach can significantly and universally improve translation quality by reducing translation errors on low-frequency words. Encouragingly, our approach achieves 28.2 and 33.9 BLEU points on the WMT14 English-German and WMT16 Romanian-English datasets, respectively. Our code, data, and trained models are available at \url{https://github.com/alphadl/RLFW-NAT}.

papers_seen.author: Robinson
papers_seen.title: Understanding and Improving Lexical Choice in Non-Autoregressive Translation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is essential for training non-autoregressive translation (NAT) models by reducing the complexity of the raw data with an autoregressive teacher model. In this study, we empirically show that as a side effect of this training, the lexical choice errors on low-frequency words are propagated to the NAT model from the teacher model. To alleviate this problem, we propose to expose the raw data to NAT models to restore the useful information of low-frequency words, which are missed in the distilled data. To this end, we introduce an extra Kullback-Leibler divergence term derived by comparing the lexical choice of NAT model and that embedded in the raw data. Experimental results across language pairs and model architectures demonstrate the effectiveness and universality of the proposed approach. Extensive analyses confirm our claim that our approach improves performance by reducing the lexical choice errors on low-frequency words. Encouragingly, our approach pushes the SOTA NAT performance on the WMT14 English-German and WMT16 Romanian-English datasets up to 27.8 and 33.8 BLEU points, respectively. The source code will be released.

papers_seen.author: Lawrence
papers_seen.title: Distilling Knowledge From a Deep Pose Regressor Network
papers_seen.abstract: This paper presents a novel method to distill knowledge from a deep pose regressor network for efficient Visual Odometry (VO). Standard distillation relies on "dark knowledge" for successful knowledge transfer. As this knowledge is not available in pose regression and the teacher prediction is not always accurate, we propose to emphasize the knowledge transfer only when we trust the teacher. We achieve this by using teacher loss as a confidence score which places variable relative importance on the teacher prediction. We inject this confidence score to the main training task via Attentive Imitation Loss (AIL) and when learning the intermediate representation of the teacher through Attentive Hint Training (AHT) approach. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work which successfully distill the knowledge from a deep pose regression network. Our evaluation on the KITTI and Malaga dataset shows that we can keep the student prediction close to the teacher with up to 92.95% parameter reduction and 2.12x faster in computation time.

papers_seen.author: Galloway
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Versatile Framework for Model Compression: Evidence, Limits, and Directions
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a broadly applicable framework for compressing and adapting deep models across modalities, deployment constraints, and learning paradigms. Empirical work shows KD can produce compact models that approach teacher performance while enabling domain adaptation, federated and privacy-aware training, multimodal-to-mono-modal transfer, and efficient generative models. However, KD is not a panacea: optimization difficulties, propagation of teacher errors, sensitivity to teacher strength and data regime, and task-specific issues (e.g., generation vs. classification) require targeted algorithmic refinements. Advances such as feature-based distillation, adversarial and curriculum-based schemes, data augmentation during distillation, meta-learned teachers, and teacher-free formulations mitigate many failure modes and extend KD to low-data, heterogeneous-device, and few-shot settings. The combination of these innovations positions KD as a central tool for practical model compression and adaptation when used with methods that explicitly address its known limitations.

papers_seen.author: Herrera
papers_seen.title: Compressing GANs using Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have been used in several machine learning tasks such as domain transfer, super resolution, and synthetic data generation. State-of-the-art GANs often use tens of millions of parameters, making them expensive to deploy for applications in low SWAP (size, weight, and power) hardware, such as mobile devices, and for applications with real time capabilities. There has been no work found to reduce the number of parameters used in GANs. Therefore, we propose a method to compress GANs using knowledge distillation techniques, in which a smaller "student" GAN learns to mimic a larger "teacher" GAN. We show that the distillation methods used on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and Celeb-A datasets can compress teacher GANs at ratios of 1669:1, 58:1, and 87:1, respectively, while retaining the quality of the generated image. From our experiments, we observe a qualitative limit for GAN's compression. Moreover, we observe that, with a fixed parameter budget, compressed GANs outperform GANs trained using standard training methods. We conjecture that this is partially owing to the optimization landscape of over-parameterized GANs which allows efficient training using alternating gradient descent. Thus, training an over-parameterized GAN followed by our proposed compression scheme provides a high quality generative model with a small number of parameters.

papers_seen.author: Allen
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Flexible Path to Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, practically effective family of techniques for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster, and often more socially or operationally suitable models. Across vision, speech, and NLP tasks KD has been shown to preserve much of teacher performance while enabling deployment on constrained hardware and in privacy-sensitive or distributed settings. KD is most effective when combined with complementary practices such as pre-training, data augmentation, careful layer-matching, ensemble guidance, and hardware-aware pruning.

papers_seen.author: Henderson
papers_seen.title: MEAL: Multi-Model Ensemble via Adversarial Learning
papers_seen.abstract: Often the best performing deep neural models are ensembles of multiple base-level networks. Unfortunately, the space required to store these many networks, and the time required to execute them at test-time, prohibits their use in applications where test sets are large (e.g., ImageNet). In this paper, we present a method for compressing large, complex trained ensembles into a single network, where knowledge from a variety of trained deep neural networks (DNNs) is distilled and transferred to a single DNN. In order to distill diverse knowledge from different trained (teacher) models, we propose to use adversarial-based learning strategy where we define a block-wise training loss to guide and optimize the predefined student network to recover the knowledge in teacher models, and to promote the discriminator network to distinguish teacher vs. student features simultaneously. The proposed ensemble method (MEAL) of transferring distilled knowledge with adversarial learning exhibits three important advantages: (1) the student network that learns the distilled knowledge with discriminators is optimized better than the original model; (2) fast inference is realized by a single forward pass, while the performance is even better than traditional ensembles from multi-original models; (3) the student network can learn the distilled knowledge from a teacher model that has arbitrary structures. Extensive experiments on CIFAR-10/100, SVHN and ImageNet datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our MEAL method. On ImageNet, our ResNet-50 based MEAL achieves top-1/5 21.79%/5.99% val error, which outperforms the original model by 2.06%/1.14%. Code and models are available at: https://github.com/AaronHeee/MEAL

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: The Case for Pragmatic, Task-Aware Knowledge Distillation in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically validated set of techniques for producing smaller, faster models from larger teachers. Across vision, language, multimodal, and distributed settings, distillation can preserve or even improve accuracy while enabling deployments with constrained compute, memory, latency, and privacy requirements. However, its success depends on matching distillation objectives and procedures to task constraints (e.g., robustness, heterogeneity, data availability). When applied thoughtfully—using feature-based objectives, ensemble or adversarial strategies, data augmentation or data-free approaches, and task-adaptive compression—KD reliably delivers practical trade-offs between efficiency and effectiveness.

papers_seen.author: Shaw
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Insights, and Applications
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model compression techniques reduce the size and computational cost of large deep models while retaining much of their performance. Across classification, sequence modeling, generation, and structured prediction, researchers have developed soft-label distillation, intermediate-feature guidance, adversarial and contrastive objectives, projector and embedding modules, and privacy-aware mechanisms to transfer knowledge from large teacher models to smaller students. Empirical and theoretical work highlights trade-offs among bias, variance, teacher quality, and data complexity, and shows that distillation interacts with pre-training, label smoothing, and modality differences. Applications span speech and machine translation to GANs and graph neural networks; complementary methods such as pruning and block-structured compression can further improve deployment on constrained hardware.

papers_seen.author: Hahn
papers_seen.title: PKD: General Distillation Framework for Object Detectors via Pearson Correlation Coefficient
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation(KD) is a widely-used technique to train compact models in object detection. However, there is still a lack of study on how to distill between heterogeneous detectors. In this paper, we empirically find that better FPN features from a heterogeneous teacher detector can help the student although their detection heads and label assignments are different. However, directly aligning the feature maps to distill detectors suffers from two problems. First, the difference in feature magnitude between the teacher and the student could enforce overly strict constraints on the student. Second, the FPN stages and channels with large feature magnitude from the teacher model could dominate the gradient of distillation loss, which will overwhelm the effects of other features in KD and introduce much noise. To address the above issues, we propose to imitate features with Pearson Correlation Coefficient to focus on the relational information from the teacher and relax constraints on the magnitude of the features. Our method consistently outperforms the existing detection KD methods and works for both homogeneous and heterogeneous student-teacher pairs. Furthermore, it converges faster. With a powerful MaskRCNN-Swin detector as the teacher, ResNet-50 based RetinaNet and FCOS achieve 41.5% and 43.9% mAP on COCO2017, which are 4.1\% and 4.8\% higher than the baseline, respectively.

papers_seen.author: Hall
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Cornerstone of Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has proven to be a broadly applicable and practical paradigm for compressing large neural models, transferring functionality across architectures, enabling deployment under data- or communication-constraints, and improving interpretability and task adaptation. Across modalities and tasks, KD variants (layer mapping, feature matching, data-free generation, progressive replacement, meta-learned teachers, multi-teacher weighting, and task-adaptive architecture search) provide complementary solutions to real-world constraints such as limited compute, limited data, privacy, and distribution shift. The most effective KD strategies select or synthesize the right supervision (soft targets, intermediate features, or distilled data), adapt the teacher–student alignment mechanism to the task, and account for practical issues such as imperfect teachers or label-smoothing interactions.

papers_seen.author: Gardner
papers_seen.title: Adversarially Robust Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is effective for producing small, high-performance neural networks for classification, but these small networks are vulnerable to adversarial attacks. This paper studies how adversarial robustness transfers from teacher to student during knowledge distillation. We find that a large amount of robustness may be inherited by the student even when distilled on only clean images. Second, we introduce Adversarially Robust Distillation (ARD) for distilling robustness onto student networks. In addition to producing small models with high test accuracy like conventional distillation, ARD also passes the superior robustness of large networks onto the student. In our experiments, we find that ARD student models decisively outperform adversarially trained networks of identical architecture in terms of robust accuracy, surpassing state-of-the-art methods on standard robustness benchmarks. Finally, we adapt recent fast adversarial training methods to ARD for accelerated robust distillation.

papers_seen.author: Wagner
papers_seen.title: Self-Knowledge Distillation in Natural Language Processing
papers_seen.abstract: Since deep learning became a key player in natural language processing (NLP), many deep learning models have been showing remarkable performances in a variety of NLP tasks, and in some cases, they are even outperforming humans. Such high performance can be explained by efficient knowledge representation of deep learning models. While many methods have been proposed to learn more efficient representation, knowledge distillation from pretrained deep networks suggest that we can use more information from the soft target probability to train other neural networks. In this paper, we propose a new knowledge distillation method self-knowledge distillation, based on the soft target probabilities of the training model itself, where multimode information is distilled from the word embedding space right below the softmax layer. Due to the time complexity, our method approximates the soft target probabilities. In experiments, we applied the proposed method to two different and fundamental NLP tasks: language model and neural machine translation. The experiment results show that our proposed method improves performance on the tasks.

papers_seen.author: Lee
papers_seen.title: Practical Principles for Effective Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and model compression are no longer just ways to reduce parameter counts; when designed thoughtfully they preserve or even improve task performance, domain robustness, and privacy while enabling real-time deployment. Effective distillation requires going beyond matching output probabilities: transferring internal representations, using task- and domain-aware selection of teacher signals, leveraging ensemble or adversarial schemes when appropriate, and adopting data-aware or data-free augmentation techniques. In application domains from NLP to vision, multi-modal systems, and graph learning, tailored distillation strategies yield substantial speedups and parameter reductions with minimal loss (and sometimes gains) in accuracy. This paper synthesizes evidence across diverse recent works to advocate a principled, task-centered approach to distillation and compression.

papers_seen.author: Ramirez
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a central technique for compressing large neural models and transferring knowledge across architectures, tasks, and deployment constraints. Work across vision, language, graphs, and generative representations shows diverse KD objectives (soft-target, feature, relational, contrastive, and layer-matching), a range of data regimes (full-data, limited-data, data-free/zero-shot), and many complementary compression mechanisms (pruning, architecture search, block-structured sparsity, and cheap operators). Empirical and theoretical studies clarify when KD helps, how it interacts with data-augmentation and teacher imperfection, and how KD can be adapted for privacy-preserving or federated scenarios. This review summarizes these practical methods, observed trade-offs, and open challenges for robust, efficient, and private model compression.

papers_seen.author: Powell
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central Tool for Model Compression and Transfer: Strengths, Limits, and Practical Directions
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a versatile set of techniques that enable model compression, domain- and task-level transfer, privacy-preserving distillation, and improvements in interpretability and fairness. Empirical and methodological work shows KD can compress large models into efficient students, transfer inductive biases, support multi-task and lifelong learning, and enable data-free or zero-shot distillation when training data are unavailable. At the same time, KD faces concrete limitations due to data heterogeneity, teacher-student capacity mismatch, and the need to select or synthesize appropriate supervision; hybrid solutions that combine feature-level matching, adversarial sample synthesis, curriculum strategies, and architectural compression achieve the best practical results. Based on evidence across domains (vision, language, graphs, retrieval, reinforcement learning), we argue that KD should be used as part of an integrated compression pipeline that is task-aware, data-aware, and often combined with pruning, layer skipping, or module replacement to meet deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Brown
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Approaches
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques have become central tools for deploying high-performing deep models in resource-constrained or privacy-sensitive settings. Work in this area has progressed beyond the original formulation of training a small student to match a teacher's output probabilities: modern approaches distill internal representations, perform many-to-many layer alignment, operate without access to original training data, combine multiple teachers or ensembles, and adapt to particular architectures and tasks (including graph networks, detectors, generative models, and language models). Practical concerns such as data heterogeneity, privacy guarantees, and robustness to distribution shift have motivated methods that use synthetic data, private perturbations, generative replay, and federated or online distillation protocols. The field continues to trade off fidelity to teacher behavior, compactness, task specificity, and deployability, with task-adaptive compression and representation-alignment methods emerging as especially effective for NLP and other structured prediction tasks.

papers_seen.author: Evans
papers_seen.title: Learning Compact Metrics for MT
papers_seen.abstract: Recent developments in machine translation and multilingual text generation have led researchers to adopt trained metrics such as COMET or BLEURT, which treat evaluation as a regression problem and use representations from multilingual pre-trained models such as XLM-RoBERTa or mBERT. Yet studies on related tasks suggest that these models are most efficient when they are large, which is costly and impractical for evaluation. We investigate the trade-off between multilinguality and model capacity with RemBERT, a state-of-the-art multilingual language model, using data from the WMT Metrics Shared Task. We present a series of experiments which show that model size is indeed a bottleneck for cross-lingual transfer, then demonstrate how distillation can help addressing this bottleneck, by leveraging synthetic data generation and transferring knowledge from one teacher to multiple students trained on related languages. Our method yields up to 10.5% improvement over vanilla fine-tuning and reaches 92.6% of RemBERT's performance using only a third of its parameters.

papers_seen.author: Gray
papers_seen.title: Improved Feature Distillation via Projector Ensemble
papers_seen.abstract: In knowledge distillation, previous feature distillation methods mainly focus on the design of loss functions and the selection of the distilled layers, while the effect of the feature projector between the student and the teacher remains under-explored. In this paper, we first discuss a plausible mechanism of the projector with empirical evidence and then propose a new feature distillation method based on a projector ensemble for further performance improvement. We observe that the student network benefits from a projector even if the feature dimensions of the student and the teacher are the same. Training a student backbone without a projector can be considered as a multi-task learning process, namely achieving discriminative feature extraction for classification and feature matching between the student and the teacher for distillation at the same time. We hypothesize and empirically verify that without a projector, the student network tends to overfit the teacher's feature distributions despite having different architecture and weights initialization. This leads to degradation on the quality of the student's deep features that are eventually used in classification. Adding a projector, on the other hand, disentangles the two learning tasks and helps the student network to focus better on the main feature extraction task while still being able to utilize teacher features as a guidance through the projector. Motivated by the positive effect of the projector in feature distillation, we propose an ensemble of projectors to further improve the quality of student features. Experimental results on different datasets with a series of teacher-student pairs illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

papers_seen.author: Robinson
papers_seen.title: Understanding and Improving Lexical Choice in Non-Autoregressive Translation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is essential for training non-autoregressive translation (NAT) models by reducing the complexity of the raw data with an autoregressive teacher model. In this study, we empirically show that as a side effect of this training, the lexical choice errors on low-frequency words are propagated to the NAT model from the teacher model. To alleviate this problem, we propose to expose the raw data to NAT models to restore the useful information of low-frequency words, which are missed in the distilled data. To this end, we introduce an extra Kullback-Leibler divergence term derived by comparing the lexical choice of NAT model and that embedded in the raw data. Experimental results across language pairs and model architectures demonstrate the effectiveness and universality of the proposed approach. Extensive analyses confirm our claim that our approach improves performance by reducing the lexical choice errors on low-frequency words. Encouragingly, our approach pushes the SOTA NAT performance on the WMT14 English-German and WMT16 Romanian-English datasets up to 27.8 and 33.8 BLEU points, respectively. The source code will be released.

papers_seen.author: Jones
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and model compression have become central strategies for deploying large deep models under resource, latency, and privacy constraints. A diverse set of methods—ranging from soft-label distillation, intermediate feature and attention matching, layer mapping, adversarial and data-free techniques, to task-adaptive architecture search and meta-learning of teachers—have been proposed to transfer performance from bulky teachers to compact students. These approaches are applied across domains including vision, language, multi-modal systems, recommender systems, and domain-specific NLP, and they trade off fidelity to the teacher, generalization, and computational efficiency. Empirical results show that properly designed distillation pipelines can recover a large fraction of teacher performance while yielding substantial speedups and memory reductions, and in some settings can even improve fairness, robustness, or downstream generalization. Remaining challenges include aligning heterogeneous inputs and representations across teacher and student, coping with absent or private training data, and automatically selecting what and how to transfer for specific tasks and deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Ryan
papers_seen.title: The Central Role of Knowledge Distillation for Practical Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Modalities, and Recommendations
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model compression techniques are now essential for deploying high-performing deep learning models under resource, privacy, and latency constraints. A broad set of distillation strategies—ranging from soft-label supervision and feature mimicking to data-free (zero-shot) distillation, adversarially guided feature transfer, self-distillation, and automated architecture search guided by teacher models—enable substantial reductions in model size and computational cost while preserving or even improving performance across vision, language, multimodal, and sequence tasks. Best practice combines input-side methods (data augmentation and mixup), representation-level transfer, and careful teacher-student design choices to match the deployment objectives (efficiency, fairness, interpretability, or privacy).

papers_seen.author: Stewart
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Foundational Tool for Compression, Robustness, and Transfer in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable technique that compresses large models into smaller, faster ones while transferring performance and often additional properties such as robustness or cross-domain adaptability. Evidence across vision, language, graph, and sequential domains shows KD enables deployable models for latency- and resource-constrained settings, supports continual and federated learning, and can be combined with pruning, architecture search, and adversarial strategies. However, distillation is not a universal panacea: it can propagate teacher errors, interact nontrivially with regularization strategies, and requires careful alignment of inputs, representations, and objectives. Best practice is to treat KD as a family of tools (logit, intermediate-layer, feature, adversarial, data-driven, self-distillation) and to adapt the distillation design to task and deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Harris
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Work
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques provide a practical path to deploy high-performing deep models under resource, latency, privacy, or domain constraints. Across vision and language, researchers have explored teacher-student training, intermediate-layer alignment, data- and label-space manipulations, data-free or few-shot settings, and architecture-aware compression. These techniques can preserve much of a teacher's performance while yielding smaller, faster models, and they can be combined with pruning, architecture search, or ensemble compression. KD also intersects with concerns about fairness, generalization, and privacy, and its effectiveness depends on design choices such as the form of distilled targets, data augmentation, and the match between teacher, student, and task.

papers_seen.author: Galloway
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Versatile Framework for Model Compression: Evidence, Limits, and Directions
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a broadly applicable framework for compressing and adapting deep models across modalities, deployment constraints, and learning paradigms. Empirical work shows KD can produce compact models that approach teacher performance while enabling domain adaptation, federated and privacy-aware training, multimodal-to-mono-modal transfer, and efficient generative models. However, KD is not a panacea: optimization difficulties, propagation of teacher errors, sensitivity to teacher strength and data regime, and task-specific issues (e.g., generation vs. classification) require targeted algorithmic refinements. Advances such as feature-based distillation, adversarial and curriculum-based schemes, data augmentation during distillation, meta-learned teachers, and teacher-free formulations mitigate many failure modes and extend KD to low-data, heterogeneous-device, and few-shot settings. The combination of these innovations positions KD as a central tool for practical model compression and adaptation when used with methods that explicitly address its known limitations.

papers_seen.author: Rios
papers_seen.title: Improving Neural Topic Models using Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Topic models are often used to identify human-interpretable topics to help make sense of large document collections. We use knowledge distillation to combine the best attributes of probabilistic topic models and pretrained transformers. Our modular method can be straightforwardly applied with any neural topic model to improve topic quality, which we demonstrate using two models having disparate architectures, obtaining state-of-the-art topic coherence. We show that our adaptable framework not only improves performance in the aggregate over all estimated topics, as is commonly reported, but also in head-to-head comparisons of aligned topics.

papers_seen.author: Hurst
papers_seen.title: Ranking Distillation: Learning Compact Ranking Models With High Performance for Recommender System
papers_seen.abstract: We propose a novel way to train ranking models, such as recommender systems, that are both effective and efficient. Knowledge distillation (KD) was shown to be successful in image recognition to achieve both effectiveness and efficiency. We propose a KD technique for learning to rank problems, called \emph{ranking distillation (RD)}. Specifically, we train a smaller student model to learn to rank documents/items from both the training data and the supervision of a larger teacher model. The student model achieves a similar ranking performance to that of the large teacher model, but its smaller model size makes the online inference more efficient. RD is flexible because it is orthogonal to the choices of ranking models for the teacher and student. We address the challenges of RD for ranking problems. The experiments on public data sets and state-of-the-art recommendation models showed that RD achieves its design purposes: the student model learnt with RD has a model size less than half of the teacher model while achieving a ranking performance similar to the teacher model and much better than the student model learnt without RD.

papers_seen.author: Morgan
papers_seen.title: The Case for Knowledge Distillation as a Core Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a practical, versatile approach to compressing large models into smaller, faster, and often more robust models across computer vision, NLP, multilingual metrics, and multimodal tasks. A range of complementary techniques — layer-wise mapping, data-free and zero-shot synthesis, self-distillation, adversarial and robust distillation, online/ensemble methods, and task-adaptive architecture search — together make distillation applicable under constraints such as limited data, privacy restrictions, heterogeneous devices, and production-scale training. I argue that adopting a portfolio of distillation strategies, chosen to match data availability and deployment constraints, yields the best trade-offs between efficiency, accuracy, robustness, and interpretability for modern deep learning systems.

papers_seen.author: Parker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Approaches and Findings
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a broad family of techniques for compressing large or expensive models into smaller, faster, or more deployable ones by transferring information from a teacher to a student. Methods differ in the form of transferred knowledge (soft logits, hidden features, contrastive distributions, synthetic data, or cross-modal alignments), in how and when distillation is applied (offline, online, layer-wise, task-adaptive, or data-free), and in the problems they target (classification, detection, generation, language tasks, graph learning, or novel-view synthesis). Empirical work demonstrates that appropriate choices about teacher signals, data manipulation, and architectural search can yield compact models that retain much of teacher performance across modalities; theoretical work begins to clarify when soft labels help and when hard labels or mixed supervision are needed. Remaining challenges include optimization gaps between teacher and student, dataset and fairness concerns, and scaling distillation reliably in large distributed settings.

papers_seen.author: Bright
papers_seen.title: Towards Practical Lipreading with Distilled and Efficient Models
papers_seen.abstract: Lipreading has witnessed a lot of progress due to the resurgence of neural networks. Recent works have placed emphasis on aspects such as improving performance by finding the optimal architecture or improving generalization. However, there is still a significant gap between the current methodologies and the requirements for an effective deployment of lipreading in practical scenarios. In this work, we propose a series of innovations that significantly bridge that gap: first, we raise the state-of-the-art performance by a wide margin on LRW and LRW-1000 to 88.5% and 46.6%, respectively using self-distillation. Secondly, we propose a series of architectural changes, including a novel Depthwise Separable Temporal Convolutional Network (DS-TCN) head, that slashes the computational cost to a fraction of the (already quite efficient) original model. Thirdly, we show that knowledge distillation is a very effective tool for recovering performance of the lightweight models. This results in a range of models with different accuracy-efficiency trade-offs. However, our most promising lightweight models are on par with the current state-of-the-art while showing a reduction of 8.2x and 3.9x in terms of computational cost and number of parameters, respectively, which we hope will enable the deployment of lipreading models in practical applications.

papers_seen.author: Davis
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Multifaceted Tool for Compression, Robustness, and Responsible NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, widely applicable approach for compressing large models into efficient students while also serving as a lever for regularization, robustness, privacy, fairness, interpretability, and continual/multi-task learning. When applied thoughtfully—combining soft-label distillation with feature- and representation-level matching, layer mapping, attention or projector modules, and task-aware curricula—KD can produce lightweight models that approach or sometimes exceed teacher performance on constrained devices and specialized tasks. However, KD is not automatic: optimization difficulties, data heterogeneity, and mismatches in the information transferred (e.g., for low-frequency tokens or internal features) limit its effectiveness unless complemented by targeted methodological choices. I argue that KD should be treated as a principled toolbox rather than a single recipe: choose distillation targets (outputs, features, internal representations), mapping strategies (many-to-many layer mapping, attention, projectors), and auxiliary safeguards (privacy-preserving noise, fairness interventions, adversarial distillation) to align compression goals with safety and utility requirements.

papers_seen.author: Yu
papers_seen.title: Best Practices and Limitations of Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a broadly applicable and powerful approach for compressing models across modalities, but its effectiveness depends on design choices spanning what is distilled (logits, features, internal representations), how inputs are prepared (augmentation, sample selection), how multiple teachers are reconciled, and whether robustness or task-specific structure is considered. Recent work shows that combining soft-target regularization with feature- and intermediate-representation matching, careful input-side interventions, and adaptive distillation objectives yields the best tradeoffs between compression, accuracy, and robustness across vision, language, multimodal, graph, and generative-model settings.

papers_seen.author: Duncan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Analyses, and Applications
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a central technique for compressing and adapting large neural models into smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained models while retaining much of their performance. A diverse set of KD approaches operate at the level of final outputs (logits), intermediate features, layer relations, or via adversarial and data-generation mechanisms. KD has been adapted across modalities and tasks — from NLP transformer compression to GAN and speech-model compression, cross-modal transfer, federated settings, and domain-specific applications — and interacts strongly with concerns about robustness, fairness, and transfer of inductive biases. Empirical and theoretical work has clarified when and why various KD variants help, and highlights open challenges in data heterogeneity, teacher-student mismatch, and automatic discovery of compact architectures.

papers_seen.author: Stewart
papers_seen.title: Private Model Compression via Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: The soaring demand for intelligent mobile applications calls for deploying powerful deep neural networks (DNNs) on mobile devices. However, the outstanding performance of DNNs notoriously relies on increasingly complex models, which in turn is associated with an increase in computational expense far surpassing mobile devices' capacity. What is worse, app service providers need to collect and utilize a large volume of users' data, which contain sensitive information, to build the sophisticated DNN models. Directly deploying these models on public mobile devices presents prohibitive privacy risk. To benefit from the on-device deep learning without the capacity and privacy concerns, we design a private model compression framework RONA. Following the knowledge distillation paradigm, we jointly use hint learning, distillation learning, and self learning to train a compact and fast neural network. The knowledge distilled from the cumbersome model is adaptively bounded and carefully perturbed to enforce differential privacy. We further propose an elegant query sample selection method to reduce the number of queries and control the privacy loss. A series of empirical evaluations as well as the implementation on an Android mobile device show that RONA can not only compress cumbersome models efficiently but also provide a strong privacy guarantee. For example, on SVHN, when a meaningful $(9.83,10^{-6})$-differential privacy is guaranteed, the compact model trained by RONA can obtain 20$\times$ compression ratio and 19$\times$ speed-up with merely 0.97% accuracy loss.

papers_seen.author: Huff
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core Tool for Practical Model Compression: Evidence, Techniques, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, broadly applicable paradigm for producing smaller, faster models that retain much of the performance of larger networks. Across modalities (vision, language, speech, graphs, and generative models) and use-cases (edge deployment, federated learning, domain adaptation, continual learning), distillation has repeatedly enabled dramatic reductions in model size and inference cost while maintaining or even improving task performance. However, distillation is not a panacea: careful design of what to transfer (logits, intermediate features, attention maps, or relational structure), how to align teacher and student inputs and layers, and when to apply supplementary strategies (adversarial examples, multi-teacher weighting, continual updates) is necessary to avoid failure modes such as propagated teacher errors, misalignment across detectors, and limits in compressing some model families. Drawing on empirical results and method innovations across the literature, I argue that KD should be treated as a foundational component of any deployment-oriented model compression pipeline, and that combining complementary distillation techniques tailored to the task and architecture yields the best balance of compactness, speed, and accuracy.

papers_seen.author: Robinson
papers_seen.title: Towards Understanding Ensemble, Knowledge Distillation and Self-Distillation in Deep Learning
papers_seen.abstract: We formally study how ensemble of deep learning models can improve test accuracy, and how the superior performance of ensemble can be distilled into a single model using knowledge distillation. We consider the challenging case where the ensemble is simply an average of the outputs of a few independently trained neural networks with the SAME architecture, trained using the SAME algorithm on the SAME data set, and they only differ by the random seeds used in the initialization.   We show that ensemble/knowledge distillation in Deep Learning works very differently from traditional learning theory (such as boosting or NTKs, neural tangent kernels). To properly understand them, we develop a theory showing that when data has a structure we refer to as ``multi-view'', then ensemble of independently trained neural networks can provably improve test accuracy, and such superior test accuracy can also be provably distilled into a single model by training a single model to match the output of the ensemble instead of the true label. Our result sheds light on how ensemble works in deep learning in a way that is completely different from traditional theorems, and how the ``dark knowledge'' is hidden in the outputs of the ensemble and can be used in distillation. In the end, we prove that self-distillation can also be viewed as implicitly combining ensemble and knowledge distillation to improve test accuracy.

papers_seen.author: Lee
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression: Practical Necessity, Limitations, and a Consolidated Best-Practice Agenda
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques are now essential for deploying high‑performing deep models in resource‑constrained settings across vision, speech, recommendation, graph, and language tasks. KD delivers large efficiency gains while often preserving much of teacher performance, but it is not a turnkey solution: teacher inference cost, data mismatches introduced by distillation, low‑frequency token degradation, privacy considerations, and heterogeneous deployment constraints each demand tailored remedies. Combining complementary strategies — multi‑teacher distillation, student‑aware teacher design, projector/feature adaptation, self‑distillation, exposure to raw data, and privacy-aware or federated KD — yields robust compressed models that approach or match teacher capabilities in practice.

papers_seen.author: Rogers
papers_seen.title: Confidence-Aware Multi-Teacher Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is initially introduced to utilize additional supervision from a single teacher model for the student model training. To boost the student performance, some recent variants attempt to exploit diverse knowledge sources from multiple teachers. However, existing studies mainly integrate knowledge from diverse sources by averaging over multiple teacher predictions or combining them using other various label-free strategies, which may mislead student in the presence of low-quality teacher predictions. To tackle this problem, we propose Confidence-Aware Multi-teacher Knowledge Distillation (CA-MKD), which adaptively assigns sample-wise reliability for each teacher prediction with the help of ground-truth labels, with those teacher predictions close to one-hot labels assigned large weights. Besides, CA-MKD incorporates intermediate layers to stable the knowledge transfer process. Extensive experiments show that our CA-MKD consistently outperforms all compared state-of-the-art methods across various teacher-student architectures.

papers_seen.author: Lynch
papers_seen.title: Revisiting Knowledge Distillation via Label Smoothing Regularization
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge Distillation (KD) aims to distill the knowledge of a cumbersome teacher model into a lightweight student model. Its success is generally attributed to the privileged information on similarities among categories provided by the teacher model, and in this sense, only strong teacher models are deployed to teach weaker students in practice. In this work, we challenge this common belief by following experimental observations: 1) beyond the acknowledgment that the teacher can improve the student, the student can also enhance the teacher significantly by reversing the KD procedure; 2) a poorly-trained teacher with much lower accuracy than the student can still improve the latter significantly. To explain these observations, we provide a theoretical analysis of the relationships between KD and label smoothing regularization. We prove that 1) KD is a type of learned label smoothing regularization and 2) label smoothing regularization provides a virtual teacher model for KD. From these results, we argue that the success of KD is not fully due to the similarity information between categories from teachers, but also to the regularization of soft targets, which is equally or even more important.   Based on these analyses, we further propose a novel Teacher-free Knowledge Distillation (Tf-KD) framework, where a student model learns from itself or manuallydesigned regularization distribution. The Tf-KD achieves comparable performance with normal KD from a superior teacher, which is well applied when a stronger teacher model is unavailable. Meanwhile, Tf-KD is generic and can be directly deployed for training deep neural networks. Without any extra computation cost, Tf-KD achieves up to 0.65\% improvement on ImageNet over well-established baseline models, which is superior to label smoothing regularization.

papers_seen.author: Herrera
papers_seen.title: Compressing GANs using Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have been used in several machine learning tasks such as domain transfer, super resolution, and synthetic data generation. State-of-the-art GANs often use tens of millions of parameters, making them expensive to deploy for applications in low SWAP (size, weight, and power) hardware, such as mobile devices, and for applications with real time capabilities. There has been no work found to reduce the number of parameters used in GANs. Therefore, we propose a method to compress GANs using knowledge distillation techniques, in which a smaller "student" GAN learns to mimic a larger "teacher" GAN. We show that the distillation methods used on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and Celeb-A datasets can compress teacher GANs at ratios of 1669:1, 58:1, and 87:1, respectively, while retaining the quality of the generated image. From our experiments, we observe a qualitative limit for GAN's compression. Moreover, we observe that, with a fixed parameter budget, compressed GANs outperform GANs trained using standard training methods. We conjecture that this is partially owing to the optimization landscape of over-parameterized GANs which allows efficient training using alternating gradient descent. Thus, training an over-parameterized GAN followed by our proposed compression scheme provides a high quality generative model with a small number of parameters.

papers_seen.author: White
papers_seen.title: Distilling portable Generative Adversarial Networks for Image Translation
papers_seen.abstract: Despite Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have been widely used in various image-to-image translation tasks, they can be hardly applied on mobile devices due to their heavy computation and storage cost. Traditional network compression methods focus on visually recognition tasks, but never deal with generation tasks. Inspired by knowledge distillation, a student generator of fewer parameters is trained by inheriting the low-level and high-level information from the original heavy teacher generator. To promote the capability of student generator, we include a student discriminator to measure the distances between real images, and images generated by student and teacher generators. An adversarial learning process is therefore established to optimize student generator and student discriminator. Qualitative and quantitative analysis by conducting experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed method can learn portable generative models with strong performance.

papers_seen.author: Baker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Mechanisms, and Applications
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a central technique for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster, and more deployable students while attempting to preserve teacher performance. Work in KD spans matching teacher outputs (soft labels), aligning internal representations and features, adversarial or data-free sample synthesis, architecture search and task-adaptive compression, privacy-aware and federated settings, and domain- or task-specific adaptations. Empirical results show KD can yield dramatic reductions in size and compute with modest drops (or even gains) in downstream performance across speech, vision, and NLP tasks, but success depends on what is distilled (outputs versus internal features), optimization and dataset choices, and problem-specific design choices. The literature also identifies limitations and failure modes—optimization difficulties, data heterogeneity, and privacy constraints—that have motivated specialized protocols and theory. This synthesis summarizes the principal approaches, mechanistic explanations, representative empirical outcomes, and practical considerations for applying KD in deep learning and NLP.

papers_seen.author: Lopez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core Tool for Model Compression, Transfer, and Robustification in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is not merely a technique for shrinking models: it is a flexible paradigm that enables model compression, domain and modality transfer, continual adaptation, and improved interpretability and fairness. A range of strategies — from many-to-many layer alignment and feature mimicking to data-free synthesis, online peer teaching, and augmentation-aware distillation — make KD applicable across tasks (classification, generation, detection, ASR, GANs) and settings (distributed training, privacy-constrained, few-shot, multi-task). However, practical use requires careful design choices (what to transfer, how to match teacher and student, and how to handle teacher–student discrepancy and label-processing artifacts). When applied with methods matched to these considerations, KD consistently yields compact models that retain much of teacher performance while unlocking deployment and research scenarios otherwise infeasible for large, monolithic networks.

papers_seen.author: Shaffer
papers_seen.title: Selective Knowledge Distillation for Neural Machine Translation
papers_seen.abstract: Neural Machine Translation (NMT) models achieve state-of-the-art performance on many translation benchmarks. As an active research field in NMT, knowledge distillation is widely applied to enhance the model's performance by transferring teacher model's knowledge on each training sample. However, previous work rarely discusses the different impacts and connections among these samples, which serve as the medium for transferring teacher knowledge. In this paper, we design a novel protocol that can effectively analyze the different impacts of samples by comparing various samples' partitions. Based on above protocol, we conduct extensive experiments and find that the teacher's knowledge is not the more, the better. Knowledge over specific samples may even hurt the whole performance of knowledge distillation. Finally, to address these issues, we propose two simple yet effective strategies, i.e., batch-level and global-level selections, to pick suitable samples for distillation. We evaluate our approaches on two large-scale machine translation tasks, WMT'14 English->German and WMT'19 Chinese->English. Experimental results show that our approaches yield up to +1.28 and +0.89 BLEU points improvements over the Transformer baseline, respectively.

papers_seen.author: Collins
papers_seen.title: The Central Role of Knowledge Distillation for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible, and widely applicable approach to compressing models for deployment in resource-constrained settings. Distillation can transfer many types of knowledge (logits, intermediate features, attention patterns, relational or contrastive signals) and can be adapted to scenarios that lack original training data, require privacy guarantees, or demand task- and hardware-aware compression. When combined with complementary techniques (pruning, architecture search, pretraining, or ensemble teaching), KD enables large reductions in model size and latency while largely preserving performance. Nevertheless, distillation can propagate biases and teacher artifacts and needs targeted remedies (feature-focused objectives, multi-teacher strategies, teacher annealing, or exposure to raw data) to avoid failure modes on rare phenomena. The literature demonstrates both the breadth of KD methods and concrete best practices to maximize effectiveness across vision, speech, graph, and NLP tasks.

papers_seen.author: Bernard
papers_seen.title: Reinforced Multi-Teacher Selection for Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: In natural language processing (NLP) tasks, slow inference speed and huge footprints in GPU usage remain the bottleneck of applying pre-trained deep models in production. As a popular method for model compression, knowledge distillation transfers knowledge from one or multiple large (teacher) models to a small (student) model. When multiple teacher models are available in distillation, the state-of-the-art methods assign a fixed weight to a teacher model in the whole distillation. Furthermore, most of the existing methods allocate an equal weight to every teacher model. In this paper, we observe that, due to the complexity of training examples and the differences in student model capability, learning differentially from teacher models can lead to better performance of student models distilled. We systematically develop a reinforced method to dynamically assign weights to teacher models for different training instances and optimize the performance of student model. Our extensive experimental results on several NLP tasks clearly verify the feasibility and effectiveness of our approach.

papers_seen.author: Hall
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Cornerstone of Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has proven to be a broadly applicable and practical paradigm for compressing large neural models, transferring functionality across architectures, enabling deployment under data- or communication-constraints, and improving interpretability and task adaptation. Across modalities and tasks, KD variants (layer mapping, feature matching, data-free generation, progressive replacement, meta-learned teachers, multi-teacher weighting, and task-adaptive architecture search) provide complementary solutions to real-world constraints such as limited compute, limited data, privacy, and distribution shift. The most effective KD strategies select or synthesize the right supervision (soft targets, intermediate features, or distilled data), adapt the teacher–student alignment mechanism to the task, and account for practical issues such as imperfect teachers or label-smoothing interactions.

papers_seen.author: Reid
papers_seen.title: Moonshine: Distilling with Cheap Convolutions
papers_seen.abstract: Many engineers wish to deploy modern neural networks in memory-limited settings; but the development of flexible methods for reducing memory use is in its infancy, and there is little knowledge of the resulting cost-benefit. We propose structural model distillation for memory reduction using a strategy that produces a student architecture that is a simple transformation of the teacher architecture: no redesign is needed, and the same hyperparameters can be used. Using attention transfer, we provide Pareto curves/tables for distillation of residual networks with four benchmark datasets, indicating the memory versus accuracy payoff. We show that substantial memory savings are possible with very little loss of accuracy, and confirm that distillation provides student network performance that is better than training that student architecture directly on data.
