papers_seen.author: Huff
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core Tool for Practical Model Compression: Evidence, Techniques, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, broadly applicable paradigm for producing smaller, faster models that retain much of the performance of larger networks. Across modalities (vision, language, speech, graphs, and generative models) and use-cases (edge deployment, federated learning, domain adaptation, continual learning), distillation has repeatedly enabled dramatic reductions in model size and inference cost while maintaining or even improving task performance. However, distillation is not a panacea: careful design of what to transfer (logits, intermediate features, attention maps, or relational structure), how to align teacher and student inputs and layers, and when to apply supplementary strategies (adversarial examples, multi-teacher weighting, continual updates) is necessary to avoid failure modes such as propagated teacher errors, misalignment across detectors, and limits in compressing some model families. Drawing on empirical results and method innovations across the literature, I argue that KD should be treated as a foundational component of any deployment-oriented model compression pipeline, and that combining complementary distillation techniques tailored to the task and architecture yields the best balance of compactness, speed, and accuracy.

papers_seen.author: Hensley
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related compression techniques are widely used to produce smaller, faster models that retain much of the performance of larger teachers. Work across theory, computer vision, natural language processing, graph learning and systems has explored why distillation works, how to make it practical under constraints (limited or no access to original data, privacy, federated settings), and how to adapt it to specialized settings (pretrained language models, non-autoregressive translation, detectors, GANs, visual-linguistic models). Empirical and theoretical studies identify benefits, failure modes, and design patterns: distillation often simplifies learning targets and stabilizes optimization; matching intermediate representations, attention patterns, or relational structure can improve transfer; mixing soft and hard targets can correct teacher errors; and specialized procedures (e.g., layer mapping, adversarial sample generation, teacher adaptation) are effective for particular tasks. Remaining challenges include handling heterogeneous or private data, preserving low-frequency or rare-token behavior in sequence tasks, and formalizing the optimal teacher-student pairing and data complexity trade-offs.

papers_seen.author: Burton
papers_seen.title: Efficient Transformer-based Large Scale Language Representations using Hardware-friendly Block Structured Pruning
papers_seen.abstract: Pre-trained large-scale language models have increasingly demonstrated high accuracy on many natural language processing (NLP) tasks. However, the limited weight storage and computational speed on hardware platforms have impeded the popularity of pre-trained models, especially in the era of edge computing. In this work, we propose an efficient transformer-based large-scale language representation using hardware-friendly block structure pruning. We incorporate the reweighted group Lasso into block-structured pruning for optimization. Besides the significantly reduced weight storage and computation, the proposed approach achieves high compression rates. Experimental results on different models (BERT, RoBERTa, and DistilBERT) on the General Language Understanding Evaluation (GLUE) benchmark tasks show that we achieve up to 5.0x with zero or minor accuracy degradation on certain task(s). Our proposed method is also orthogonal to existing compact pre-trained language models such as DistilBERT using knowledge distillation, since a further 1.79x average compression rate can be achieved on top of DistilBERT with zero or minor accuracy degradation. It is suitable to deploy the final compressed model on resource-constrained edge devices.

papers_seen.author: Cohen
papers_seen.title: ALP-KD: Attention-Based Layer Projection for Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is considered as a training and compression strategy in which two neural networks, namely a teacher and a student, are coupled together during training. The teacher network is supposed to be a trustworthy predictor and the student tries to mimic its predictions. Usually, a student with a lighter architecture is selected so we can achieve compression and yet deliver high-quality results. In such a setting, distillation only happens for final predictions whereas the student could also benefit from teacher's supervision for internal components.   Motivated by this, we studied the problem of distillation for intermediate layers. Since there might not be a one-to-one alignment between student and teacher layers, existing techniques skip some teacher layers and only distill from a subset of them. This shortcoming directly impacts quality, so we instead propose a combinatorial technique which relies on attention. Our model fuses teacher-side information and takes each layer's significance into consideration, then performs distillation between combined teacher layers and those of the student. Using our technique, we distilled a 12-layer BERT (Devlin et al. 2019) into 6-, 4-, and 2-layer counterparts and evaluated them on GLUE tasks (Wang et al. 2018). Experimental results show that our combinatorial approach is able to outperform other existing techniques.

papers_seen.author: Johnson
papers_seen.title: Mitigating Gender Bias in Distilled Language Models via Counterfactual Role Reversal
papers_seen.abstract: Language models excel at generating coherent text, and model compression techniques such as knowledge distillation have enabled their use in resource-constrained settings. However, these models can be biased in multiple ways, including the unfounded association of male and female genders with gender-neutral professions. Therefore, knowledge distillation without any fairness constraints may preserve or exaggerate the teacher model's biases onto the distilled model. To this end, we present a novel approach to mitigate gender disparity in text generation by learning a fair model during knowledge distillation. We propose two modifications to the base knowledge distillation based on counterfactual role reversal$\unicode{x2014}$modifying teacher probabilities and augmenting the training set. We evaluate gender polarity across professions in open-ended text generated from the resulting distilled and finetuned GPT$\unicode{x2012}$2 models and demonstrate a substantial reduction in gender disparity with only a minor compromise in utility. Finally, we observe that language models that reduce gender polarity in language generation do not improve embedding fairness or downstream classification fairness.

papers_seen.author: Parsons
papers_seen.title: Curriculum Learning for Dense Retrieval Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Recent work has shown that more effective dense retrieval models can be obtained by distilling ranking knowledge from an existing base re-ranking model. In this paper, we propose a generic curriculum learning based optimization framework called CL-DRD that controls the difficulty level of training data produced by the re-ranking (teacher) model. CL-DRD iteratively optimizes the dense retrieval (student) model by increasing the difficulty of the knowledge distillation data made available to it. In more detail, we initially provide the student model coarse-grained preference pairs between documents in the teacher's ranking and progressively move towards finer-grained pairwise document ordering requirements. In our experiments, we apply a simple implementation of the CL-DRD framework to enhance two state-of-the-art dense retrieval models. Experiments on three public passage retrieval datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed framework.

papers_seen.author: Moore
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression: Powerful, Versatile, but Context-Dependent
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a core technique for compressing large models and transferring their knowledge into smaller, faster models for deployment in resource-constrained settings and domain-specific applications. Advances in layer- and feature-level transfer, many-to-many layer mapping, data- and augmentation-aware practices, and federated or privacy-sensitive adaptations have expanded KD's applicability across vision, NLP, and graph domains. However, KD is not a universal remedy: it can propagate teacher errors, struggle under data heterogeneity, and depend critically on teacher quality, data choices, and optimization design. Best outcomes follow when practitioners combine KD with complementary techniques (careful layer matching, feature mimicking, data selection/augmentation, and pruning or quantization) and explicitly address heterogeneity and teacher reliability.

papers_seen.author: Foster
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Approaches
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation has emerged as a broad set of techniques to compress large or ensemble models into smaller, faster, or more deployable models while preserving performance. Research spans logits-based distillation, feature and representation matching, intermediate-layer alignment, adversarial and self-supervised schemes, curriculum and online protocols, and task-adaptive or privacy-preserving variants. Practical work demonstrates successful applications across NLP (including compressing BERT), vision, graph learning, retrieval, object detection, and large-scale distributed training, with ongoing research focused on teacher design, data augmentation, and robustness under limited or heterogeneous data.

papers_seen.author: Fowler
papers_seen.title: SEED: Self-supervised Distillation For Visual Representation
papers_seen.abstract: This paper is concerned with self-supervised learning for small models. The problem is motivated by our empirical studies that while the widely used contrastive self-supervised learning method has shown great progress on large model training, it does not work well for small models. To address this problem, we propose a new learning paradigm, named SElf-SupErvised Distillation (SEED), where we leverage a larger network (as Teacher) to transfer its representational knowledge into a smaller architecture (as Student) in a self-supervised fashion. Instead of directly learning from unlabeled data, we train a student encoder to mimic the similarity score distribution inferred by a teacher over a set of instances. We show that SEED dramatically boosts the performance of small networks on downstream tasks. Compared with self-supervised baselines, SEED improves the top-1 accuracy from 42.2% to 67.6% on EfficientNet-B0 and from 36.3% to 68.2% on MobileNet-v3-Large on the ImageNet-1k dataset.

papers_seen.author: Walls
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related compression techniques have been adapted across modalities (vision, language, graphs, and generative models) to produce smaller, faster, or more robust models while attempting to retain performance of larger teachers. Approaches vary in what is transferred (soft logits, intermediate features, relational information, or structural/topological properties), how transfer is scheduled or weighted (confidence-aware, progressive replacement, or multi-teacher aggregation), and how distillation is combined with other compression methods (pruning, architecture search, or compact operator substitution). Empirical work shows strong practical benefits—improved runtime, memory, and sometimes robustness or fairness—while theoretical and analytical work begins to explain when and why distillation helps (e.g., role of soft targets, label smoothing analogies, and behavior with imperfect teachers). Remaining challenges include transferring rare-word or low-frequency information in sequence tasks, preserving relational/global structure in graph and link tasks, adapting to evolving domains, and automating generator compression for GANs. This synthesis summarizes key methods, insights, and open directions from recent literature.

papers_seen.author: Martin
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Settings, and Findings
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression strategies are now widespread across computer vision, natural language processing, recommendation systems, and specialized settings (federated, few-shot, multi-modal, generative). Research has advanced along multiple axes: what to transfer (logits, features, attention, latent modules), how to shape the transfer (sample selection, adversarially-informed examples, curriculum, teacher ensembles, meta-learning), and special protocols for constrained environments (federated/black-box, few-shot, on-device inference). Empirical work shows KD can substantially close the performance gap between small and large models, enable practical deployment of generative and discriminative models, and, when extended, transfer robustness and interpretability. Remaining challenges include error propagation from teachers (especially for low-frequency phenomena), limitations under data heterogeneity in federated settings, and task-specific design choices for complex outputs (e.g., detection, segmentation, set outputs), motivating continued work on tailored distillation objectives and teacher-student co-design.

papers_seen.author: James
papers_seen.title: Robust Cross-Modal Representation Learning with Progressive Self-Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: The learning objective of vision-language approach of CLIP does not effectively account for the noisy many-to-many correspondences found in web-harvested image captioning datasets, which contributes to its compute and data inefficiency. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel training framework based on cross-modal contrastive learning that uses progressive self-distillation and soft image-text alignments to more efficiently learn robust representations from noisy data. Our model distills its own knowledge to dynamically generate soft-alignment targets for a subset of images and captions in every minibatch, which are then used to update its parameters. Extensive evaluation across 14 benchmark datasets shows that our method consistently outperforms its CLIP counterpart in multiple settings, including: (a) zero-shot classification, (b) linear probe transfer, and (c) image-text retrieval, without incurring added computational cost. Analysis using an ImageNet-based robustness test-bed reveals that our method offers better effective robustness to natural distribution shifts compared to both ImageNet-trained models and CLIP itself. Lastly, pretraining with datasets spanning two orders of magnitude in size shows that our improvements over CLIP tend to scale with number of training examples.

papers_seen.author: Miller
papers_seen.title: Understanding BERT Rankers Under Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Deep language models such as BERT pre-trained on large corpus have given a huge performance boost to the state-of-the-art information retrieval ranking systems. Knowledge embedded in such models allows them to pick up complex matching signals between passages and queries. However, the high computation cost during inference limits their deployment in real-world search scenarios. In this paper, we study if and how the knowledge for search within BERT can be transferred to a smaller ranker through distillation. Our experiments demonstrate that it is crucial to use a proper distillation procedure, which produces up to nine times speedup while preserving the state-of-the-art performance.

papers_seen.author: Hernandez
papers_seen.title: R2L: Distilling Neural Radiance Field to Neural Light Field for Efficient Novel View Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Recent research explosion on Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) shows the encouraging potential to represent complex scenes with neural networks. One major drawback of NeRF is its prohibitive inference time: Rendering a single pixel requires querying the NeRF network hundreds of times. To resolve it, existing efforts mainly attempt to reduce the number of required sampled points. However, the problem of iterative sampling still exists. On the other hand, Neural Light Field (NeLF) presents a more straightforward representation over NeRF in novel view synthesis -- the rendering of a pixel amounts to one single forward pass without ray-marching. In this work, we present a deep residual MLP network (88 layers) to effectively learn the light field. We show the key to successfully learning such a deep NeLF network is to have sufficient data, for which we transfer the knowledge from a pre-trained NeRF model via data distillation. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world scenes show the merits of our method over other counterpart algorithms. On the synthetic scenes, we achieve 26-35x FLOPs reduction (per camera ray) and 28-31x runtime speedup, meanwhile delivering significantly better (1.4-2.8 dB average PSNR improvement) rendering quality than NeRF without any customized parallelism requirement.

papers_seen.author: Mueller
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Work
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a central technique for compressing and accelerating deep models by transferring knowledge from larger (teacher) models to smaller (student) models. Beyond straightforward parameter reduction, KD is used to improve student generalization, robustness, interpretability, domain adaptation, continual learning, and to enable deployment in latency- or resource-constrained settings. The literature shows a wide variety of KD objectives (logit/soft-label matching, feature imitation, relational losses), training protocols (multi-teacher, curriculum, adversarial or zero-shot data generation, teacher-free/self-distillation), and application-specific adaptations (detection, retrieval, GANs, speech, lipreading, 3D vision, recommender systems, and NLP). Empirical results demonstrate that carefully designed distillation pipelines can recover much of teacher performance and in some cases surpass teachers on efficiency-accuracy trade-offs, but raise challenges including heterogeneous teacher-student alignment, data availability, preserving low-frequency or fine-grained behaviors, and transferring robustness and domain-general knowledge.

papers_seen.author: Garcia
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Methods and Applications
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques have become central tools for deploying high-performance deep models in resource-constrained settings. Across computer vision, generative modeling, 3D rendering, graph learning, and natural language processing, researchers employ a range of distillation paradigms — including teacher-student soft-label transfer, intermediate representation matching, self-distillation, data-free and privacy-preserving distillation, and automated architecture search guided by teacher models — to produce smaller, faster, or more interpretable students while retaining much of the teacher performance. Practical concerns such as limited or unavailable training data, domain shifts, adversarial robustness, and the need for interpretable or low-precision models have driven specific adaptations of KD. Empirical results across tasks show that (1) distillation can greatly reduce model size or runtime with small accuracy loss, (2) internal- and feature-level matching often improves transfer beyond logits-only approaches, and (3) novel protocols (e.g., ensemble teachers, generative pseudo-replay, many-to-many layer alignment) expand KD applicability to privacy-sensitive, multimodal, and generation tasks.

papers_seen.author: Pierce
papers_seen.title: Survey of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP (Selected 2017–2022 Literature)
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model-compression techniques have become central tools for producing compact, efficient models from larger teachers across vision, language, and multimodal tasks. Methods include soft-label distillation, feature- and representation-level matching, adversarial and ensemble-based transfer, data-free or privacy-aware distillation, curriculum and selective-sample strategies, and task-adaptive architecture search. These approaches target deployment constraints (latency, memory, on-device compute), data-availability and privacy limitations, robustness, and domain-continuity, and have been adapted to detectors, generative models, retrieval systems, federated settings, and pre-trained language models. Empirical work demonstrates that careful choice of what to transfer (logits, internal features, relational/contrastive signals) and when/how to train (online, teacher-free, curriculum, few-shot) materially affects student performance and robustness. Open challenges include heterogeneity of data and architectures in distributed settings, theoretical understanding of what aspects of teacher knowledge are most valuable across tasks, and extending distillation to privacy- and domain-constrained deployments.

papers_seen.author: Hoffman
papers_seen.title: Federated Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Distributed learning frameworks often rely on exchanging model parameters across workers, instead of revealing their raw data. A prime example is federated learning that exchanges the gradients or weights of each neural network model. Under limited communication resources, however, such a method becomes extremely costly particularly for modern deep neural networks having a huge number of model parameters. In this regard, federated distillation (FD) is a compelling distributed learning solution that only exchanges the model outputs whose dimensions are commonly much smaller than the model sizes (e.g., 10 labels in the MNIST dataset). The goal of this chapter is to provide a deep understanding of FD while demonstrating its communication efficiency and applicability to a variety of tasks. To this end, towards demystifying the operational principle of FD, the first part of this chapter provides a novel asymptotic analysis for two foundational algorithms of FD, namely knowledge distillation (KD) and co-distillation (CD), by exploiting the theory of neural tangent kernel (NTK). Next, the second part elaborates on a baseline implementation of FD for a classification task, and illustrates its performance in terms of accuracy and communication efficiency compared to FL. Lastly, to demonstrate the applicability of FD to various distributed learning tasks and environments, the third part presents two selected applications, namely FD over asymmetric uplink-and-downlink wireless channels and FD for reinforcement learning.

papers_seen.author: Rodriguez
papers_seen.title: Releasing Graph Neural Networks with Differential Privacy Guarantees
papers_seen.abstract: With the increasing popularity of graph neural networks (GNNs) in several sensitive applications like healthcare and medicine, concerns have been raised over the privacy aspects of trained GNNs. More notably, GNNs are vulnerable to privacy attacks, such as membership inference attacks, even if only black-box access to the trained model is granted. We propose PrivGNN, a privacy-preserving framework for releasing GNN models in a centralized setting. Assuming an access to a public unlabeled graph, PrivGNN provides a framework to release GNN models trained explicitly on public data along with knowledge obtained from the private data in a privacy preserving manner. PrivGNN combines the knowledge-distillation framework with the two noise mechanisms, random subsampling, and noisy labeling, to ensure rigorous privacy guarantees. We theoretically analyze our approach in the Renyi differential privacy framework. Besides, we show the solid experimental performance of our method compared to several baselines adapted for graph-structured data. Our code is available at https://github.com/iyempissy/privGnn.

papers_seen.author: Doyle
papers_seen.title: DE-RRD: A Knowledge Distillation Framework for Recommender System
papers_seen.abstract: Recent recommender systems have started to employ knowledge distillation, which is a model compression technique distilling knowledge from a cumbersome model (teacher) to a compact model (student), to reduce inference latency while maintaining performance. The state-of-the-art methods have only focused on making the student model accurately imitate the predictions of the teacher model. They have a limitation in that the prediction results incompletely reveal the teacher's knowledge. In this paper, we propose a novel knowledge distillation framework for recommender system, called DE-RRD, which enables the student model to learn from the latent knowledge encoded in the teacher model as well as from the teacher's predictions. Concretely, DE-RRD consists of two methods: 1) Distillation Experts (DE) that directly transfers the latent knowledge from the teacher model. DE exploits "experts" and a novel expert selection strategy for effectively distilling the vast teacher's knowledge to the student with limited capacity. 2) Relaxed Ranking Distillation (RRD) that transfers the knowledge revealed from the teacher's prediction with consideration of the relaxed ranking orders among items. Our extensive experiments show that DE-RRD outperforms the state-of-the-art competitors and achieves comparable or even better performance to that of the teacher model with faster inference time.

papers_seen.author: Humphrey
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Multi-Modal Tool for Compression and Adaptation in Deep Learning: Strengths, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a broadly applicable approach for compressing and adapting deep models across modalities (text, vision, graphs, speech) and deployment scenarios (edge devices, federated clients, domain shifts). Empirical evidence shows KD can improve student generalization, enable small-footprint models, and facilitate domain- or modality-transfer when combined with representation-level objectives or adversarial/contrastive methods. However, its success depends on optimization, teacher-student design, data availability, and fairness considerations. I argue that KD should be treated as a flexible framework—one that combines logit-level supervision with representation-aware objectives, domain-aware selection of teacher signals, and explicit measures to mitigate undesirable side effects (e.g., lexical errors or bias)—to reliably produce compact, high-quality models for NLP and beyond.

papers_seen.author: Mcclain
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation from Internal Representations
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is typically conducted by training a small model (the student) to mimic a large and cumbersome model (the teacher). The idea is to compress the knowledge from the teacher by using its output probabilities as soft-labels to optimize the student. However, when the teacher is considerably large, there is no guarantee that the internal knowledge of the teacher will be transferred into the student; even if the student closely matches the soft-labels, its internal representations may be considerably different. This internal mismatch can undermine the generalization capabilities originally intended to be transferred from the teacher to the student. In this paper, we propose to distill the internal representations of a large model such as BERT into a simplified version of it. We formulate two ways to distill such representations and various algorithms to conduct the distillation. We experiment with datasets from the GLUE benchmark and consistently show that adding knowledge distillation from internal representations is a more powerful method than only using soft-label distillation.

papers_seen.author: Santos
papers_seen.title: Channel Distillation: Channel-Wise Attention for Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is to transfer the knowledge from the data learned by the teacher network to the student network, so that the student has the advantage of less parameters and less calculations, and the accuracy is close to the teacher. In this paper, we propose a new distillation method, which contains two transfer distillation strategies and a loss decay strategy. The first transfer strategy is based on channel-wise attention, called Channel Distillation (CD). CD transfers the channel information from the teacher to the student. The second is Guided Knowledge Distillation (GKD). Unlike Knowledge Distillation (KD), which allows the student to mimic each sample's prediction distribution of the teacher, GKD only enables the student to mimic the correct output of the teacher. The last part is Early Decay Teacher (EDT). During the training process, we gradually decay the weight of the distillation loss. The purpose is to enable the student to gradually control the optimization rather than the teacher. Our proposed method is evaluated on ImageNet and CIFAR100. On ImageNet, we achieve 27.68% of top-1 error with ResNet18, which outperforms state-of-the-art methods. On CIFAR100, we achieve surprising result that the student outperforms the teacher. Code is available at https://github.com/zhouzaida/channel-distillation.

papers_seen.author: Mckay
papers_seen.title: MixKD: Towards Efficient Distillation of Large-scale Language Models
papers_seen.abstract: Large-scale language models have recently demonstrated impressive empirical performance. Nevertheless, the improved results are attained at the price of bigger models, more power consumption, and slower inference, which hinder their applicability to low-resource (both memory and computation) platforms. Knowledge distillation (KD) has been demonstrated as an effective framework for compressing such big models. However, large-scale neural network systems are prone to memorize training instances, and thus tend to make inconsistent predictions when the data distribution is altered slightly. Moreover, the student model has few opportunities to request useful information from the teacher model when there is limited task-specific data available. To address these issues, we propose MixKD, a data-agnostic distillation framework that leverages mixup, a simple yet efficient data augmentation approach, to endow the resulting model with stronger generalization ability. Concretely, in addition to the original training examples, the student model is encouraged to mimic the teacher's behavior on the linear interpolation of example pairs as well. We prove from a theoretical perspective that under reasonable conditions MixKD gives rise to a smaller gap between the generalization error and the empirical error. To verify its effectiveness, we conduct experiments on the GLUE benchmark, where MixKD consistently leads to significant gains over the standard KD training, and outperforms several competitive baselines. Experiments under a limited-data setting and ablation studies further demonstrate the advantages of the proposed approach.

papers_seen.author: Leblanc
papers_seen.title: The Case for Knowledge Distillation as a Universal Tool for Model Compression and Practical Deployment
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible technique that enables model compression, deployment efficiency, and task- or domain-specific adaptation across a wide range of deep learning settings. Empirical work shows KD can reduce memory and compute with small accuracy loss, enable low-precision inference, compress specialized generative or multi-modal models, and provide routes to interpretability and data- or privacy-constrained scenarios. Best results arise when KD is adapted to the task (choice of objectives, teacher ensembles, data augmentation, or data-free strategies) and when student architectures or training protocols explicitly account for heterogeneity between teacher and student.

papers_seen.author: Daniels
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Methods, Applications, and Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques enable deployment of high-performing but large deep models by transferring knowledge from larger or more complex models (teachers) to smaller, efficient models (students). Across vision, speech, recommendation, retrieval, and NLP tasks, KD has been adapted into many forms—single- and multi-teacher schemes, data-free and federated variants, task-adaptive compression, and methods that target robustness, fairness, or cross-modal transfer. Empirical results show KD can yield large speed and size gains with modest performance loss and in some cases match or exceed teacher performance when combined with architectural or training strategies. Open challenges remain around teacher quality and heterogeneity, data availability, distribution shift, low-frequency phenomena, adversarial robustness, and deploying distillation in privacy-sensitive or resource-constrained environments.

papers_seen.author: Herrera
papers_seen.title: Distilling Object Detectors with Fine-grained Feature Imitation
papers_seen.abstract: State-of-the-art CNN based recognition models are often computationally prohibitive to deploy on low-end devices. A promising high level approach tackling this limitation is knowledge distillation, which let small student model mimic cumbersome teacher model's output to get improved generalization. However, related methods mainly focus on simple task of classification while do not consider complex tasks like object detection. We show applying the vanilla knowledge distillation to detection model gets minor gain. To address the challenge of distilling knowledge in detection model, we propose a fine-grained feature imitation method exploiting the cross-location discrepancy of feature response. Our intuition is that detectors care more about local near object regions. Thus the discrepancy of feature response on the near object anchor locations reveals important information of how teacher model tends to generalize. We design a novel mechanism to estimate those locations and let student model imitate the teacher on them to get enhanced performance. We first validate the idea on a developed lightweight toy detector which carries simplest notion of current state-of-the-art anchor based detection models on challenging KITTI dataset, our method generates up to 15% boost of mAP for the student model compared to the non-imitated counterpart. We then extensively evaluate the method with Faster R-CNN model under various scenarios with common object detection benchmark of Pascal VOC and COCO, imitation alleviates up to 74% performance drop of student model compared to teacher. Codes released at https://github.com/twangnh/Distilling-Object-Detectors

papers_seen.author: Miller
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Improved Accuracy in Spoken Question Answering
papers_seen.abstract: Spoken question answering (SQA) is a challenging task that requires the machine to fully understand the complex spoken documents. Automatic speech recognition (ASR) plays a significant role in the development of QA systems. However, the recent work shows that ASR systems generate highly noisy transcripts, which critically limit the capability of machine comprehension on the SQA task. To address the issue, we present a novel distillation framework. Specifically, we devise a training strategy to perform knowledge distillation (KD) from spoken documents and written counterparts. Our work makes a step towards distilling knowledge from the language model as a supervision signal to lead to better student accuracy by reducing the misalignment between automatic and manual transcriptions. Experiments demonstrate that our approach outperforms several state-of-the-art language models on the Spoken-SQuAD dataset.

papers_seen.author: Walker
papers_seen.title: BERT Learns to Teach: Knowledge Distillation with Meta Learning
papers_seen.abstract: We present Knowledge Distillation with Meta Learning (MetaDistil), a simple yet effective alternative to traditional knowledge distillation (KD) methods where the teacher model is fixed during training. We show the teacher network can learn to better transfer knowledge to the student network (i.e., learning to teach) with the feedback from the performance of the distilled student network in a meta learning framework. Moreover, we introduce a pilot update mechanism to improve the alignment between the inner-learner and meta-learner in meta learning algorithms that focus on an improved inner-learner. Experiments on various benchmarks show that MetaDistil can yield significant improvements compared with traditional KD algorithms and is less sensitive to the choice of different student capacity and hyperparameters, facilitating the use of KD on different tasks and models.

papers_seen.author: Wagner
papers_seen.title: Self-Knowledge Distillation in Natural Language Processing
papers_seen.abstract: Since deep learning became a key player in natural language processing (NLP), many deep learning models have been showing remarkable performances in a variety of NLP tasks, and in some cases, they are even outperforming humans. Such high performance can be explained by efficient knowledge representation of deep learning models. While many methods have been proposed to learn more efficient representation, knowledge distillation from pretrained deep networks suggest that we can use more information from the soft target probability to train other neural networks. In this paper, we propose a new knowledge distillation method self-knowledge distillation, based on the soft target probabilities of the training model itself, where multimode information is distilled from the word embedding space right below the softmax layer. Due to the time complexity, our method approximates the soft target probabilities. In experiments, we applied the proposed method to two different and fundamental NLP tasks: language model and neural machine translation. The experiment results show that our proposed method improves performance on the tasks.

papers_seen.author: Hall
papers_seen.title: FedZKT: Zero-Shot Knowledge Transfer towards Resource-Constrained Federated Learning with Heterogeneous On-Device Models
papers_seen.abstract: Federated learning enables multiple distributed devices to collaboratively learn a shared prediction model without centralizing their on-device data. Most of the current algorithms require comparable individual efforts for local training with the same structure and size of on-device models, which, however, impedes participation from resource-constrained devices. Given the widespread yet heterogeneous devices nowadays, in this paper, we propose an innovative federated learning framework with heterogeneous on-device models through Zero-shot Knowledge Transfer, named by FedZKT. Specifically, FedZKT allows devices to independently determine the on-device models upon their local resources. To achieve knowledge transfer across these heterogeneous on-device models, a zero-shot distillation approach is designed without any prerequisites for private on-device data, which is contrary to certain prior research based on a public dataset or a pre-trained data generator. Moreover, this compute-intensive distillation task is assigned to the server to allow the participation of resource-constrained devices, where a generator is adversarially learned with the ensemble of collected on-device models. The distilled central knowledge is then sent back in the form of the corresponding on-device model parameters, which can be easily absorbed on the device side. Extensive experimental studies demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of FedZKT towards on-device knowledge agnostic, on-device model heterogeneity, and other challenging federated learning scenarios, such as heterogeneous on-device data and straggler effects.

papers_seen.author: Montgomery
papers_seen.title: Object DGCNN: 3D Object Detection using Dynamic Graphs
papers_seen.abstract: 3D object detection often involves complicated training and testing pipelines, which require substantial domain knowledge about individual datasets. Inspired by recent non-maximum suppression-free 2D object detection models, we propose a 3D object detection architecture on point clouds. Our method models 3D object detection as message passing on a dynamic graph, generalizing the DGCNN framework to predict a set of objects. In our construction, we remove the necessity of post-processing via object confidence aggregation or non-maximum suppression. To facilitate object detection from sparse point clouds, we also propose a set-to-set distillation approach customized to 3D detection. This approach aligns the outputs of the teacher model and the student model in a permutation-invariant fashion, significantly simplifying knowledge distillation for the 3D detection task. Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on autonomous driving benchmarks. We also provide abundant analysis of the detection model and distillation framework.

papers_seen.author: Henderson
papers_seen.title: The Case for Knowledge Distillation as a Central Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation has emerged as a practical, flexible approach to compressing large neural models into resource-efficient students while preserving much of the teachers' performance. Across modalities and tasks — from language and retrieval to vision, generation, and graph learning — distillation techniques enable trade-offs between accuracy, compute, and memory that make deployment feasible on constrained hardware. However, the effectiveness of distillation depends strongly on the distillation objective, the information transferred (probabilities, internal representations, or structured signals), availability of original data, and care to avoid transferring undesirable teacher properties. When combined with complementary compression techniques (quantization, architecture search, low-precision training, or curriculum strategies), distillation can yield compact models that approach or sometimes even exceed teacher performance while meeting practical latency and size constraints.

papers_seen.author: Ryan
papers_seen.title: The Central Role of Knowledge Distillation for Practical Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Modalities, and Recommendations
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model compression techniques are now essential for deploying high-performing deep learning models under resource, privacy, and latency constraints. A broad set of distillation strategies—ranging from soft-label supervision and feature mimicking to data-free (zero-shot) distillation, adversarially guided feature transfer, self-distillation, and automated architecture search guided by teacher models—enable substantial reductions in model size and computational cost while preserving or even improving performance across vision, language, multimodal, and sequence tasks. Best practice combines input-side methods (data augmentation and mixup), representation-level transfer, and careful teacher-student design choices to match the deployment objectives (efficiency, fairness, interpretability, or privacy).

papers_seen.author: Ray
papers_seen.title: Transferring Inductive Biases through Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Having the right inductive biases can be crucial in many tasks or scenarios where data or computing resources are a limiting factor, or where training data is not perfectly representative of the conditions at test time. However, defining, designing and efficiently adapting inductive biases is not necessarily straightforward. In this paper, we explore the power of knowledge distillation for transferring the effect of inductive biases from one model to another. We consider families of models with different inductive biases, LSTMs vs. Transformers and CNNs vs. MLPs, in the context of tasks and scenarios where having the right inductive biases is critical. We study the effect of inductive biases on the solutions the models converge to and investigate how and to what extent the effect of inductive biases is transferred through knowledge distillation, in terms of not only performance but also different aspects of converged solutions.

papers_seen.author: Hoffman
papers_seen.title: Federated Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Distributed learning frameworks often rely on exchanging model parameters across workers, instead of revealing their raw data. A prime example is federated learning that exchanges the gradients or weights of each neural network model. Under limited communication resources, however, such a method becomes extremely costly particularly for modern deep neural networks having a huge number of model parameters. In this regard, federated distillation (FD) is a compelling distributed learning solution that only exchanges the model outputs whose dimensions are commonly much smaller than the model sizes (e.g., 10 labels in the MNIST dataset). The goal of this chapter is to provide a deep understanding of FD while demonstrating its communication efficiency and applicability to a variety of tasks. To this end, towards demystifying the operational principle of FD, the first part of this chapter provides a novel asymptotic analysis for two foundational algorithms of FD, namely knowledge distillation (KD) and co-distillation (CD), by exploiting the theory of neural tangent kernel (NTK). Next, the second part elaborates on a baseline implementation of FD for a classification task, and illustrates its performance in terms of accuracy and communication efficiency compared to FL. Lastly, to demonstrate the applicability of FD to various distributed learning tasks and environments, the third part presents two selected applications, namely FD over asymmetric uplink-and-downlink wireless channels and FD for reinforcement learning.

papers_seen.author: Robinson
papers_seen.title: Learning Student-Friendly Teacher Networks for Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: We propose a novel knowledge distillation approach to facilitate the transfer of dark knowledge from a teacher to a student. Contrary to most of the existing methods that rely on effective training of student models given pretrained teachers, we aim to learn the teacher models that are friendly to students and, consequently, more appropriate for knowledge transfer. In other words, at the time of optimizing a teacher model, the proposed algorithm learns the student branches jointly to obtain student-friendly representations. Since the main goal of our approach lies in training teacher models and the subsequent knowledge distillation procedure is straightforward, most of the existing knowledge distillation methods can adopt this technique to improve the performance of diverse student models in terms of accuracy and convergence speed. The proposed algorithm demonstrates outstanding accuracy in several well-known knowledge distillation techniques with various combinations of teacher and student models even in the case that their architectures are heterogeneous and there is no prior knowledge about student models at the time of training teacher networks.

papers_seen.author: Chapman
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Approaches and Findings
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a practical and versatile family of techniques for producing smaller, faster, or otherwise specialized models by transferring information from larger or alternative teacher models. KD variants include offline teacher-student distillation, online mutual distillation, ensemble-to-student distillation, cross-task distillation, and teacher-aware or student-aware training. Beyond the canonical logit-matching objective, modern work distills intermediate representations, relational and contrastive structures, and task-specific signals to improve accuracy, robustness, fairness, privacy, generation, and inference latency. Empirical results across computer vision, speech, machine translation, retrieval, graph learning, and routing problems show KD can both compress models without large accuracy loss and improve distilled students in multiple dimensions (robustness, fairness, generalization, and deployment cost). However, distillation is not a panacea: its effectiveness depends on teacher quality and compatibility, the choice of distilled knowledge (logits vs features vs relations), data complexity, and careful training strategies (sample selection, curriculum, annealing, or joint teacher-student learning). This synthesis summarizes methods, motivations, practical techniques, and empirical patterns observed across recent studies.

papers_seen.author: Walls
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related compression techniques have been adapted across modalities (vision, language, graphs, and generative models) to produce smaller, faster, or more robust models while attempting to retain performance of larger teachers. Approaches vary in what is transferred (soft logits, intermediate features, relational information, or structural/topological properties), how transfer is scheduled or weighted (confidence-aware, progressive replacement, or multi-teacher aggregation), and how distillation is combined with other compression methods (pruning, architecture search, or compact operator substitution). Empirical work shows strong practical benefits—improved runtime, memory, and sometimes robustness or fairness—while theoretical and analytical work begins to explain when and why distillation helps (e.g., role of soft targets, label smoothing analogies, and behavior with imperfect teachers). Remaining challenges include transferring rare-word or low-frequency information in sequence tasks, preserving relational/global structure in graph and link tasks, adapting to evolving domains, and automating generator compression for GANs. This synthesis summarizes key methods, insights, and open directions from recent literature.

papers_seen.author: Welch
papers_seen.title: The Central Role of Knowledge Distillation in Practical Model Compression and Generalization
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured from a niche compression trick into a broadly applicable paradigm that enables deployment of large models across modalities, supports privacy- and resource-constrained federated scenarios, and improves generalization when combined with task- and architecture-specific techniques. Empirical evidence shows that KD alone yields large gains for small students, while hybrid approaches that distill internal representations, use curriculum or meta-learning, augment data, or jointly optimize architecture and distillation produce state-of-the-art trade-offs between size, speed, and task performance. KD is therefore a foundational tool for modern model compression strategies and should be used in concert with complementary methods (e.g., pretraining, low-precision numerics, structural compression, and privacy-aware distillation) to meet real-world deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Perez
papers_seen.title: BAM! Born-Again Multi-Task Networks for Natural Language Understanding
papers_seen.abstract: It can be challenging to train multi-task neural networks that outperform or even match their single-task counterparts. To help address this, we propose using knowledge distillation where single-task models teach a multi-task model. We enhance this training with teacher annealing, a novel method that gradually transitions the model from distillation to supervised learning, helping the multi-task model surpass its single-task teachers. We evaluate our approach by multi-task fine-tuning BERT on the GLUE benchmark. Our method consistently improves over standard single-task and multi-task training.

papers_seen.author: Caldwell
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Effectiveness, Limitations, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a practical and flexible method for compressing large models into smaller, faster, and often more interpretable models across vision, language, speech, and recommendation systems. KD works both as a stand-alone compression technique and as a complementary tool that combines well with pruning, quantization, multi-teacher strategies, and privacy-aware or federated settings. While highly effective in practice, KD has limits—especially around data availability, heterogeneity, and theoretical understanding—that recent work addresses with data-free methods, meta-learning teachers, and principled analyses.

papers_seen.author: Rocha
papers_seen.title: Few Shot Network Compression via Cross Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Model compression has been widely adopted to obtain light-weighted deep neural networks. Most prevalent methods, however, require fine-tuning with sufficient training data to ensure accuracy, which could be challenged by privacy and security issues. As a compromise between privacy and performance, in this paper we investigate few shot network compression: given few samples per class, how can we effectively compress the network with negligible performance drop? The core challenge of few shot network compression lies in high estimation errors from the original network during inference, since the compressed network can easily over-fits on the few training instances. The estimation errors could propagate and accumulate layer-wisely and finally deteriorate the network output. To address the problem, we propose cross distillation, a novel layer-wise knowledge distillation approach. By interweaving hidden layers of teacher and student network, layer-wisely accumulated estimation errors can be effectively reduced.The proposed method offers a general framework compatible with prevalent network compression techniques such as pruning. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that cross distillation can significantly improve the student network's accuracy when only a few training instances are available.

papers_seen.author: Evans
papers_seen.title: Learning Compact Metrics for MT
papers_seen.abstract: Recent developments in machine translation and multilingual text generation have led researchers to adopt trained metrics such as COMET or BLEURT, which treat evaluation as a regression problem and use representations from multilingual pre-trained models such as XLM-RoBERTa or mBERT. Yet studies on related tasks suggest that these models are most efficient when they are large, which is costly and impractical for evaluation. We investigate the trade-off between multilinguality and model capacity with RemBERT, a state-of-the-art multilingual language model, using data from the WMT Metrics Shared Task. We present a series of experiments which show that model size is indeed a bottleneck for cross-lingual transfer, then demonstrate how distillation can help addressing this bottleneck, by leveraging synthetic data generation and transferring knowledge from one teacher to multiple students trained on related languages. Our method yields up to 10.5% improvement over vanilla fine-tuning and reaches 92.6% of RemBERT's performance using only a third of its parameters.

papers_seen.author: Jordan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central Tool for Compression and Robust Transfer in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically essential technique for compressing large models and transferring useful knowledge to smaller or specialized models. Across vision, speech, graph, and language tasks, distillation enables faster inference, reduced memory footprint, and sometimes improved generalization when combined with complementary strategies (e.g., architecture search, pruning, or data management). However, distillation outcomes depend on data, teacher-student alignment, and training design; success requires adapting KD objectives and pipelines to the task and deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Santos
papers_seen.title: Channel Distillation: Channel-Wise Attention for Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is to transfer the knowledge from the data learned by the teacher network to the student network, so that the student has the advantage of less parameters and less calculations, and the accuracy is close to the teacher. In this paper, we propose a new distillation method, which contains two transfer distillation strategies and a loss decay strategy. The first transfer strategy is based on channel-wise attention, called Channel Distillation (CD). CD transfers the channel information from the teacher to the student. The second is Guided Knowledge Distillation (GKD). Unlike Knowledge Distillation (KD), which allows the student to mimic each sample's prediction distribution of the teacher, GKD only enables the student to mimic the correct output of the teacher. The last part is Early Decay Teacher (EDT). During the training process, we gradually decay the weight of the distillation loss. The purpose is to enable the student to gradually control the optimization rather than the teacher. Our proposed method is evaluated on ImageNet and CIFAR100. On ImageNet, we achieve 27.68% of top-1 error with ResNet18, which outperforms state-of-the-art methods. On CIFAR100, we achieve surprising result that the student outperforms the teacher. Code is available at https://github.com/zhouzaida/channel-distillation.

papers_seen.author: Ramos
papers_seen.title: The Case for Knowledge Distillation: A Versatile Framework for Model Compression, Robustness, and Privacy in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and broadly applicable approach for compressing large models into smaller, faster, and often more robust models. Beyond mere size reduction, contemporary KD techniques transfer internal representations, enable deployment under data- and privacy-constrained conditions, mitigate architectural and modality mismatches, and interact non-trivially with regularization practices. I argue that KD should be treated as a foundational toolchain in applied deep learning and NLP systems—one that must be combined with tailored alignment, privacy-preserving, and teacher-selection strategies to fully realize its benefits in production settings.

papers_seen.author: Conner
papers_seen.title: Distilling Task-Specific Knowledge from BERT into Simple Neural Networks
papers_seen.abstract: In the natural language processing literature, neural networks are becoming increasingly deeper and complex. The recent poster child of this trend is the deep language representation model, which includes BERT, ELMo, and GPT. These developments have led to the conviction that previous-generation, shallower neural networks for language understanding are obsolete. In this paper, however, we demonstrate that rudimentary, lightweight neural networks can still be made competitive without architecture changes, external training data, or additional input features. We propose to distill knowledge from BERT, a state-of-the-art language representation model, into a single-layer BiLSTM, as well as its siamese counterpart for sentence-pair tasks. Across multiple datasets in paraphrasing, natural language inference, and sentiment classification, we achieve comparable results with ELMo, while using roughly 100 times fewer parameters and 15 times less inference time.

papers_seen.author: Brown
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Approaches
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques have become central tools for deploying high-performing deep models in resource-constrained or privacy-sensitive settings. Work in this area has progressed beyond the original formulation of training a small student to match a teacher's output probabilities: modern approaches distill internal representations, perform many-to-many layer alignment, operate without access to original training data, combine multiple teachers or ensembles, and adapt to particular architectures and tasks (including graph networks, detectors, generative models, and language models). Practical concerns such as data heterogeneity, privacy guarantees, and robustness to distribution shift have motivated methods that use synthetic data, private perturbations, generative replay, and federated or online distillation protocols. The field continues to trade off fidelity to teacher behavior, compactness, task specificity, and deployability, with task-adaptive compression and representation-alignment methods emerging as especially effective for NLP and other structured prediction tasks.

papers_seen.author: Duncan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Analyses, and Applications
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a central technique for compressing and adapting large neural models into smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained models while retaining much of their performance. A diverse set of KD approaches operate at the level of final outputs (logits), intermediate features, layer relations, or via adversarial and data-generation mechanisms. KD has been adapted across modalities and tasks — from NLP transformer compression to GAN and speech-model compression, cross-modal transfer, federated settings, and domain-specific applications — and interacts strongly with concerns about robustness, fairness, and transfer of inductive biases. Empirical and theoretical work has clarified when and why various KD variants help, and highlights open challenges in data heterogeneity, teacher-student mismatch, and automatic discovery of compact architectures.

papers_seen.author: Liu
papers_seen.title: Enabling Multimodal Generation on CLIP via Vision-Language Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: The recent large-scale vision-language pre-training (VLP) of dual-stream architectures (e.g., CLIP) with a tremendous amount of image-text pair data, has shown its superiority on various multimodal alignment tasks. Despite its success, the resulting models are not capable of multimodal generative tasks due to the weak text encoder. To tackle this problem, we propose to augment the dual-stream VLP model with a textual pre-trained language model (PLM) via vision-language knowledge distillation (VLKD), enabling the capability for multimodal generation. VLKD is pretty data- and computation-efficient compared to the pre-training from scratch. Experimental results show that the resulting model has strong zero-shot performance on multimodal generation tasks, such as open-ended visual question answering and image captioning. For example, it achieves 44.5% zero-shot accuracy on the VQAv2 dataset, surpassing the previous state-of-the-art zero-shot model with $7\times$ fewer parameters. Furthermore, the original textual language understanding and generation ability of the PLM is maintained after VLKD, which makes our model versatile for both multimodal and unimodal tasks.

papers_seen.author: Holmes
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques are widely used to produce smaller, faster models while preserving much of the performance of large teachers. Approaches vary from matching final logits to transferring internal representations, attention maps, or layer-wise information, and they are applied across modalities including NLP, vision, speech, and reinforcement learning. Practical extensions address multi-teacher setups, data-free scenarios, domain adaptation, quantization, and architecture-aware compression; remaining challenges include handling heterogeneous architectures, data heterogeneity, fairness, and reliably preserving inductive biases.

papers_seen.author: Santos
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Approaches and Findings
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applied framework for compressing large models, improving generalization, and transferring capabilities across modalities and deployment constraints. Research spans teacher-student paradigms (including multi-teacher and self-distillation), data-free and zero-shot distillation, task-adaptive compression, and applications to specialized tasks (detection, retrieval, translation, multimodal learning, federated settings, and graph problems). Empirical work shows KD can yield large speed and size gains while retaining much of the teacher's performance, but also exposes important limitations tied to optimization, data used for distillation, and potential bias transfer. Recent methods address these limitations via curriculum scheduling, confidence- or reinforcement-based teacher weighting, task-adaptive architecture search, domain- and modality-aware losses, and efficient label-generation or student-focused training regimes.

papers_seen.author: Henderson
papers_seen.title: MEAL: Multi-Model Ensemble via Adversarial Learning
papers_seen.abstract: Often the best performing deep neural models are ensembles of multiple base-level networks. Unfortunately, the space required to store these many networks, and the time required to execute them at test-time, prohibits their use in applications where test sets are large (e.g., ImageNet). In this paper, we present a method for compressing large, complex trained ensembles into a single network, where knowledge from a variety of trained deep neural networks (DNNs) is distilled and transferred to a single DNN. In order to distill diverse knowledge from different trained (teacher) models, we propose to use adversarial-based learning strategy where we define a block-wise training loss to guide and optimize the predefined student network to recover the knowledge in teacher models, and to promote the discriminator network to distinguish teacher vs. student features simultaneously. The proposed ensemble method (MEAL) of transferring distilled knowledge with adversarial learning exhibits three important advantages: (1) the student network that learns the distilled knowledge with discriminators is optimized better than the original model; (2) fast inference is realized by a single forward pass, while the performance is even better than traditional ensembles from multi-original models; (3) the student network can learn the distilled knowledge from a teacher model that has arbitrary structures. Extensive experiments on CIFAR-10/100, SVHN and ImageNet datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our MEAL method. On ImageNet, our ResNet-50 based MEAL achieves top-1/5 21.79%/5.99% val error, which outperforms the original model by 2.06%/1.14%. Code and models are available at: https://github.com/AaronHeee/MEAL

papers_seen.author: Silva
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large models into smaller, faster models by transferring information from a teacher to a student. Approaches vary from matching output soft-labels to imitating internal representations, attention maps, or relational structure. Distillation has been applied across modalities and tasks — NLP, vision, detection, generation, ranking, CTR prediction, graph learning, reinforcement learning and federated settings — and can be combined with architecture search and task- or domain-adaptation to produce compact models that preserve much of the teacher’s performance while reducing latency, memory and compute. Practical constraints such as unavailable training data, mismatched inputs or architectures, privacy requirements, and distribution shift motivate specialized techniques including data-free distillation, student-friendly teacher training, adversarial sample generation, many-to-many layer mapping, and generative replay. Empirical results show substantial size and speed gains with modest degradation in performance in many settings, but trade-offs remain and several directions for more robust, automated and privacy-aware distillation remain active.

papers_seen.author: Mayo
papers_seen.title: Rethinking Soft Labels for Knowledge Distillation: A Bias-Variance Tradeoff Perspective
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is an effective approach to leverage a well-trained network or an ensemble of them, named as the teacher, to guide the training of a student network. The outputs from the teacher network are used as soft labels for supervising the training of a new network. Recent studies \citep{muller2019does,yuan2020revisiting} revealed an intriguing property of the soft labels that making labels soft serves as a good regularization to the student network. From the perspective of statistical learning, regularization aims to reduce the variance, however how bias and variance change is not clear for training with soft labels. In this paper, we investigate the bias-variance tradeoff brought by distillation with soft labels. Specifically, we observe that during training the bias-variance tradeoff varies sample-wisely. Further, under the same distillation temperature setting, we observe that the distillation performance is negatively associated with the number of some specific samples, which are named as regularization samples since these samples lead to bias increasing and variance decreasing. Nevertheless, we empirically find that completely filtering out regularization samples also deteriorates distillation performance. Our discoveries inspired us to propose the novel weighted soft labels to help the network adaptively handle the sample-wise bias-variance tradeoff. Experiments on standard evaluation benchmarks validate the effectiveness of our method. Our code is available at \url{https://github.com/bellymonster/Weighted-Soft-Label-Distillation}.

papers_seen.author: Munoz
papers_seen.title: Zero-Shot Knowledge Distillation in Deep Networks
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation deals with the problem of training a smaller model (Student) from a high capacity source model (Teacher) so as to retain most of its performance. Existing approaches use either the training data or meta-data extracted from it in order to train the Student. However, accessing the dataset on which the Teacher has been trained may not always be feasible if the dataset is very large or it poses privacy or safety concerns (e.g., bio-metric or medical data). Hence, in this paper, we propose a novel data-free method to train the Student from the Teacher. Without even using any meta-data, we synthesize the Data Impressions from the complex Teacher model and utilize these as surrogates for the original training data samples to transfer its learning to Student via knowledge distillation. We, therefore, dub our method "Zero-Shot Knowledge Distillation" and demonstrate that our framework results in competitive generalization performance as achieved by distillation using the actual training data samples on multiple benchmark datasets.

papers_seen.author: Ramirez
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a central technique for compressing large neural models and transferring knowledge across architectures, tasks, and deployment constraints. Work across vision, language, graphs, and generative representations shows diverse KD objectives (soft-target, feature, relational, contrastive, and layer-matching), a range of data regimes (full-data, limited-data, data-free/zero-shot), and many complementary compression mechanisms (pruning, architecture search, block-structured sparsity, and cheap operators). Empirical and theoretical studies clarify when KD helps, how it interacts with data-augmentation and teacher imperfection, and how KD can be adapted for privacy-preserving or federated scenarios. This review summarizes these practical methods, observed trade-offs, and open challenges for robust, efficient, and private model compression.

papers_seen.author: Powell
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central Tool for Model Compression and Transfer: Strengths, Limits, and Practical Directions
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a versatile set of techniques that enable model compression, domain- and task-level transfer, privacy-preserving distillation, and improvements in interpretability and fairness. Empirical and methodological work shows KD can compress large models into efficient students, transfer inductive biases, support multi-task and lifelong learning, and enable data-free or zero-shot distillation when training data are unavailable. At the same time, KD faces concrete limitations due to data heterogeneity, teacher-student capacity mismatch, and the need to select or synthesize appropriate supervision; hybrid solutions that combine feature-level matching, adversarial sample synthesis, curriculum strategies, and architectural compression achieve the best practical results. Based on evidence across domains (vision, language, graphs, retrieval, reinforcement learning), we argue that KD should be used as part of an integrated compression pipeline that is task-aware, data-aware, and often combined with pruning, layer skipping, or module replacement to meet deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Young
papers_seen.title: The Case for Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Multifaceted Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature and flexible approach to compress large or ensemble models into smaller, faster models while preserving much of their performance. Across supervised, self-supervised, and cross-modal settings, distillation can recover accuracy for lightweight architectures, enable deployment on resource-constrained devices, and transfer specialized properties (e.g., temporal, structural, or ensemble knowledge). However, distillation is not a panacea: its success depends on the choice of teacher, student architecture and capacity, the training protocol (including data augmentation and sample selection), and implementation details that affect optimization. When these factors are treated carefully, KD complements other compression techniques (pruning, architecture design, quantization) and can be adapted to domain-specific needs such as federated learning, retrieval, and vision-language tasks.
